## Highlights

*   •Factors that shape implementation primarily originate from within the organisation. 
*   •Key successes include communication, team structures, and tools and resources. 
*   •Key challenges include staffing availability and role continuity. 
*   •Recommendations relate to streamlining delivery and project management tasks. 
*   •Priority areas include staff and resource availability, and effective communication. 

## Abstract

Zoo conservation-education programs have potential to address biodiversity loss, although evidence of their effectiveness to encourage social change is in its infancy. Moreover, how a program is implemented may influence program efficacy, yet there is little evidence of the factors that shape this process in zoos. Accordingly, through a process evaluation of Zoos Victoria’s ‘When Balloons Fly” (WBF) conservation-education program against marine debris, we identified barriers and enablers to the implementation of the program which can be addressed to improve future initiatives. Between April-May 2018, 24 Zoos Victoria professionals completed an online survey focussed on identifying challenges and successes in implementing WBF. Four participants additionally completed a follow-up telephone interview. Themes were identified and organised according to the model of diffusion in service organisations ([Greenhalgh, Robert, Macfarlane, Bate, & Kyriakidou, 2004](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0149718921000458#bib0120)). Our results illuminate that features of the organisation (e.g., structure, culture) rather than features of individuals (e.g., skills, motivation) or characteristics of the conservation-education program itself (e.g., messaging), were most influential to implementation success. Based on these findings, attention to the organisational context is critical for promoting and evaluating the success of conservation-education programs and must be given significant attention alongside program characteristics and staff capability to deliver them.

## Introduction

Biodiversity is the total variability of life on Earth (DeLong, 1996; Morton, Sheppard, & Lonsdale, 2014) and the _“engine room”_ for a functioning global ecosystem that delivers life-supporting provisions including oxygen, and clean air and water (Close, Zammit, Boshier, Gainer, & Mednis, 2009, p. 4). Of concern, biodiversity is declining rapidly (Barnosky et al., 2011; Dirzo et al., 2014; Pimm et al., 2014), and this trend is largely driven by human activity (Ceballos et al., 2015; Niemelä et al., 2000; Vitousek, Mooney, Lubchenco, & Melillo, 1997). With hundreds of millions of annual visitors worldwide (Gusset & Dick, 2011; Smith, 2013), well-run modern zoos and aquariums (hereafter ‘zoos’; Gray, 2017) are change agents with enormous potential to promote sustainability and thus protect biodiversity. Through conservation education, zoos can teach the public about the plights faced by non-human species, foster connections between people and nature, and help people build knowledge and develop skills for post-visit conservation action (Clayton, Fraser, & Saunders, 2009; Grajal et al., 2017; Packer & Ballantyne, 2010; Patrick & Caplow, 2018).

A variety of educational approaches and communication strategies to promote environmental sustainability are increasingly being employed in zoos. One example is conservation-education programs. These offerings typically comprise the delivery of a series of planned activities, experiences, interactions, and/or interpretations (e.g., keeper presentations, animations, static signage displays, educator screens, touch tables) that communicate information about a specific conservation issue. Such programs often appoint an ambassador species to act as an icon for the environmental issue at hand.

One example is “Don’t Palm Us Off” (DPUO), a program that has been implemented at several Australian zoos including Melbourne Zoo, Perth Zoo, and Taronga Zoo (see: [https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=oRQWj4H9nH0](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=oRQWj4H9nH0) [accessed February 8, 2019] for an overview of the initiative). DPUO seeks to raise awareness about the biodiversity-detrimental impacts of unsustainably grown palm oil (principally, the rapid clearing of rainforests to plant palm oil trees), and to advocate for mandatory labelling of palm oil in Australia thus create pressure for food production businesses to source palm oil sustainably. An evaluation of this program at Melbourne Zoo revealed significant increases in self‐reported conservation behaviour throughout the 12-month campaign and 6-months after the campaign had ended (see Pearson, Lowry, Dorrian, & Litchfield, 2014 for an evaluation of the program at Melbourne Zoo). One ambassador species for the program is the orang-utan, which serves as an icon for several other species also affected by unsustainable palm oil development, including rhinos and elephants. Onsite interpretation at Melbourne Zoo includes static signage displays, a looping 1-minute narrated video containing information explaining the connection between palm oil and orang-utan habitat destruction, and a “Zoopermarket”, where visitors can ‘scan’ common food items to determine if the product contains unsustainable palm oil. This program serves as a good illustration of how zoo conservation education can promote widespread environmental sustainability.

Like the evaluation of DPUO, there is a small, yet growing body of published scholarly work that has investigated the effect of zoo conservation-education on a variety of visitor outcomes. As outlined in a recent review (Thomas, Teel, Bruyere, & Laurence, 2019), common outcome domains of interest include cognition (e.g., knowledge, understanding); affect (e.g., attitudes, social norms, values, emotion); and behaviour (e.g., intent to act and action). Yet findings concerning the nature and extent of the impact of zoo-based conservation education have been mixed, even within a single outcome domain. For example, in terms of impact on conservation action, a handful of zoo conservation-education evaluations have reported that the programs or materials of interest had some post-visit effect on behaviour (MacDonald, 2015; Mann, Ballantyne, & Packer, 2018; Smith, Broad, & Weiler, 2008), while others yielded little or no evidence of any post-visit influence on behaviour (Adelman, Falk, & James, 2000; Dierking et al., 2004).

There are several explanations for variance in evaluation results. One set of obstacles are those embedded in evaluation methodology and reporting of evaluation outcomes. In their review of research methods and reporting practices in zoo conservation education evaluation, Mellish, Ryan, Pearson, and Tuckey (2019) identified problems pertaining to construct validity (e.g., limited use of validated measures), external validity (e.g., limited reporting of response rates), internal validity (e.g., few study designs with random allocation), and statistical conclusion validity (e.g., absence of reporting effect sizes or triangulating data) that, if addressed, would help clarify what and how components of zoo conservation education might influence visitor psychosocial outcomes. Variances in program success could additionally be explained by contextual factors specific to the program setting and/or features of the target behaviour. In terms of setting, for instance, naturalistically-designed enclosures appear to more effectively improve attitudes toward the conservation of African apes than traditional exhibits (Lukas & Ross, 2014). With regard to differences in target behaviour, translation into action might be more successful when the desired actions are: performed on-site; not physically, mentally, or time demanding (e.g., recycling waste vs. riding a bike to work to reduce carbon footprint); new or based on new knowledge; and accompanied with an explanation of the effect of the behaviour (Smith, Curtis, & Van Dijk, 2010). These contextual factors become variables of substantive interest among researchers and evaluation practitioners in their own right.

A final consideration when seeking to explain the mixed outcomes in evaluation studies is factors in the organisational context that can shape conservation-education programs. Such factors include a variety of influences on how an organisation functions, including: organisational culture and structure; communication channels; strategy; policies and procedures; and the external business environment (Project Management Institute, 2013; Scott & Vessey, 2002). These organisational factors can influence different stages of a program life cycle. Broadly, these factors include the: (a) initiation phase (project idea is explored and a project proposal is approved); (b) definition phase (project requirements, scope, and expectations are identified); (c) design phase (design choices are made e.g., design of signage); (d) development phase (suppliers or subcontractors are arranged, materials are ordered, schedules are created); (e) implementation/execution phase (the program is put into action/moved to production); and (f) follow-up/evaluation phase (e.g., Archibald, Di Filippo, & Di Filippo, 2012; Baars, Harmsen, Kramer, Sesink, & van Zundert, 2006).

Of zoo-related work investigating program evaluation from an organisational perspective, studies appear to have focused exclusively on the _evaluation_ phase of the program life cycle, highlighting issues regarding evaluation design and resourcing. In their seminal review paper concerning the challenges and successes faced during the evaluation of environmental education programs, Carleton-Hug and Hug (2010) discovered that three major issues hindered the quality of program evaluations: short evaluation time frames; lack of diverse research approaches, including overreliance on short-term objective-focused evaluations; and overlooked differences in participant background variables. Growing interest in understanding the impacts of environmental education among evaluators, the need for an informed population, and a national interest in education accountability, were identified as opportunities. A similar focus was taken by Luebke and Grajal (2011), who investigated challenges when evaluating operational performance (e.g., visitor satisfaction) and mission-related learning outcomes (e.g., cognitive gains, affective reactions, or intended conservation action) among Association of Zoo and Aquarium (AZA) accredited conservation organisations. Challenges to emerge included: few staff or few staff with appropriate expertise; no or limited budget; lack of understanding about when/what/how to evaluate; difficulty attaining good responses and poor survey completion rates; and limited technology to aid data analysis. Similarly, time, cost, and know-how were further revealed as challenges to research assessing the evaluation processes of school or curriculum-aligned zoo education efforts (Roe, McConney, & Mansfield, 2014). Further, Khalil, Ardoin, and Wojcik (2017) explored how zoo education professionals engage with each other during evaluation and highlighted that open flow of information and easy opportunities for collaboration were the most valued mechanisms when performing tasks. Evidently there exists a variety of challenges to overcome when evaluating different types of conservation-and-environmental education interventions (Monroe, 2010).

Less is known about the organisational factors that may help or obstruct the _development_ and _implementation_ stages of a zoo conservation-education program life cycle. These stages are closely linked, with the development stage typically addressing the “how” component of implementation, and the implementation stage involving the “doing” (activation) element. Together they comprise the steps undertaken to arrange, build, or produce each idea generated in the _design_ stage (Baars et al., 2006). For zoo conservation-education programs, such activities might involve script creation and rehearsal for a keeper presentation, assembly and placement of signage material, or acquisition of partners to promote the program messaging.

Integrating both an outcome-focus and a process-focus into a single, more holistic evaluation could help to: (1) obtain a more comprehensive understanding of the mechanisms that can influence the successes of a conservation-education program; (2) provide future developers with an evidence-base for what practices to embrace and avoid; (3) discover alternative or new methods and tools for implementation; and (4) pinpoint areas for improvement and/or change. Indeed, school-based education innovations (e.g., Forman, Olin, Hoagwood, Crowe, & Saka, 2009; Plotner & Marshall, 2015) and health-related interventions (Ageberg, Bunke, Lucander, Nilsen, & Donaldson, 2019; Cotner, Ottomanelli, O’Connor, & Trainor, 2018; Kadu & Stolee, 2015) have benefitted from similar research approaches. Taken together, identifying helpful and unhelpful processes that might impact program implementation could help to create programs that have greater effects on visitors’ cognition, affect, and behaviour, and subsequently mitigate biodiversity loss.

Understanding of the factors that influence the implementation of zoo conservation-education programs can be strengthened if explored with the application of an existing framework; application of an existing framework offers a robust and transferable methodology (Greenhalgh et al., 2004) and can permit moving beyond simply describing to generalising about a phenomenon (Grant & Osanloo, 2014).

Drawing upon Roger’s pioneering diffusion of innovation theory (which explains that the spread of ideas during innovation is influenced by features of the innovation itself, communication methods, time, and social systems; 1962; 2010), one applicable determinant framework is the model of diffusion in service organisations (Greenhalgh et al., 2004). The application of this model to zoo conservation education is suitable for two reasons. First, sustainability, a key goal of zoos, is considered an innovative idea (Dibra, 2015), which broadly refers to any new changes or improvements to products and processes that advance performance or outcomes (Rogers, 1998). Second, zoos are service organisation in the sense that they seek to provide several services to society including public conservation education and in-situ and ex-situ wildlife conservation, both of which are critically important to preserving global biodiversity.

The model of diffusion in service organisations was developed from a review of theoretical and empirical studies concerning innovation (in this case, new behaviours and routines) in health care service delivery (Greenhalgh et al., 2004). This model is not a prescriptive formula, but rather, a conceptual framework that highlights key areas for consideration when seeking to explore the nuances of innovation in service organisations (Greenhalgh et al., 2004). The model lists several main components for consideration: (1) innovation; (2) adopters and adoption, (3) dissemination and social influence; (4) the organisational context, (5) system readiness for innovation, (6) the outer context, and (7) implementation. Table 1 provides a more detailed description of each component and sub-topics of the model, and the definitions for a new re-contextualised version: -the _model of diffusion in conservation organisations_, which was developed to guide the current research.

Program implementation can influence program success. Given that the outcomes of zoo conservation-education programs are inconsistent, according to the evaluation evidence, the area of inquiry that seeks to evaluate these experiences could benefit (a) from understanding the challenges and successes that occur during the implementation phase of a program’s life cycle; and (b) from the provision of recommendations for the best course of action for future program implementation. As such, using a re-contextualised version of the model of diffusion in service organisations, this research sought to: (1) examine the challenges and successes to implementing Zoos Victoria’s “When Balloons Fly” conservation-education program; and (2) provide a practitioner-informed course of action for future conservation-education program implementation. We use the terms _challenge_ and _success_ to refer to any human (e.g., labour, management) and non-human (e.g., technology, financial resources) tool or process that hindered or helped (respectively) the implementation of WBF. In recognition that implementation can be a non-linear process - especially when setbacks are experienced, in the context of this research, _implementation_ describes any activity, process, or task related to the “how” and “doing” components of implementation.

When Balloons Fly (WBF) is a conservation-education program delivered at Zoos Victoria (Melbourne, Australia), a Zoo and Aquarium Association-accredited conservation-organisation. WBF seeks to (a) raise awareness about the anthropogenic threat of marine debris affecting marine and aquatic species, and (b) encourage the use of wildlife-friendly bubbles instead of balloons outdoors. At the time of this research, the program had multiple interpretation components on site, including a keeper-led seal presentation, static signage displays, ‘pledge’ boards and books, promise points (staff-manned areas where visitors could make the pledge to use bubbles not balloons outdoors), bubble play areas (staff-manned areas where visitors could blow, and play with, bubbles), as well as a growing presence in the wider community through the campaign’s partner organisation Phillip Island Nature Parks and numerous local organisations who promoted the campaign in their businesses and communities.

args.summary:
This academic article, published in *Evaluation and Program Planning* (Volume 88, October 2021), investigates the challenges and successes of implementing a zoo conservation-education program called "When Balloons Fly" (WBF) at Zoos Victoria in Melbourne, Australia. The program aims to raise awareness about marine debris and encourage the use of bubbles instead of balloons outdoors.

The study used a process evaluation approach, surveying 24 Zoos Victoria professionals (April-May 2018) and conducting follow-up interviews with 4 participants. The research applied a re-contextualized version of Greenhalgh et al.'s (2004) model of diffusion in service organisations to identify barriers and enablers to implementation.

**Key findings:**
- Factors shaping implementation success primarily originate from within the organization (structure, culture, readiness) rather than from individual staff capabilities or the program's characteristics.
- The most influential domains were "organisational readiness for innovation" and "organisational antecedents for innovation" (both within "the inner/organisational context").
- Key successes: effective communication, team structures, and tools/resources.
- Key challenges: staffing availability, role continuity, and resource constraints.
- Recommendations focus on streamlining delivery, improving project management, and prioritizing staff/resource availability alongside effective communication.

**Background context:** The study notes that evaluation of zoo conservation-education programs has yielded mixed results. The authors argue that understanding implementation processes (not just outcomes) is critical for program effectiveness. The paper highlights that while zoos have enormous potential to promote sustainability (with hundreds of millions of annual visitors worldwide), evidence of their effectiveness in encouraging social change is still developing.

**Conclusion:** Attention to the organisational context is critical for promoting and evaluating the success of conservation-education programs, and must be given significant attention alongside program characteristics and staff capability.

# Conservation Education

Studies have shown that [AZA-accredited zoos and aquariums](https://www.aza.org/current-accreditation-list) enhance the public’s understanding of wildlife and the need to conserve the places animals live. Visitors believe zoos and aquariums play an important role in conservation education and that when they experience a stronger connection to nature, are prompted to reconsider their role in environmental problems and conservation action and see themselves as part of the solution as a result of their visit.

AZA-accredited zoos and aquariums play a vital role in educating over 180 million visitors, including 51 million students, each year, about wild animals, their habitats, their related conservation issues, and the ways in which they can contribute to their preservation. Over the past ten years, AZA-accredited institutions have also trained more than 400,000 teachers with award-winning and proven science curricula.

AZA and its [Conservation Education Committee](/conservation_education_committee "Hyperlink to the AZA web page titled Conservation Education Committee") provide information, protocols, and tools through the [AZA Network](https://network.aza.org/communities/community-home?CommunityKey=96b40174-f0af-4333-98ec-e25ce1d2f85f "Hyperlink to the AZA Network Education Group") to help educators facilitate nature play opportunities; manage animal ambassador presentations; deliver consistent conservation messages; advocate for the educational impact of zoos and aquariums, and serve on AZA committees, advisory groups, or animal programs as a means to enhance their education program planning and raise public awareness about, and actions towards, conservation concerns.

[Core Competencies for Conservation Education](/assets/2332/aza_core-competencies_final-2025062501542019.pdf)

Join the [Conservation Education Committee](https://www.aza.org/conservation_education_committee) - The Committee Call for Service opens in March of each year.

Join the [Ambassador Animal Scientific Advisory Group](https://www.aza.org/ambassador-animal-scientific-advisory-group) (AASAG)

Become an [Education Advisor](https://www.aza.org/education-advisors)

#### Conservation Education Standards and Policies

AZA is committed to promoting high standards of excellence in all aspects of conservation education. [Accreditation Standards](/accreditation) and [Board-Approved Policies](/board-approved-policies-and-position-statements "Hyperlink to the AZA web page title Board Approved Policies and Position Statements") have been established to ensure this objective is achieved and often evolve to meet increasingly rigorous criteria. All AZA-accredited institutions must ensure that education is a central tenet in their mission, must develop a written education plan that matches current industry standards, and must regularly evaluate their education programs.

#### Conservation Engagement Framework

[From Caring to Action: A Unified Framework for Conservation Action](/assets/2332/aza_cons-engagement_framework_final_web_(1).pdf "CARE Framework") is intended as a brief introduction to principles of effective audience conservation engagement. A companion document, [From Theory to Practice: The CARE Conservation Engagement Roadmap](/assets/2332/aza_cons-engagement_care-roadmap_final_web_(1).pdf "CARE Roadmap") provides a practical guide to applying the principles to practice.

#### Education Programs Database

The web-based Education Programs database collects information about our member's individual and collective education program contributions to help tell the story of the educational impact of AZA Zoos & Aquariums as part of the [Annual Report on Conservation and Science](/annual-report-on-conservation-and-science). [Learn More](http://ams.aza.org/eweb/DynamicPage.aspx?Site=AZA&WebKey=e0590d74-74e7-4efb-bc53-21f2d288247d)

#### Advocating for Education

A vital part of AZA’s government affairs strategy is the continuing education of all Members of Congress as to the value of accredited zoos and aquariums, the vital role they play in conservation, education, recreation, tourism, job creation, and collectively as major contributors to the economy and AZA educators are ideal advocates for their institution. # The Impact of COVID-19 on Zoos and Aquariums

Published: July 29, 2020studio98

[display\_gallery\_copyright\_text]

![Featured Image](https://iges.us/wp-content/uploads/2020/07/covid-19-impact-aquariums.jpg)

Just weeks into the beginning of this year, it seems as if the world came to a bit of a screeching halt thanks to COVID-19. Unfortunately, visits to zoos and aquariums, popular spots during the spring and summer months, were no exception.

Statistics show that over [700 million people visit aquariums and zoos](https://www.waza.org/) worldwide. This means that human interaction is a near constant for the animals who call those places home. However, the pandemic forced these places to close, leaving the animals and their human visitors without that usual interaction.

Zoo workers have continued to care for the animals and have noticed a change in how many of them are handling this isolation. While some animals, like foxes and hippos, seem happy with the quiet spell due to the frolicking and splashing they’ve been seen enjoying, others seem to miss their human visitors. Primates have been reported to appear to be [looking for visitors](https://www.leicestermercury.co.uk/news/local-news/animals-twycross-zoo-are-missing-4119435) that cannot be found.

## **Finding Alternative Ways to Let People Experience Zoos & Aquariums**

Just as offices, restaurants, and other businesses have been forced to adapt to this new environment, zoos and aquariums have as well. Though the zoos and aquariums have closed to outside visitors, the zookeepers are still going in to provide medical care and feed the animals. Many have tried their best to keep the animals on the same schedule they had before the lockdown started.

![Receive our monthly newsletter 'Gifted,' and show emails that feature curated highlights, exhibitor spotlights, event updates, and valuable tips on maximizing your IGES experience!](https://no-cache.hubspot.com/cta/default/23836458/interactive-214172642655.png)

While the zookeepers are inside the zoos and aquariums, many have opened virtually to continue to allow people to see inside the facilities from the comfort of their home. These virtual peeks inside include behind-the-scenes photos and videos, and more. Some of the most popular virtual attractions include the following:

* **Online Cams – The San Diego Zoo** is one of the organizations that has seen a substantial increase in the people that are viewing exhibits from home. Webcams were added to the **Safari Park’s Butterfly Jungle** as well as other habitats throughout the zoo and zoo officials say they have seen a 1000% increase in virtual viewers. **Monterey Bay Aquarium’s** virtual viewers are loving the moon jelly cam according to officials there. Zoos and aquariums can add their online events to [the AZA master calendar](https://www.aza.org/livestreams-and-activities) here.
* **Social Media –** Social media campaigns and viewers of the campaigns have increased exponentially to create a connection with visitors that can’t come to the zoos and aquariums physically. Organizations say this has been a way to engage with visitors and donors during this trying time.
* **Education –** Many aquariums and zoos are offering educational materials and plans free of charge to teachers and homeschoolers during this time. The Association f Zoos and Aquariums created a library of [conservation and climate education materials](https://www.aza.org/conservation-education-materials).

These online platforms allow organizations to continue their missions for conservation, education, and research even though they aren’t able to be open to the public. In fact, they say it has been the perfect opportunity to teach people about how the world is connected and that we must take care of it.

## **What About Zoos & Aquariums Reopening?**

Although some zoos and aquariums have been able to resume some sort of in-house visits, the reopenings may have come too late for some. **Oakland Zoo** in California is one of those that has been hit hard. The facility reported that they have been [losing roughly $2 million per month](https://abc7news.com/oakland-zoo-in-danger-of-closing-out-money-coronavirus-bay-area/6292206/) since they were forced to close in March. They are hoping they can be reclassified as outdoor museums, similar to botanical gardens and parks that have already been allowed to reopen.

The **National Aquarium in Baltimore** is also seeing similar struggles. They say they have lost over $8 million over the past three month period and have been forced to furlough one-third of their staff. It is one of [200 major U.S. aquariums and zoos](https://www.washingtonpost.com/science/2020/06/08/coronavirus-zoos-aquariums/) that have suffered huge losses due to the loss in ticket sales – their main source of revenue. The dilemma, they say, is because not only have they had to shut down, but their occupants still need water, cooling, heating, food, and veterinary care.

Although many zoos and aquariums have been closed for several months, they are looking to [local, state, and federal guidelines](https://asdonline.com/blog/retail-news/reopening-your-retail-store/) when it comes to reopening. For many, this looks like limited admissions, social distancing, and restricted hours when visitors are allowed to return. And the current resurgence of the virus isn’t making reopening in any capacity very easy. Many people anticipate, and hope, that the visitor experience will once again return to normal, not just for the people, but for the animals that miss the visitors too. Until then, we encourage you to think outside the box on how you can bring the experience online and social media channels. Get creative with online fundraising ideas and don’t be afraid to go outside the box. We’ll be covering this in an upcoming post so stay tuned.

args.summary: This is the homepage of the Association of Zoos and Aquariums (AZA), the primary professional organization for zoos and aquariums in the United States and beyond. The AZA's website serves as a comprehensive resource hub covering six main areas: About Us (including governance, strategic plan, bylaws, press room, and partners), Accreditation (including the accreditation process, application, materials, accredited members, and awards), Animal Care & Management (including Taxon Advisory Groups, Species Survival Plan Programs, animal wellbeing, aquatic sustainability, and ambassador animal resources), Conservation (including SAFE: Saving Animals From Extinction, conservation funding, field conservation, green practices, research and science, and conservation education), Equity & Inclusion (including the MoZAICS program), and the Wildlife Trafficking Alliance (including initiatives, campaigns, partners, and action resources). The site also offers AZA Services such as membership options, conferences, professional development courses, scholarships, honors and awards, safety resources, member benefits, and data/trends. Additional features include a job board, a zoo/aquarium finder, a calendar, and a donation portal.

Crossroads blog  13 Jan, 2021

# Progressive zoos and aquariums must be part of the world’s response to COVID-19

Many zoos and aquariums face challenges as lockdowns mean the loss of vital income from visitors. As the international community looks to stimulate economic recovery whilst addressing other global goals, the love of nature that zoos and aquariums inspire and the ex situ conservation techniques they pioneer have never been more important writes Dr Martín Zordan, CEO of the World Association of Zoos and Aquariums (WAZA), an IUCN Member organisation.

![author iamge](/sites/default/files/m_zordan_-_portrait-850.jpg)

Martín Zordan

Dr Martín Zordan is a Chilean Veterinary Doctor and Chief Executive Officer (CEO) of the World Association of Zoos and Aquariums (WAZA), an IUCN Member organisation. He was Executive Director of the Latin American Association of Zoos and Aquariums (ALPZA) between 2014 and 2017, and joined WAZA in 2018 initially as Conservation Coordinator. Now as WAZA CEO, Dr Zordan represents a global network of over 330 members in more than 50 countries. He also serves as Trustee of Species360, an international non-profit that maintains a database of wild animals in human care to aid conservation.

Dr Martín Zordan is a Chilean Veterinary Doctor and Chief Executive Officer (CEO) of the World Association of Zoos and Aquariums (WAZA), an IUCN Member organisation. He was Executive Director of the Latin American Association of Zoos and Aquariums (ALPZA) between 2014 and 2017, and joined WAZA in 2018 initially as Conservation Coordinator. Now as WAZA CEO, Dr Zordan represents a global network of over 330 members in more than 50 countries. He also serves as Trustee of Species360, an international non-profit that maintains a database of wild animals in human care to aid conservation.

![content hero image](/sites/default/files/styles/article_image/public/2022-07/im3-georgia-aquarium-manta-ray.jpg?itok=pzYlBrO5)

Photo: Georgia Aquarium

A manta ray (*Mobula sp. cf. birostris*) surprises visitors to Georgia Aquarium, USA. Researchers study their behaviour in the aquarium to inform field conservation.

We will not forget 2020. For decades, even centuries, humans have taken nature for granted. It was only a matter of time before human activity exposed us to another zoonotic pathogen and, given the speed of modern travel, a pandemic was perhaps, tragically, inevitable. Just as with climate change, difficult scenarios we predicted for future generations are happening much earlier. Individuals are responding to these urgent challenges, and our institutions must too. For the progressive community of zoos and aquariums, of which I am proudly part, there is now even more urgency to act.

The World Association of Zoos and Aquariums (WAZA), an IUCN Member since 1949, includes among its own members more than 280 zoos and aquariums from over 50 countries, and 23 national and regional associations. In a normal year we estimate more than 700 million people visit zoos and aquariums worldwide, with many millions following their work online too (the only option during lockdown). With this huge and growing audience, we nurture strong relationships with the wider public. We foster love for animals and advocate for them to have their habitats protected. Where science often struggles to find the words to engage people, zoos and aquariums bridge the gap. To that end, jointly with the International Zoo Educators Association, WAZA has published [Social Change for Conservation: The World Zoo and Aquarium Conservation Education Strategy](https://www.waza.org/priorities/community-conservation/the-waza-education-strategy/). Inspiring conservation action in the wake of the pandemic is essential if we are to reform humanity’s relationship with the natural world.

> **In a normal year we estimate more than 700 million people visit zoos and aquariums worldwide. Inspiring conservation action in the wake of the pandemic is essential if we are to reform humanity’s relationship with the natural world.**

Alongside ex situ conservation like the breeding of threatened species, every year progressive zoos and aquariums invest hundreds of millions of dollars in field programmes. With other IUCN Members, we are part of the larger puzzle that makes conservation work but, as COVID-19 has shown so clearly, more must be done. So, how does such a complex network come together to level-up our impact?

Put simply, I believe the need is for better connections between the pieces of the puzzle, and this is where initiatives like [Reverse the Red](https://www.reversethered.org/) fit in. Founded by IUCN, WAZA and our partners, Reverse the Red is a global movement to build cooperation and action that ensures the survival of species and ecosystems. Whether government agencies, NGOs, zoos, aquariums, botanical gardens or parties to multinational agreements, we all have a role to play.

![](/sites/default/files/2022-07/im2-chester-zoo-sunda-gharial-crocodile.jpg)

Chester Zoo

At the heart of the movement is the Assess, Plan, Act methodology, and we need IUCN at every stage. To Assess, the IUCN Red List of Threatened SpeciesTM is our main tool. To Plan, the IUCN Species Survival Commission (IUCN SSC) Conservation Planning Specialist Group has demonstrated how to integrate ecological and social sciences to engage diverse stakeholders with comprehensive conservation strategies. When the time comes to Act, a conservation programme must convene and mobilise those stakeholders to deliver actions, and those actions must be based on the best available tools and practices. IUCN SSC has developed many of them. Through training and other capacity building efforts, WAZA zoos and aquariums are working with IUCN SSC to assist in these three areas; a powerful example of the strength of unions.

> **Global conservation efforts and indicators are complicated and potentially unachievable without national strategies, goals and metrics.**

When the partnership discussed what we need to do differently to reverse current extinction rates, two themes emerged:

1. National-scale approach: Global conservation efforts and indicators are complicated and potentially unachievable without national strategies, goals and metrics.
2. Representation: Everyone needs to feel included.

In my view, the wounds of colonialism and misogyny must be healed. Nothing can do this more than seeing people everyone can relate to at the centre of the action. This is essential to engage new generations.

Again, WAZA and our members are helping to achieve both. Zoos and aquariums have access to governments, private sector partners, and academia, but also to educators, families, communities, youth groups and grassroots movements. We have yet to harness the full potential of these networks.

![](/sites/default/files/2022-07/im1-education-at-the-uganda-wildlife-conservation-education-centre.jpg)

Uganda Wildlife Conservation Education Centre

In the context of the pandemic, wildlife trade is receiving much more attention. Zoos and aquariums are no stranger to the work of stopping illegal wildlife trade. Through education programmes we encourage people to avoid the consumption of illegal wildlife products and when illegal trade is suspected, the expertise of zoos and aquariums is needed. Our specialists are called upon to differentiate legal from illegal trade, identify species, provide care for confiscated animals and train enforcement agencies. Two recent IUCN Motions led by zoo and aquarium associations aim to further our work on this matter:

* Resolution 57, [Law enforcement regarding commercial trade in tigers and tiger parts](https://www.iucncongress2020.org/motion/057),led by the European Association of Zoos and Aquaria (EAZA)
* Resolution 65, [Engaging the private sector to combat wildlife trafficking](https://www.iucncongress2020.org/motion/065), led by the Association of Zoos and Aquariums (AZA)

On a final note, if you are a follower of the Crossroads Blog you know that each comes with a call to action. Mine is to all IUCN Members: we must find a way to foster networks and, given the limited time and resources we have to address our most urgent global challenges, we should pay special attention to national ones. If every nation has strong national conservation networks, supported by an engaged public, the international community has a much stronger base from which to act and achieve our global goals. With the organisation I represent in mind, I invite you all to consider an inclusive approach to these networks; one that brings in the ex situ community (zoos, aquariums, museums, and botanical gardens amongst others).

> **Given the limited time and resources we have to address our most urgent global challenges, we should pay special attention to national conservation networks and bring in the ex situ community of zoos, aquariums, museums and botanical gardens amongst others.**

Recognition of the value of ex situ conservation is growing, for example through [Article 9](https://www.cbd.int/kb/record/article/6885?RecordType=article) of the UN Convention on Biological Diversity (CBD). In addition to [IUCN SSC guidelines on the use of ex situ management for species conservation](https://portals.iucn.org/library/node/44952), approved in 2014, ex situ is now acknowledged as a valuable tool through Resolution 94, [Linking in situ and ex situ efforts to save threatened species](https://www.iucncongress2020.org/motion/094). Just as with Article 9, a continuum between in situ and ex situ action is encouraged. Resolution 119, [Improving process and action to identify and recover ‘Extinct in the Wild’ species](https://www.iucncongress2020.org/motion/119), goes further, and highlights the need for further ex situ measures particularly for those species on the verge of extinction.

![](/sites/default/files/2022-07/im4-dusky-gopher-froglet-courtesy-steve-reichling-memphis-zoo-min-min.jpg)

Steve Reichling, Memphis Zoo

I hope this cooperation builds. We are all part of the conservation puzzle. To make our recovery from this dreadful pandemic a sustainable one, the ex situ community has distinct tools, skills and expertise that we are glad to and need to share. Like biodiversity, those of us working to protect it need a diverse set of resources and strong networks to thrive.

args.summary:
This blog post, published on January 13, 2021, by Dr. Martín Zordan, CEO of the World Association of Zoos and Aquariums (WAZA), argues that progressive zoos and aquariums must be part of the global response to COVID-19. Dr. Zordan represents WAZA, an IUCN Member since 1949, with over 330 members in more than 50 countries. In a normal year, over 700 million people visit zoos and aquariums worldwide.

Key points include:
- Zoos and aquariums invest hundreds of millions of dollars annually in field conservation programmes alongside ex situ conservation (e.g., breeding threatened species).
- WAZA is part of the "Reverse the Red" initiative (founded by IUCN, WAZA, and partners), which uses the "Assess, Plan, Act" methodology.
- Two themes emerged for reversing extinction rates: (1) a national-scale approach with national strategies, goals, and metrics, and (2) ensuring representation and inclusion.
- In the context of the pandemic, zoos and aquariums work to stop illegal wildlife trade through education, species identification, confiscated animal care, and training enforcement agencies.
- Two recent IUCN Motions led by zoo associations: Resolution 57 (law enforcement on tiger trade, led by EAZA) and Resolution 65 (engaging private sector against wildlife trafficking, led by AZA).
- The author calls on IUCN Members to foster national conservation networks that include the ex situ community (zoos, aquariums, museums, botanical gardens).
- Ex situ conservation is recognized through Article 9 of the UN Convention on Biological Diversity and IUCN SSC guidelines, as well as IUCN Resolution 94 (linking in situ and ex situ efforts) and Resolution 119 (recovering 'Extinct in the Wild' species).
- The author emphasizes that the ex situ community has distinct tools, skills, and expertise to share for a sustainable recovery from the pandemic.

args.summary:
The webpage is the main navigation/sitemap of the Association of Zoos and Aquariums (AZA) website (aza.org). AZA is the primary accrediting body for zoos and aquariums in the United States. The site structure covers the following major areas:

1. **About Us** — Information about AZA's leadership (Board of Directors, Staff, Ethics Board), numerous committees (Accreditation Commission, Animal Health, Animal Welfare, Conservation Education, etc.), Scientific Advisory Groups (Avian, Behavior, Nutrition, Veterinary, etc.), Strategic Plan 2024-2029, Annual Reports, Bylaws, Policies (Code of Conduct, Code of Professional Ethics), Press Room, and Partners.

2. **Accreditation** — Details on becoming accredited, benefits, FAQs, how to apply (including the Pathway Toward Membership Program), accreditation materials, lists of accredited members, awards (Half Century and Quarter Century Awards), the Accreditation Commission, inspectors, and the Accreditation Resource Center with guidelines and sample documents.

3. **Animal Care & Management** — Covers Animal Programs (Taxon Advisory Groups, Species Survival Plan Programs, Studbooks, Global Species Management Plans), Animal Program Resources, Animal Wellbeing (strategic frameworks, guiding principles, care manuals, ambassador animal guidelines, welfare assessments), funding opportunities, Aquatic Sustainability, and the Ambassador Animal Resource & Information Center.

4. **Conservation** — SAFE: Saving Animals From Extinction program with SAFE Species, conservation initiatives (Annual Report on Conservation and Science, Reduce the Risk, Climate Change, Citizen Science, Florida Reef Tract Rescue Project, Black-footed Ferret Recovery), Conservation Funding (Conservation Grants Fund, SAFE Granting Program, ARPA-Related Grants), Field Conservation, Green Practices, Research and Science, and Conservation Education.

5. **Equity & Inclusion** — Includes the MoZAICS (Modeling Zoos and Aquariums of Inclusive Communities of Science) program.

6. **Wildlife Trafficking Alliance** — Information about the problem of wildlife trafficking, initiatives and campaigns (Wildlife Confiscations Network, I Travel for Wildlife, Not A Pet, Toss the Tusk, Buy Informed, Reduce the Risk), partners, what you can do, and funding opportunities.

7. **AZA Services** — Membership options (Individual, Organization, Commercial, Student, Advocate), Conferences (Annual Conference, Mid-Year Meeting), Government Affairs, Professional Development (courses, scholarships, executive leadership programs), Honors & Awards, Safety & Preparedness (Antivenom Index), and Member Resources & Benefits (data, surveys, trends, discounted admissions, logos).

8. **Connect** — Connect Stories, archives, photo contests, and holiday gift guide.

9. **Utility Navigation** — Jobs/careers, Find a Zoo or Aquarium, Calendar, Donate, and Login.

# Economic Impact and Tourism Analysis of The Florida Aquarium’s Business Activities

[Home](https://tbrpc.org/) > Economic Impact and Tourism Analysis of The Florida Aquarium’s Business Activities

This report analyzes the economic and tourism impact of [The Florida Aquarium](https://www.flaquarium.org/) on Hillsborough County and the broader Tampa Bay region in 2023. Conducted by the [Tampa Bay Regional Planning Council](https://tbrpc.org) (TBRPC), the study underscores the Aquarium’s pivotal role in driving local economic growth, supporting employment, and bolstering the region’s tourism sector.

![](https://tbrpc.org/wp-content/uploads/2024/10/Economic-Impact-and-Tourism-Analysis-of-The-Florida-Aquariums-Business-Activities_Page_01-1024x791.jpg)

[Download Resources](https://tampabayplanning.sharepoint.com/:b:/s/Public/EQ-0OA8HkkhHpkoDcFIzJb4BgBsIKAwl3u0HF-c3Tz9Qtg?e=NoNIGr)

**Key Insights**

* Record-Breaking Attendance: In 2023, The Florida Aquarium welcomed over one million visitors, indicating its continued popularity as a tourist destination.
* Visitor Spending: Out-of-town visitors, who accounted for 45% of total attendance in 2023, made a significant contribution to the local economy, particularly benefiting the hospitality and retail sectors.
* Employment Impact: The Florida Aquarium directly supported 249 full-time equivalent jobs in 2023 and contributed to a total of 407 jobs when including indirect and induced employment.
* Economic Output: The Florida Aquarium generated a total economic output of $53.6 million in Hillsborough County, with a Gross County Product (GCP) contribution of $28.8 million.
* Local Spending: The Florida Aquarium’s operational spending within Hillsborough County totaled $5.2 million, supporting an additional 39 jobs and generating $7.7 million in economic output.
* Future Growth: The planned expansion of The Florida Aquarium is projected to increase its economic impact by creating additional jobs and attracting more visitors in the coming years.

# Study Shows Zoo Investment Leads to $659 Million Economic Impact

* [Latest News](https://www.littlerockzoo.com/zoo-blog/blog-posts/category/latest-news/)

**Monday, Apr 26, 2021**

**Study Shows Zoo Investment Leads to $659 Million Economic Impact***Overall Impact Nears $1 Billion Over 15 Years as Zoo Draws Large Tourism Market*

LITTLE ROCK (April 26, 2021) – The Little Rock Zoo released **[a study](https://littlerockzoo.com/media/1998/little-rock-zoo-economic-impact-analysis-to-lrz-42121.pdf)** today showing that a $50 million dollar investment from the Rebuild the Rock initiative would create economic activity in the Little Rock area of more than $659 million. Overall economic activity related to the Zoo from 2015 to 2030 would amount to close to $1 billion dollars.

The study conducted by Intelligent Analytics and Modeling (IAMECON) and Zoo Advisors, a Zoo industry analytic firm, showed tourism uniquely created by the Little Rock Zoo has a significant impact on the local economy.  For the analysis, they reviewed the impact of the increase in attendance to the Zoo that would be created by the investment of $50 million.

Families travel to visit zoos. The city of Little Rock is currently losing tourism dollars to Tulsa, Memphis and St. Louis as tourists travel to these areas to visit their zoos. When the Little Rock Zoo builds on its Master Plan and becomes a regionally competitive zoo, more families will travel to Little Rock to visit the Little Rock Zoo. Other economic activity is created by capital expenditures and operational spending. This spending increases employment activity and other associated economic activity. Because the Little Rock Zoo is the only zoo in the state and one of the largest attractions in the state it uniquely has the potential to create this impact.

Zoo Director Susan Altrui said the results of the study were exciting and showed the tremendous economic value of the Little Rock Zoo beyond its value as a place for conservation learning and family recreation. “Investment in the Zoo has a real financial return and it’s about more than just making kids smile and providing great learning experiences. This is about driving real, tangible tourism dollars to our city and fueling economic opportunity,” said Altrui.

Owner of Allegra and Image 360 Little Rock and Zoo Foundation board chair, Lisa Buehler, echoed Altrui’s sentiment. “The Little Rock Zoo has untapped potential and there is good reason to invest in our Zoo. This economic impact study shows how investment in our Zoo helps grow our local economy and that’s something any resident or business person should be excited about,” said Buehler.

**About the Zoo**

The Little Rock Zoo is accredited by the Association of Zoos and Aquariums.  Look for the AZA logo whenever you visit a zoo or aquarium as your assurance that you are supporting a facility dedicated to providing excellent care for animals, a great experience for you and a better future for all living things.  With its more than 200 accredited members, AZA is a leader in global wildlife conservation and your link to helping animals in their native habitats.  For more information, visit [www.aza.org](http://www.aza.org/).

**About the Arkansas Zoological Foundation**

The Arkansas Zoological Foundation is a 501 (c) (3) organization raising funds for the growth and development of the Little Rock Zoo. The Zoo Foundation has helped fund several projects at the Little Rock Zoo including the Laura P. Nichols Penguin Pointe habitat, the Cheetah Outpost, the Arkansas Heritage Farm, the Diamond Express Train and the soon to open Conservation Learning Center and Eastern collared lizard habitat. The Zoo Foundation hosts fundraisers throughout the year including the popular Wild Wines and Zoo Brew events. For more information, visit [arkzoofoundation.org](https://www.arkzoofoundation.org/).

# Travel & Tourism Economic Impact Research (EIR)

WTTC produces reports annually on the economic and employment impact of Travel & Tourism for 184 countries/economies and 28 geographic and economic regions across the world.

[Our Data](/research)

Economic Impact Research (EIR)

Alongside our other Insights reports, WTTC produces reports annually on the economic and employment impact of Travel & Tourism for 184 countries/economies and 28 geographic and economic regions across the world. These reports, in collaboration with [Oxford Economics](https://www.oxfordeconomics.com/), are a vital tool in helping us to equip public and private sector bodies with hard evidence of the huge value Travel & Tourism brings to the economy so that their policymaking and investment decisions support our sector.  
  
For all of our latest EIR data, please visit the [WTTC Research Hub](https://researchhub.wttc.org/).

### What is the economic impact of Travel & Tourism?

WTTC’s latest annual research shows:

9.8%
:   In 2025, Travel & Tourism’s contribution to global GDP totalled US$11.6 trillion. It grew at 4.1% year on year, exceeding overall global economic growth (2.8%) by almost 50%. This includes direct, indirect, and induced impacts of the sector. As a share, Travel & Tourism represented 9.8% of the global economy.

366m
:   Travel & Tourism is also an important source of employment. In 2025, the sector supported a total of 366 million jobs globally, which is approximately 1 in 9 jobs. The sector also accounted for 1 in 3 new jobs created globally.

3.2%
:   Domestic visitors spent US$5.63 trillion, growing 3.7% over the 2024 level. At the same time, spending by international visitors increased 3.2% annually to reach US$2.02 trillion.

## Recent EIR Reports and Factsheets

Below are some of our recent and popular Travel & Tourism Economic Impact Research (EIR) publications. You can find many more on specific regions and economies/countries on our [Research Hub](https://researchhub.wttc.org/category/economic-impact).

**The data for these, including historic data, gets updated every year.**

[Click here](/research/economic-impact/tourism-data-statistics-regions-countries) for links to the different economy/country and regional reports. Or use the buttons below to go to our Research Hub.

[View Our EIR reports](https://researchhub.wttc.org/category/economic-impact)   [View Our EIR Factsheets](https://researchhub.wttc.org/factsheets)

### World Travel & Tourism Economic Impact Factsheet

 [View more](https://researchhub.wttc.org/product/factsheet-world-travel-tourism-economic-impact-research)

## Why our Economic Impact Research (EIR) matters

From the inception of WTTC in 1990, our [Members](/membership/our-members) realised that hard economic facts were needed to help governments and policymakers truly understand the potential of Travel & Tourism. Measuring the size and growth of Travel & Tourism and its contribution to society, therefore, plays a vital part in underpinning [WTTC's work](/about).

## What does an EIR report look like?

Each EIR (Economic Impact Research) report reveals the importance of Travel & Tourism to a specific economy/country or economic region in granular detail across many metrics. The report’s features include:

* Absolute and relative contributions of Travel & Tourism to GDP and employment, international and domestic spending
* Data on leisure and business spending, capital investment, government spending and outbound spending
* Tables ranking the economy against other competing destinations and benchmarked against the world and regional average across various metrics
* Charts comparing data across every year from 2015 to 2025 and 2035
* Detailed data tables for the years 2019-2024 plus forecasts for 2025 and 2035

[View Our EIR Factsheets](https://researchhub.wttc.org/factsheets)   [View Our EIR reports](https://researchhub.wttc.org/category/economic-impact)

## What other economic impact research does WTTC carry out?

As well as producing its annual EIR reports for 184 countries/ economies and 28 regions globally, WTTC also produces an annual [Global Trends report](https://researchhub.wttc.org/product/travel-tourism-economic-impact-2025-global-trends). This report provides a comprehensive analysis of the economic impact of the Travel & Tourism sector globally and regionally, and discussion of emerging themes and global trends in Travel & Tourism. In recent years, WTTC has also published [EIR data for more than 80 cities](/research/economic-impact/cities) and has benchmarked Travel & Tourism against other economic sectors. WTTC also presents thought leadership reports – often focused on a specific region or theme – that include an analysis of the economic impact of government policies affecting the sector such as investment, visa facilitation, investment and incentivising training and careers.

Visit our [Research Hub](https://researchhub.wttc.org/) to find all our Economic Impact Research reports, as well as other reports on Travel and Tourism.

## What other research does WTTC produce?

On top of research into the economic impact of Travel & Tourism, WTTC also carries out research into many other topics that are crucial to the sector. Another key focus is [Sustainability](https://wttc.org/sustainability), which includes the areas of [Environmental & Social Research (ESR)](https://globaltravelfootprint.wttc.org/), our Net-Zero Roadmap, Sustainable Aviation Fuel, Destination Stewardship, and Nature Positive Tourism. We also research technology trends, diversity, specific segments – such as retail tourism - and global tourism trends.

Visit our Research Hub via the button below to find all our Economic Impact Reports, as well as other reports on Travel and Tourism.

[WTTC Research Hub](https://researchhub.wttc.org/)

The projects spotlighted as part of the capital raise included cosmetic updates, new bear and giraffe exhibits, and a general refresh that ﬁt the order of the day – and the Erie community stepped up. COVID-19 hit in March 2020 interrupting the yet to be closed capital campaign. Visitors were no longer able to visit the Erie Zoo for months and the main revenue source dried up – the Zoo took a ﬁnancial hit. In its resilient and what can only be described as Erie-like style, the Zoo opened its gates hosting students, so parents without childcare could make it to work and found creative ways to remain relevant during a confusing time. The Erie Zoo wasn’t alone – zoos across the country were emerging as part of virtual classrooms ﬁnding ways to create ﬁeld trips for students stuck at home. These zoos were equipped with livestream capability and put their fascinating creatures and charismatic zookeepers in the spotlight – a difﬁcult task without mobile cameras and campus-wide broadband, which was the case at the Erie Zoo.
Also, unlike other zoos across the country facing similar COVID-induced challenges, inside the Erie Zoo a reckoning was underway, as its Association of Zoos and Aquariums (AZA) accreditation, long held together through its commitment to conservation and years of transactional support, was beginning to buckle. In November 2021, a consequential outcome than could not have been imagined prior to the pandemic was about to bear down on the beloved city asset – an AZA inspection resulted in an interruption that could change the course of the Erie Zoo.
3 AN ECONOMIC AND COMMUNITY ASSET The Erie Zoo generates $21.2 million annually in the PA economy. 84% of this impact ($17.8 million) stays in the Erie County economy. The Erie Zoo generated nearly $100 million in economic impact over the past 5 years. • Operational and capital spending of the Erie Zoo generates $8.5 million annually. • Visitor spending generates $12.7 million annually on a direct and indirect basis.
Most visitors to the Erie Zoo live within a 50-mile radius (80.4%), and 19.6% of visitors are from 50+ miles away. It is assumed that all visitors to the Erie Zoo are day visitors and local day visitors (living within a 50-mile radius) spend $28.49 per visit and non-local day visitors (living 50 or more miles away) spend $51.28 per visit.

4 SUPPORTING AND SUSTAINING JOBS The Erie Zoo’s operations and visitors support and sustain an estimated 250 jobs annually. • The day-to-day operations of the Zoo support 109 jobs with an average of 85 direct jobs annually.1 • Visitors to the Erie Zoo are an important driver of the Zoo’s impact. The Zoo has level set and is opting to use this pivotal moment as an opportunity to update aging exhibits to match speciﬁcations of modern zoological design and move the Zoo into the 21st Century.
While the AZA is currently the Zoo’s ﬁercest critic – they are also the Zoo’s biggest cheerleader. Through mentorship and side-by-side guidance, the AZA has expressed its desire to have the Zoo back as a member and has given the beloved Erie County asset a path forward to reentry. The visitors are coming for the beach, but there is signiﬁcant opportunity to get them to stay in Erie County longer and spend more money thereby beneﬁting the economy. The Erie Zoo leadership is approaching the upgrades and modernization requirements as an opportunity to transform the Zoo into an attraction that appeals to people beyond the region. A review of the AZA economic impact study[1], shows that compared to other zoos across the country, the capital and operational investment required to continually invest in its facilities and operational funding required to stay on course with its peers across the nation are lacking at the Erie Zoo. Technology is a major deﬁcit when compared to regional attractions.
Interactive displays and live camera feeds are hindered by the fact that the Erie Zoo doesn’t have access to campus-wide broadband, resulting in a limited visitor experience.
Erie loves the Erie Zoo – as evidenced by the fact that the Wild Open Spaces campaign drew $8 million in private and corporate support. That funding can be used to leverage outside investments, which could transform this community asset into a regional attraction and economic engine.

In 2011, the average attendance of the Akron Zoo was 100,000 visitors and grew to over 400,000 in 2019. Visitors to the Akron Zoo are 40% from Summit County and 60% from surrounding counties and states. A deliberate decision in 2001 to provide public funds for the Akron Zoo has yielded results with an annual economic impact of $56.2 million per year – the zoo is a tourist destination rather than a local attraction. The Akron Zoo is publicly supported through a tax levy that passed in 2010 and successfully passed on the November 3, 2020, ballot requesting a 0.8 mil renewal levy and 0.4 mil increase. Two-hours south of Erie, PA, in Pittsburgh, local ﬁnancial support of two regional assets makes a signiﬁcant impact in operations and destination status. Support for the Pittsburgh Zoo and National Aviary in Allegheny County, Pennsylvania, comes from the Regional Asset District (RAD) which provides funding for over 100 assets in the county including the Carnegie Library System, Allegheny County Parks, and Phipps Conservatory. The Pittsburgh Zoo and the National Aviary in Pittsburgh (AZA accredited) are considered contractual assets and are guaranteed a share of the RAD, which is reviewable every 5 years. The current operating and capital budget is about $5 million annually. As way of perspective, total operating and capital budget for the Akron Zoo in 2019 was almost $15 million ($14.9 million). It draws the highest percentage of ECGRA dollars, because it attracts the most visitors among all lead assets in the county. "By investing in lead assets like the Erie Zoo, we're investing in Erie's ability to attract and retain creative talent and innovative businesses. The vitality and continued excellence of the Erie Zoo is a part of the region’s renaissance." Perry Wood, Ed.D.
Executive Director, Erie County Gaming Revenue Authority Currently, the Erie Zoo maintains its operations through visitor revenues and spending, which was laid bare during COVID when the ticket sales dried up forcing the leadership of the Erie Zoo to get creative. A season of change brings opportunity, and the staff and Board of the Erie Zoo are preparing to undertake the task of modernizing the near century old Zoo through a new lens of reaccreditation.
The Erie Zoo is a pride point for the county and Northwestern Pennsylvania – regaining accreditation by AZA will help restore it to its former glory as both an economic and community building block. This economic analysis shows that the Erie Zoo is an economic asset that could become a powerful economic engine, but a major investment is critical to its long-term success.

args.summary:
The Erie Zoo, a 98-year-old City of Erie-owned asset, is a beloved regional attraction generating $21.2 million in annual economic impact, supporting 250 jobs, and contributing $1.3 million in state and local taxes. Despite attracting 310,000+ yearly visitors, the Zoo faces a critical challenge: it lost its AZA accreditation in November 2021, partly due to COVID-19 disruptions. The AZA has provided a path to reaccreditation requiring investments in technology (broadband), capital upgrades (veterinary center), infrastructure (modern exhibits), and operations (competitive salaries).

The Zoo's current operating/capital budget (~$5 million) lags significantly behind peers. For comparison, the Akron Zoo—which received public funding support—grew from 100,000 to 400,000 annual visitors and now generates $56.2 million in economic impact. Erie Zoo receives only 4% of its revenue from government support, compared to 57% for Akron, 25% for Pittsburgh Zoo, and 20% for Buffalo Zoo.

A modernization effort (the Wild Open Spaces campaign raised $8 million privately) could transform the Zoo from a local attraction to a regional destination. Doubling the budget to be competitive could conservatively double its economic impact to $46.1 million annually. The report concludes that the Erie Zoo is a worthy investment—a self-sustaining community asset that needs public funding support to reach its full potential as an economic engine for Northwest Pennsylvania.

## Animal Health & Physiology

#### Scientific Papers

© Rory Harper

#### Identification and Validation of Operational Pain Indicators in Anurans (González et al., 2025)

September 2025

How can we identify and assess pain in anurans? New research published in the Journal of Zoological and Botanical Gardens aimed to validate pain indicators in this taxon by using a four-phase approach (literature review, expert validation, field validation in a zoo, and development of a preliminary pain index):  
   
 ✔Literature Review: 158 papers = 16 potential pain indicators identified.  
 ✔28 experts refined the list to 7 indicators (>60% agreement):  
      - Feeding behaviour changes,  
      - Abnormal behaviour,  
      - Impaired locomotion,  
      - Oedema,  
      - Reduced movement,  
      - Retained skin post-moulting,  
      - Altered respiration.  
 ✔Field validation in 53 zoo-housed anurans: high observability and ease of measurement for the 7 indicators (feeding behaviour changes & oenema scoring were the most practical).  
 ✔Applications to health and welfare assessments and interventions.

#### Effect of brushing on heart rate variability in Malayan tapirs: Does brushing contribute toward alleviating puncture stress? (Ishida et al., 2025)

July 2025

Research published in Journal of Zoo & Aquarium Research assessed stress in Malayan tapirs during invasive veterinary procedures, and whether brushing can alleviate stress during those procedures:  
 ✔Heart-rate variability (HRV) measured - increased during and after punctures, also matching with stress behaviours (valid stress indicator?).  
 ✔HRV during husbandry training (blood collection and brushing) varied across individuals and days - no clear negative effect of puncture.  
 ✔HRV during brushing was closer to standing position than other postures - brushing may have a rewarding effect on tapirs.  
 ✔More research needed, but first HRV analysis of Malayan tapirs conducted, and brushing shown to potentially alleviate stress during veterinary procedures.

[Paper](https://www.jzar.org/jzar/article/view/787)

#### Body mass of adult zoo hippos Hippopotamidae and how they compare to data from populations in the wild (Meireles et al., 2025)

April 2025

A study published in the Journal of Zoo and Aquarium Research (JZAR) compared the body mass of zoo-housed common and pygmy hippopotamuses with available data from wild populations:   
 ✔Zoo hippos heavier on average than wild counterparts: both species but more pronounced differences in pygmy hippos.  
 ✔Zoo adult males heavier than females, with common hippos showing more prominent sexual body mass dimorphism than their wild counterparts.  
 ✔Unlike wild hippos, zoo hippos show no consistent seasonal fluctuations in body mass.  
 ✔No immediate weight-related health problems detected in zoo populations, but may affect management and breeding.  
 ✔Applications to ex-situ husbandry and management of this taxon.

[Paper](https://www.jzar.org/jzar/article/view/905)

#### Composition of White Rhinoceros Colostrum and Changes During Early Lactation to Mature Milk (Osthoff, Hugo & Nieuwoudt, 2025)

January 2025

The early-lactation milk composition of seven free-ranging white rhinoceros was described in a paper published in Zoo Biology:  
 ✔Detailed analysis of minerals and fatty acids of milk during first 20 days of lactation.  
 ✔Gross energy: 123.2 kCal/100 g.  
 ✔Top 3 minerals: Sodium (24 mg/100 g), Potassium (55.2 mg/100 g), Calcium (33.4 mg/100 g).  
 ✔Colostrum phase ends after 2 days of lactation.  
 ✔Mature milk phase starts after 5 days.  
 ✔Fat content peaked at days 3 and 4 (1.6 g/100 g milk).  
 ✔Applications to ex-situ breeding and rearing of calves.

[Paper](https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1002/zoo.21907)

#### Investigating African swine fever virus susceptibility across seven genera of pigs and peccaries using peripheral blood mononuclear cells (Friedrichs et al., 2025)

January 2025

A study in the new issue of JZAR investigated the susceptibility of seven genera of pigs and peccaries to African Swine Fever (ASF):  
 ✔Susceptibility assessed using macrophages from peripheral blood mononuclear cells of different species.  
 ✔Suidae: all species of pigs were susceptible to ASF, including highly threatened Asian wild pigs (e.g. Visayan warty pig).  
 ✔Tayassuidae (peccaries): Macrophages did not support ASFV replication - susceptibility is unlikely.  
 ✔Applications to health management of both in situ and ex situ populations.

[Paper](https://www.jzar.org/jzar/article/view/850)

#### A New Soil-Based Solution for Reducing the Persistence of Parasites in Zoos  (Hernández et al., 2024)

December 2024

A new study in Journal of Zoological and Botanical Gardens tested a novel solution using parasitophagous fungi-treated forage seeds to reduce soil parasite persistence in zoos:  
 ✔Forage seeds were immersed in a submerged culture and sown in plastic trays (trial 1) and demarcated ground plots framed with wood (trial 2).  
 ✔Parasite (roundworm and cyathostomin) eggs placed above germinated vegetation after 15 days.  
 ✔Viability of roundworm eggs reduced by 62% (trial 1) and 55% (trial 2), while counts of cyasthostomin decreased by 64% and 57% in trial 1 and 2, respectively.  
 ✔Sowing soil with forage seeds pre-treated with fungi can reduce risk of parasite infection, and may be a solution for parasite control in zoos.

[Paper](https://www.mdpi.com/2673-5636/5/4/54)

#### Venous blood gas and lactate values in adult giraffe trained for voluntary jugular phlebotomy (Cole et al., 2024)

April 2024

A paper in Zoo Biology described the use of a point-of-care blood gas and lactate analyser to take blood from the veins (venepuncture/phlebotomy) of 20 trained giraffes, without anaesthesia or physical restraint:  
 ✔Reference values for venous blood gas and lactate concentrations were established.  
 ✔Blood gas values differed across giraffes at different altitudes.  
 ✔Quick and accurate assessments of giraffe physiological indicators can be obtained with a point-of-care blood gas analyser.  
 ✔This method, with voluntary training programmes, can facilitate medical care, husbandry and welfare of captive giraffes.

March 2024

The weights of zoo-housed and wild-caught Livingstone's fruit bats were compared in a paper published in Zoo Biology:  
 ✔Wild males heavier and have longer forearms than females.  
 ✔Zoo-housed bats heavier than wild counterparts, particularly those housed in enclosures that restrict flight.  
 ✔Females are particularly vulnerable to weight gain when housed in enclosures that restrict flight, as they get heavier than males under those conditions.  
 ✔Aviary-style enclosures that enable flight reduce weight gain in captive fruit bats - applications to ex situ management of species.

A case study published in the new issue of Journal of Zoo Aquarium Research investigated infection-related abnormal swimming in an aquarium-housed yellow stingray:  
 ✔An inner ear infection was thought to be causing the abnormal swimming behaviour.  
 ✔A meclizine treatment resulted in reduction of abnormal swimming, and increased normal swimming and resting.

✔Further reduction in abnormal behaviours after the stingray returned to its more complex home habitat, from the isolated treatment tank.
