# Coral Reef Restoration Guidelines

![](data:image/gif;base64,R0lGODlhAQABAAAAACH5BAEKAAEALAAAAAABAAEAAAICTAEAOw==)

Restoration activities are becoming more and more popular across the world, in an attempt to restore/sustain the function and services associated with coral reef ecosystems. It should be noted that these efforts are unlikely to be effective as a stand-alone action, they should always be done as part of a larger integrated management strategy.

Below we have compiled some of the most recent guidelines on coral reef restoration. Should you know of any additional guidelines that are relevant please send them to [Thomas Dallison](/cdn-cgi/l/email-protection#cebaa6a1a3afbde0aaafa2a2a7bda1a08ea7adbca7a8a1bcbba3e0a1bca9).

![](data:image/gif;base64,R0lGODlhAQABAAAAACH5BAEKAAEALAAAAAABAAEAAAICTAEAOw==)

![](data:image/gif;base64,R0lGODlhAQABAAAAACH5BAEKAAEALAAAAAABAAEAAAICTAEAOw==)

##### Guide to Coral Reef Restoration: Optimizing efficiency and scale for in situ nurseries and outplanting (2025).

Developed by the Coral Restoration Consortium’s (CRC) Field-based Propagation Working Group — a team of dedicated practitioners who worked together from 2018 to 2023.

This guide brings together the most relevant, widely used methods and lessons learned from years of hands-on experience around the globe. Whether you’re just starting out or looking to scale up your coral restoration program, this guide is designed to support success across diverse goals, environments, and resource levels.

![](data:image/gif;base64,R0lGODlhAQABAAAAACH5BAEKAAEALAAAAAABAAEAAAICTAEAOw==)

![](data:image/gif;base64,R0lGODlhAQABAAAAACH5BAEKAAEALAAAAAABAAEAAAICTAEAOw==)

##### **A Practical Guide to Restoration and Rehabilitation of Rubble on Coral Reefs: guidelines from the Rubble Stabilisation Subprogram, summarising recommendations for rubble rehabilitation (2024).**

The RRAP Rubble Stabilisation R&D Subprogram is investigating methods to stabilise damaged reef surfaces where dead or degraded corals have become loose and unconsolidated rubble, preventing or slowing reef recovery.

Natural and man-made disturbances (for example, cyclones, ship groundings, crown-of-thorns starfish outbreaks or coral bleaching) can reduce functional and diverse coral reefs to fields of rubble, with an unstable and mobile surface. The lack of stability and frequent motion inhibits recruitment (settlement and regrowth) of young corals back onto reefs and hampers recovery.

Rubble stabilisation, as a reef restoration technique, is in its infancy.

It is also important to be able to identify coral reefs that can most benefit from restoration strategies: those most vulnerable to rubble formation, and those where prevailing wave regimes can make mobile rubble persist and hinder recovery.

![](data:image/gif;base64,R0lGODlhAQABAAAAACH5BAEKAAEALAAAAAABAAEAAAICTAEAOw==)

![](data:image/gif;base64,R0lGODlhAQABAAAAACH5BAEKAAEALAAAAAABAAEAAAICTAEAOw==)

##### **Standard operating procedures for larval-based restoration of Maldivian coral reefs (2023)**

The Standard Operating Procedure (SOP) for larval-based restoration has been developed in collaboration between CSIRO and the Maldives Marine Research Institute (MMRI). to provide a practical guide for the use of larval-based restoration in the Maldives. The SOP is separated into four main sections: 1) Before coral spawning, 2) During coral spawning, 3) After coral spawning, 4) Deploying coral larvae. While the report focuses on case studies in the Maldives, it is broadly applicable to larval-based restoration across the Indo-Pacific region.

![](data:image/gif;base64,R0lGODlhAQABAAAAACH5BAEKAAEALAAAAAABAAEAAAICTAEAOw==)

![](data:image/gif;base64,R0lGODlhAQABAAAAACH5BAEKAAEALAAAAAABAAEAAAICTAEAOw==)

##### **Meeting 30 by 30: The Role of Coral Reef Restoration (2022)**

The whitepaper reviews the role of coral reef restoration in the context of climate change and global 30 by 30 targets arguing that while restoration is not the only response to global declines, it has an important role to play to deliver social and ecological goals. The whitepaper also reviews current limitations, barriers, and opportunities, and provides avenues for improving the effectiveness of coral reef restoration and assist evidence-based investment and decision making.

[![](data:image/gif;base64,R0lGODlhAQABAAAAACH5BAEKAAEALAAAAAABAAEAAAICTAEAOw==)](https://www.decadeonrestoration.org/publications/principles-ecosystem-restoration-guide-united-nations-decade-2021-2030)

![](data:image/gif;base64,R0lGODlhAQABAAAAACH5BAEKAAEALAAAAAABAAEAAAICTAEAOw==)

##### **Principles for ecosystem restoration to guide the United Nations Decade 2021–2030 (2022)**

To support the implementation of the UN Decade on Ecosystem Restoration and help achieve its goals, there is a need for a shared vision of ecosystem restoration. A key step in creating a shared vision of ecosystem restoration is to adopt principles that underpin the full set of ecosystem restoration activities. These principles detail the essential tenets of ecosystem restoration that should be followed to maximize net gain for biodiversity, ecosystem health and integrity, and human health and well-being across all biomes, sectors and regions.

Although not directly pertaining to reef restoration, these principles for a shared vision of ecosystem restoration are still highly relevant for managers and implementers.

*Available in Arabic, Chinese, English, French, Spanish.*

![](data:image/gif;base64,R0lGODlhAQABAAAAACH5BAEKAAEALAAAAAABAAEAAAICTAEAOw==)

![](data:image/gif;base64,R0lGODlhAQABAAAAACH5BAEKAAEALAAAAAABAAEAAAICTAEAOw==)

##### A guide to coral reef restoration for the tourism sector (2022)

These guidelines provide an overview of the tourism sector’s engagement with coral reef conservation efforts in the Caribbean region, including results of the public opinion research, considerations before implementing a coral reef restoration project, and guiding principles and best practices for the tourism sector to implement coral reef protection and restoration efforts more effectively.

##### Translating the ten golden rules of reforestation for coral reef restoration (2022)

A new study has aimed to translate the ten golden rules of reforestation for coral reef restoration. It seeks to apply lessons from restoring terrestrial ecosystems to coral reefs.

[![](data:image/gif;base64,R0lGODlhAQABAAAAACH5BAEKAAEALAAAAAABAAEAAAICTAEAOw==)](https://icriforum.org/wp-content/uploads/2021/01/Screenshot-2021-01-18-at-15.39.37.webp)

![](data:image/gif;base64,R0lGODlhAQABAAAAACH5BAEKAAEALAAAAAABAAEAAAICTAEAOw==)

##### Coral reef restoration as a strategy to improve ecosystem services (2020)

This document presents an overview of the best- available knowledge in the field and provides realistic recommendations for the use of restoration as a management strategy for coral reefs to assist managers, practitioners, policy makers, and funding agencies to make informed decisions. Whilst not designed to reduce climate impacts, coral reef restoration can be a useful tool to support resilience, especially at local scales where coral recruitment is limited, and disturbances can be mitigated. Ongoing investment in coral reef restoration research and development globally will improve the scale and cost-efficiency of the methods currently applied. You can read the policy brief [here](https://icriforum.org/wp-content/uploads/2021/01/Policy-brief.pdf).

Watch the webinar from the Reef Resilience Network about the guide [here](https://reefresilience.org/restoration-report/).

[![](data:image/gif;base64,R0lGODlhAQABAAAAACH5BAEKAAEALAAAAAABAAEAAAICTAEAOw==)](https://icriforum.org/wp-content/uploads/2020/11/Screenshot-2020-11-25-at-15.43.11.webp)

![](data:image/gif;base64,R0lGODlhAQABAAAAACH5BAEKAAEALAAAAAABAAEAAAICTAEAOw==)

##### Managers Guide for coral restoration (2020)

The **Manager’s Guide to Coral Reef Restoration Planning and Design** supports the needs of reef managers seeking to begin restoration or assess their current restoration program. Based on global best practices, the Guide was developed for reef managers and practitioners, and anyone who plans, implements, and monitors reef restoration activities. Together with a suite of tools and templates, the Guide maps out a six-step, iterative process to help users gather relevant data, ask critical questions, and have important conversations about restoration in their location, culminating in the creation of a Restoration Action Plan to enhance reef resilience and recovery. Within the guide are two Appendices and other tools that can (and should) be used to assist readers in developing a restoration action plan;

Watch the webinar from the Reef Resilience Network about the guide [here](https://reefresilience.org/a-managers-guide-to-coral-reef-restoration-planning-and-design/).

[![](data:image/gif;base64,R0lGODlhAQABAAAAACH5BAEKAAEALAAAAAABAAEAAAICTAEAOw==)](https://icriforum.org/wp-content/uploads/2020/11/Screenshot-2020-11-09-at-14.41.19.webp)

![](data:image/gif;base64,R0lGODlhAQABAAAAACH5BAEKAAEALAAAAAABAAEAAAICTAEAOw==)

##### Coral reef restoration monitoring guide: Methods to evaluate restoration success from local to ecosystem scales (2020)

The **Coral reef restoration monitoring guide: Methods to evaluate restoration success from local to ecosystem scales.** This guide will help any restoration group or government – large or small – decide on a monitoring regimen that fits their budget and capacity. The guide took more than two years to put together – and we are sure this will be a crucial resource to the community as more and more countries engage in coral restoration.

[![](data:image/gif;base64,R0lGODlhAQABAAAAACH5BAEKAAEALAAAAAABAAEAAAICTAEAOw==)](https://icriforum.org/wp-content/uploads/2020/11/Screenshot-2020-11-09-at-14.46.54.webp)

![](data:image/gif;base64,R0lGODlhAQABAAAAACH5BAEKAAEALAAAAAABAAEAAAICTAEAOw==)

##### Guide to ecological engineering: the restoration of coral reefs and associated ecosystems (2020)

This guide provides an inventory of ecological engineering techniques employed mainly in France, but also worldwide. It is devoted to the restoration of coral reefs and their associated ecosystems: seagrasses and mangroves. It was produced by the French Coral Reef Initiative (IFRECOR) in French and has recently been translated into English by UNEP.

[![](data:image/gif;base64,R0lGODlhAQABAAAAACH5BAEKAAEALAAAAAABAAEAAAICTAEAOw==)](https://icriforum.org/wp-content/uploads/2020/11/Screenshot-2020-11-23-at-12.40.53.webp)

![](data:image/gif;base64,R0lGODlhAQABAAAAACH5BAEKAAEALAAAAAABAAEAAAICTAEAOw==)

##### Training Guide for Coral Reef Restoration (2020)

This Guide is a practical, complementary tool for coral reef restoration training. Any individuals wishing to start a restoration project must contact local authorities to learn about the legal implications and obtain the corresponding permits, as well as join working groups with restoration experience to receive proper training. It was produced the Mesoamerican Reef Fund (MAR Fund), Mesoamerican Reef Rescue Initiative (RRI) with the support of ICRI and the UN Environment Programme Small Grants Program.

[![](data:image/gif;base64,R0lGODlhAQABAAAAACH5BAEKAAEALAAAAAABAAEAAAICTAEAOw==)](https://icriforum.org/wp-content/uploads/2020/11/Screenshot-2020-11-30-at-09.26.03.webp)

![](data:image/gif;base64,R0lGODlhAQABAAAAACH5BAEKAAEALAAAAAABAAEAAAICTAEAOw==)

##### Protocol for the restoration of reefs and coral communities in Costa Rica (2020)

This technical document is aimed to support officials of the National System of Conservation Areas (SINAC), non-governmental non-profit organisations (NGOs) related to the sea, academic centres, diving centres and in general, including any person who loves the ocean and is an enthusiast of coral ecosystems and their conservation.

[![](data:image/gif;base64,R0lGODlhAQABAAAAACH5BAEKAAEALAAAAAABAAEAAAICTAEAOw==)](https://icriforum.org/wp-content/uploads/2020/11/Screenshot-2020-11-09-at-15.01.26.webp)

![](data:image/gif;base64,R0lGODlhAQABAAAAACH5BAEKAAEALAAAAAABAAEAAAICTAEAOw==)

##### A guidebook for coral propagation through asexual reproduction- revised version (2019)

The English translation of the Japanese coral restoration guidelines. These guidelines provide an overview of the characteristics, functions, and current state of corals in Japan, coral propagation plans and how to go about it. In chapter two it details whole-area propagation techniques for corals and the different methods that could be utilised.

*Note: all the text was translated by James Cook University from the Japanese publication of “A guidebook for coral propagation through asexual reproduction- revised version” produced by the Fisheries Agency, the Ministry of Agriculture, Forestry and Fisheries of Japan on their web site (<https://www.jfa.maff.go.jp/j/seibi/sango_tebiki.html>). All the responsibility of the English text is on the James Cook University, but not the Fisheries Agency.*

[![](data:image/gif;base64,R0lGODlhAQABAAAAACH5BAEKAAEALAAAAAABAAEAAAICTAEAOw==)](https://icriforum.org/wp-content/uploads/2020/12/Screenshot-2020-12-16-at-13.52.16.webp)

![](data:image/gif;base64,R0lGODlhAQABAAAAACH5BAEKAAEALAAAAAABAAEAAAICTAEAOw==)

##### Early Warning and Rapid Response Protocol (2019)

The Early Warning and Rapid Response Protocol: Actions to mitigate the Impact of Tropical Cyclones on Coral Reefs presents a step wise approach to guide First Responders and reef managers in terms of what needs to be done before, during and after a tropical cyclone to mitigate the impacts to coral reefs in an orderly and timely manner. It is also available in Spanish [here](https://icriforum.org/wp-content/uploads/2020/12/Protocolo-Generico-2.pdf).

[![](data:image/gif;base64,R0lGODlhAQABAAAAACH5BAEKAAEALAAAAAABAAEAAAICTAEAOw==)](https://icriforum.org/wp-content/uploads/2020/11/Screenshot-2020-11-18-at-10.18.19.webp)

![](data:image/gif;base64,R0lGODlhAQABAAAAACH5BAEKAAEALAAAAAABAAEAAAICTAEAOw==)

##### Belize Coral Reef Replenishment Manual (2018)

This manual was designed to be used by fisherfolk, licensed tour guides, those involved inMPAs in Belize either for the government or an NGO, students and community members. It presents coral restoration methods that have been working successfully in southern Belize since 2006.

[![](data:image/gif;base64,R0lGODlhAQABAAAAACH5BAEKAAEALAAAAAABAAEAAAICTAEAOw==)](https://icriforum.org/wp-content/uploads/2020/11/Screenshot-2020-11-09-at-14.43.28.webp)

![](data:image/gif;base64,R0lGODlhAQABAAAAACH5BAEKAAEALAAAAAABAAEAAAICTAEAOw==)

##### Coral Reef Restoration Toolkit: A Field-Oriented Guide Developed in the Seychelles Islands (2018)

Produced by Nature Seychelles in 2018, the purpose of this Toolkit is to describe how to complete a coral reef restoration project, using the ‘coral gardening’ concept and aims to be a companion for scientists, managers, practitioners and local communities who are facing a coral reef restoration challenge and require guidance using low cost, ﬁeld-tested methods.

[![](data:image/gif;base64,R0lGODlhAQABAAAAACH5BAEKAAEALAAAAAABAAEAAAICTAEAOw==)](https://icriforum.org/wp-content/uploads/2020/11/Screenshot-2020-11-09-at-15.36.11.webp)

![](data:image/gif;base64,R0lGODlhAQABAAAAACH5BAEKAAEALAAAAAABAAEAAAICTAEAOw==)

##### Methodology for scaling mitigation and compensatory measures in tropical marine ecosystems (2018)

The French Coral Reef Initiative (IFRECOR) has developed MERCI-Cor a method to assess the significance of an ecological impact, to ensure better avoidance and reduction of ecological losses in the mitigation hierarchy, and sizing compensatory measures, to offset last residual losses.

[![](data:image/gif;base64,R0lGODlhAQABAAAAACH5BAEKAAEALAAAAAABAAEAAAICTAEAOw==)](https://icriforum.org/wp-content/uploads/2020/11/Screenshot-2020-11-09-at-15.49.13.webp)

![](data:image/gif;base64,R0lGODlhAQABAAAAACH5BAEKAAEALAAAAAABAAEAAAICTAEAOw==)

##### Guidance document for reef management and restoration to improve coastal protection (2018)

This guidance document aims to provide a review and recommendations on reef management and restoration for risk reduction. It synthesizes evidence of the role coral reefs play in coastal protection and the reduction of risks during disasters. It presents ecological, geological, and oceanographic factors that contribute to the coastal protection capacity of reefs and the factors that reduce this capacity. It also presents an array of risk reduction solutions to restore reef protection services, and management approaches that can help support its coastal protection values.

[![](data:image/gif;base64,R0lGODlhAQABAAAAACH5BAEKAAEALAAAAAABAAEAAAICTAEAOw==)](https://icriforum.org/wp-content/uploads/2020/11/Screenshot-2020-11-16-at-15.56.36.webp)

![](data:image/gif;base64,R0lGODlhAQABAAAAACH5BAEKAAEALAAAAAABAAEAAAICTAEAOw==)

##### Practical guide to restoration based on the production of coral sexual recruits with an emphasis on Acropora palmata (2018)

This is a practical guide (in Spanish) that provides information on the production and use of coral sex recruits for reef restoration. This guide is aimed at people interested and/or involved in reef restoration and brings together a compilation of experiences acquired over ten years by the team under  Dr Anastazia T. Banaszak at the Academic Unit of Reef Systems of the Institute of Marine Sciences and Limnology, of the National Autonomous University of Mexico.

[![](data:image/gif;base64,R0lGODlhAQABAAAAACH5BAEKAAEALAAAAAABAAEAAAICTAEAOw==)](https://icriforum.org/wp-content/uploads/2020/11/Screenshot-2020-11-25-at-12.26.49.webp)

![](data:image/gif;base64,R0lGODlhAQABAAAAACH5BAEKAAEALAAAAAABAAEAAAICTAEAOw==)

##### Coral Restoration Techniques in the Western Pacific Region (2014)

The guide was produced by the Indian Ocean Commission Western Pacific (IOC/WESTPAC) project on Coastal Marine Biodiversity and Conservation with the aim of consolidating techniques that are used and available for coral restoration in the Western Pacific Region.

[![](data:image/gif;base64,R0lGODlhAQABAAAAACH5BAEKAAEALAAAAAABAAEAAAICTAEAOw==)](https://icriforum.org/wp-content/uploads/2020/11/Screenshot-2020-11-11-at-15.28.42.webp)

![](data:image/gif;base64,R0lGODlhAQABAAAAACH5BAEKAAEALAAAAAABAAEAAAICTAEAOw==)

##### Methods of farming sexually propagated corals and outplanting for coral reef rehabilitation (2014)

The English translation of the Japanese document on farming sexually propagated corals and how to outplant these corals. The document provides detailed step by step instruction on how to get from the spawning of corals all the way to outplanting of the new corals.

[![](data:image/gif;base64,R0lGODlhAQABAAAAACH5BAEKAAEALAAAAAABAAEAAAICTAEAOw==)](https://icriforum.org/wp-content/uploads/2020/12/Screenshot-2020-12-03-at-14.57.30.webp)

![](data:image/gif;base64,R0lGODlhAQABAAAAACH5BAEKAAEALAAAAAABAAEAAAICTAEAOw==)

##### Caribbean Acropora Restoration Guide: Best Practices for Propagation and Population Enhancement (2011)

This Practitioner’s Guide was developed out of a workshop held at the University of Miami Rosenstiel School of Marine and Atmospheric Science (RSMAS) in April 2011. The purpose of this guide is to share the collective knowledge of a community of scientists and restoration practitioners who have been working both independently and collaboratively to restore populations of Acropora corals throughout the Caribbean.

##### 

[![](data:image/gif;base64,R0lGODlhAQABAAAAACH5BAEKAAEALAAAAAABAAEAAAICTAEAOw==)](https://icriforum.org/wp-content/uploads/2020/11/Screenshot-2020-11-09-at-14.48.23.webp)

![](data:image/gif;base64,R0lGODlhAQABAAAAACH5BAEKAAEALAAAAAABAAEAAAICTAEAOw==)

##### Reef rehabilitation manual (2010)

This Reef Rehabilitation Manual is intended to complement the Reef Restoration Concepts & Guidelines and provide more detailed hands-on advice, based on lessons learnt from previous experience, on how to carry out coral reef rehabilitation in a responsible and cost-effective manner.

# 2026 Global Zoo Overview and Economic Impact

![](https://www.ottoenvironmental.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/01/pexels-doug-1770706-scaled.jpg)

# As we enter 2026, the zoo industry continues to evolve, driven by technological advancements, shifting visitor demographics, and a focus on sustainability.

Globally, the [AZA](https://www.aza.org/) (Association of Zoos and Aquariums) [reports](https://www.aza.org/zoo-and-aquarium-statistics) over 700 million annual visitors to zoos and aquariums, contributing $350 million to conservation. The U.S. market size is projected at [$3.0 billion](https://www.ibisworld.com/united-states/industry/zoos-aquariums/4990/), with revenue growing at a compound annual growth rate of 6.0% through 2025, expected to continue modestly into 2026.

### International Zoo Attendance Projections

![](https://www.ottoenvironmental.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/01/1-A-1-Cologne-Zoo-300x188.png)Cologne Zoo

Attendance projections for 2026 show steady growth. In the U.S., zoos, aquariums, and animal parks attract millions annually. For example, the [Milwaukee County Zoo](https://milwaukeezoo.org/) is targeting 1,302,379 visitors, a 2% increase ([report](https://county.milwaukee.gov/files/county/administrative-services/PSB/BudgetsCopy-1/2026-Budget/Recommended-Operating/950---Zoological.pdf)). Globally, [Cologne Zoo](https://koelnerzoo.de/en/home-en) in Germany anticipates over 1.2 million visitors, supporting €3 million in conservation since 2010. Denver Zoo anticipates 1.85 million attendees, reflecting post-pandemic recovery trends ([Executive summary](https://denverzoo.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/05/CHJC_DenverZoo_Impacts_ExecSummary.pdf)).

[Nassal](https://www.nassal.com/), an international specialty theming fabricator and program manager, has revealed four major trends that are reshaping the zoo and aquarium industry, transforming how these institutions operate, engage, and evolve. The [four pillars](https://www.nassal.com/insights) involve designing facilities  for peak animal welfare, promoting conservation education and ethical interaction (enrichment vs flashy presentations), immersive experiences, and building and programming for all ages and abilities.

### Shifting Visitor Expectations and Enhanced Experiences

![](https://www.ottoenvironmental.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/01/1-A-1-Penguins-300x168.jpg)Empire of the Penguin at Seaworld (Nassal)

Visitor expectations are [shifting](https://www.statista.com/outlook/amo/entertainment/zoos-and-aquariums/worldwide?srsltid=AfmBOoqK775ank1OGTFVkS8FIvkpbtBgk5-rSmkKbIxruPODIc9s9o4L) toward immersive and diverse offerings. Augmented Reality ([AV](https://www.brandxr.io/augmented-reality-roars-into-zoos)) and Virtual Reality ([VR](https://texaszoos.com/virtual-reality-in-zoos/)) are poised to be a [major addition](https://www.classvr.com/us/virtual-reality-in-education/virtual-reality-industry-work/vr-ar-for-public-attractions/) to parks that can afford the technology.

![](https://www.ottoenvironmental.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/01/1-A-1-Class-VR-300x272.png)ClassVR

Internationally, European Association of Zoos and Aquaria ([EAZA](https://www.eaza.net/home/))’s 2026 [Welfare Forum](https://www.eaza.net/events/animal-welfare-forum-2026/) in Belgium focuses on evidence-based welfare, meeting demands for ethical experiences. Increasingly, food options are key, with events like Houston Zoo’s [Feast with the Beasts](https://www.houstonzoo.org/feast-restaurants-2024) spreading in major cities. Entertainment beyond animals is rising, including music and beer gardens at U.S. events like [Brews Around the Zoo](https://www.centralfloridazoo.org/event/brews/) at Central Florida [Zoo & Botanical Gardens](https://www.centralfloridazoo.org/).

### Zoos & Aquariums: Frontlines in Global Wildlife Conservation

In 2026, zoos and aquariums are advancing high-impact conservation initiatives that span research, species protection, and community engagement. For example, the San Antonio Zoo is launching the [Brewer Ocean Conservation Lab](https://www.expressnews.com/business/article/san-antonio-zoo-coral-conservation-lab-21020591.php) in summer 2026, a new facility dedicated to growing and restoring damaged coral reefs in partnership with NOAA and educating the public about marine ecosystems. Meanwhile, Woodland Park Zoo continues to support transformative [wildlife projects](https://blog.zoo.org/2025/04/woodland-park-zoo-announces-grant-to.html) through its grant programs that fund conservation projects across multiple institutions, helping deepen human-wildlife connections and support field work.

### Admission Pricing Strategies

Admission pricing trends lean toward [dynamic models](https://www.wcnc.com/article/news/local/connect-the-dots/dynamic-pricing-impacting-zoos-museums-aquariums-family-attractions/275-5582fa99-b7cd-4d5e-85f4-9fc65ec512cc). Globally, [16%](https://www.nbcnews.com/business/economy/museums-zoos-aquariums-are-embracing-dynamic-pricing-rcna210877) of attractions prioritize dynamic pricing for 2026 to optimize revenue. In the UK, London Zoo’s 2026 rates vary by season, starting at £31 for adults. U.S. examples include Fresno [Chaffee Zoo](https://thebusinessjournal.com/fresno-chaffee-zoo-raises-ticket-prices-for-2026-announces-return-of-zoorasic-park-this-spring/)‘s $25.95-$33.95. Woodland Park Zoo proposed tiered pricing ([Proposal](https://zoo.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/12/WoodlandParkZoo-2026-Draft-Annual-Plan_For-Public-Comment.pdf)).

### Advancements in Animal Healthcare and University Partnerships

![](https://www.ottoenvironmental.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/01/1-A-1-Midwestern-Uni-300x172.jpg)Midwestern University

A key trend in 2026 is the expansion of in-house animal healthcare through strategic university partnerships. The [Phoenix Zoo’s](https://www.phoenixzoo.org/) new Veterinary Medical Center, opening late 2026, will house the Midwestern University [Zoological Medical Institute](https://www.midwestern.edu/news-stories/midwestern-university-zoological-medical-institute-open-2026-new-phoenix-zoo-veterinary-medical), advancing diagnostics, research, and student training. Zoo Atlanta’s collaboration with Fort Valley State University provides hands-on experience for veterinary students at the Rollins Animal Health Center. Mississippi State University partners with Loop Abroad for global [veterinary programs](https://www.dvm360.com/view/education-partnership-provides-more-global-learning-opportunities) starting summer 2026, focusing on companion and wildlife medicine. These initiatives, supported by AZA’s emphasis on [science-based collaborations](https://www.aza.org/research-and-science), enhance animal welfare and conservation efforts.

### Otto Environmental’s Commitment to the Future

At Otto Environmental, we are excited about these important trends and look forward to continuing to serve our international partners in animal conservation and animal health research. With over 31 years of experience supporting zoos worldwide in enhancing animal welfare through innovative caging, housing, and enrichment solutions, we remain committed to helping facilities create engaging, ethical environments that benefit both animals and visitors.

### Save your cart?

For annual bibliographies of WCS-authored publications or to search our database of WCS publications, use the links above. Media inquiries about these and other WCS publications can be directed to [WCS Communications staff](https://programs.wcs.org/newsroom/Contacts.aspx). For all other inquiries, please [contact the WCS Library](/staff.aspx).

If you are a WCS staff member who has authored a publication this year and it is not listed below, please [contact the WCS Library](/staff.aspx) so that we can add it.  WCS staff can find additional Library services to support research publications [here](/en-us/research/staff-services.aspx).

#### **WCS-AUTHORED PUBLICATIONS, 10-16 August 2026**

### **Peer-Reviewed Literature Citations**

##### **Peer-Reviewed Literature Citation 1 of 4**

Botero-Cañola, S., **W. Bonell-Rojas**, J. D. Sánchez-Londoño, ..., **L. D. Acevedo-Cendales** et al. (2026). "Forest integrity and elevation as drivers of habitat use by medium to large mammals in a conservation priority site in the Northern Andes." *Global Ecology and Conservation* 70, e04354. <https://doi.org/10.1016/j.gecco.2026.e04354>

Abstract: Understanding the environmental drivers of habitat use by medium to large (M–L) mammals is essential for tropical forest conservation. In the Neotropics, survey data for this group remain spatially incomplete, and species’ responses to natural and anthropogenic habitat characteristics are still poorly understood. We used camera-trap data to evaluate M–L mammal occurrence in the Serranía de San Lucas (SSL), an understudied mountain range in the northern Andes of Colombia identified as an urgent conservation priority. We assessed the influence of elevation, forest structure, human accessibility, and ecosystem integrity on species occurrence. Our surveys documented 24 M–L mammal species, five of global or national conservation concern: the lowland tapir, jaguar, giant anteater, Andean bear, and the varied white-fronted capuchin. Using spatial multispecies occupancy models, we identified elevation and the Forest Integrity Index (FII) as the strongest predictors of habitat use. Many species exhibited their highest probabilities of occurrence at intermediate elevations, supporting a mid-elevation peak in M–L mammal diversity along the gradient. Several species showed positive responses to forest integrity, with threatened terrestrial mammals displaying the strongest associations. Our findings suggest that the FII is a valuable predictor of M–L mammal occurrence and a potentially relevant target for forest conservation and restoration. We highlight the SSL as a critical refuge for species extirpated from other regions and underscore the importance of large-scale conservation strategies that maintain forest integrity and minimize human disturbance across its full elevation gradient to support wide-ranging species such as the jaguar and Andean bear. / Para conservar efectivamente los bosques tropicales es importante entender los determinantes del uso del hábitat de los mamíferos medianos y grandes (M G) . En el Neotrópico, la información sobre este grupo sigue siendo espacialmente incompleta y las respuestas de las especies a características naturales y antropogénicas del hábitat aún no se comprenden plenamente. En este estudio utilizamos datos de cámaras trampa para evaluar la ocurrencia de mamíferos M–G en la Serranía de San Lucas (SSL), un área poco estudiada del norte de los Andes colombianos identificada como una prioridad urgente de conservación. Para esto, evaluamos la influencia de la elevación, la estructura del bosque, la accesibilidad humana y la integridad del ecosistema sobre la ocurrencia de estas especies. Registramos 24 especies de mamíferos M–G, cinco de las cuales son de importancia global o nacional para la conservación: la danta de tierras bajas, el jaguar, el oso hormiguero gigante, el oso andino y el capuchino cariblanco variado. Mediante modelos espaciales de ocupación multiespecie, identificamos la elevación y el Índice de Integridad Forestal (Forest Integrity Index, FII) como los predictores más importantes del uso del hábitat. La mayoría de especies presentaron sus mayores probabilidades de ocurrencia en elevaciones intermedias, lo que sugiere la existencia de un pico de diversidad de mamíferos M–G en niveles intermedios del gradiente altitudinal. Varias especies respondieron positivamente a la integridad del bosque, siendo las especies terrestres amenazadas las que mostraron las asociaciones más fuertes. Nuestros resultados sugieren que el FII es un predictor valioso de la ocurrencia de mamíferos M–G y un objetivo relevante para estrategias de conservación y restauración forestal. Este trabajo destaca la importancia de la SSL como un refugio crítico para especies que han sido extirpadas de otras regiones y subraya la importancia de implementar medidas de conservación a gran escala que mantengan la integridad del bosque y minimicen la perturbación humana a lo largo de todo el gradiente altitudinal.

##### **Peer-Reviewed Literature Citation 2 of 4**

Millicent, O. O., A. C. Jonah, A. D. Chinedu, U. A. Kenneth, **O. C. C. Sanctus** and O. D. F. Chinyelu (2026). "Assessment of environmentally suitable sites for solid waste sanitary landfill using analytical hierarchy process (AHP) and GIS in Uyo and environs, South-South Nigeria." *Smart Construction and Sustainable Cities* 4(1), e18. <https://doi.org/10.1007/s44268-026-00098-6>

Abstract: Rapid urban growth in the Global South makes it harder to choose infrastructure corridors, especially in sensitive coastal basins. This study introduces a spatial decision-support framework tailored to local conditions. It combines the Delphi technique, Analytical Hierarchy Process (AHP), and Geographic Information Systems (GIS) to improve sanitary landfill site selection in Uyo and nearby areas in South-South Nigeria. The region sits on the highly permeable Benin Formation and gets heavy annual rainfall of 2,500 mm. Ten environmental experts participated in a three-round Delphi process to agree on key parameters, which were subsequently measured using a pairwise AHP matrix to ensure consistency (CR < 0.10). Hydrogeological factors, mainly Lithology and Soil Permeability (31.4%), were given the greatest weight, followed by infrastructure and proximity factors. Using Weighted Linear Combination (WLC), the spatial analysis showed a strong urban buffer effect: only 210.5 km2 (9.2%) of the 2,289.41 km2 area is classified as “Highly Suitable” for engineering, mostly in remote parts of Ikono, Ibiono, Uruan, and Etinan. The rest of the land is limited by required exclusion zones around growing peri-urban homes (1,000 m) and surface drainage networks (500 m). The model was checked with fifteen independent ground-truth points, showing an overall accuracy of 86.67% and a Cohen’s Kappa coefficient (ǩ) of 0.762, which means there was strong spatial agreement. The findings show that standard site selection methods often underestimate aquifer risks in tropical sedimentary areas. The protocol developed here offers a practical framework for infrastructure planning in humid, vulnerable regions with limited data.

##### **Peer-Reviewed Literature Citation 3 of 4**

Rey Faura, D., **A. Raya Rey**, K. Pütz and **S. Harris** (2026). "From individual movement patterns to colony-level costs: Foraging energetics of Magellanic penguins (*Spheniscus magellanicus*) at the southern edge of their distribution." *Polar Biology* 49(3), e97. <https://doi.org/10.1007/s00300-026-03536-4>

Abstract: The energetic costs associated with foraging activity were quantified for breeding Magellanic penguins from Martillo Island, located in the Beagle Channel, Tierra del Fuego, Argentina (54°54′ S, 67°23′ W). Individuals were equipped in 2023–2024 with multi-sensor biologging devices that recorded body acceleration, pressure and location during the early chick-rearing period. These data were used to characterize the structure of foraging trips and rates of energy expenditure and later upscaled to estimate prey-intake of the whole colony. Foraging trips were found to last slightly less than one day and to cover up to more than a hundred kilometers within the Beagle Channel. Estimates of metabolic power, derived from Overall Dynamic Body Acceleration (ODBA), indicated relatively consistent energetic expenditure rates among individuals (~ 63 W), although total energy expenditure increased with trip duration up to 7000 kJ per trip. Diving patterns showed that foraging activity occurred throughout most of the transit and central phase of trips, suggesting that no clear separation between those occur, whereas higher travel speeds defined the return to the colony. Energetic estimates were subsequently converted into prey consumption requirements to evaluate the trophic demand generated by breeding adults. When extrapolated to the colony scale, these requirements indicate a substantial energy flow (6–15 tons of prey) from local marine resources to the penguin population. These results highlight the ecological importance of the Beagle Channel as a productive feeding environment supporting this colony and other seabird populations.

##### **Peer-Reviewed Literature Citation 4 of 4**

Sousa, L. L., R. Kotze, L. Fanikiso, ..., **R. Lines** et al. (2026). "Multispecies transboundary landscape connectivity in the KAZA TFCA." *Scientific Reports* 16(1), e24330. <https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-026-58440-y>

Abstract: This study aimed to delineate multi-species corridors across the KAZA landscape to be included in land use planning and identify which wildlife dispersal areas (WDA) are most critical for seven key mammal species across KAZA. For each species, we modelled habitat suitability across KAZA using ~ 48,000 occurrence points, from both camera trap and spoor surveys. Data from different sources were individually analysed, combined in an ensemble model and final outputs overlayed to form a multi-species layer, with which we assessed connectivity identifying core areas (KDE), corridors (LCP) and functional habitat in KAZA. The central KAZA region, from the Okavango Delta and Chobe National Park to Hwange National Park, supports the most extensive, well-connected core habitat for multiple species. Connectivity weakens toward the Sebungwe region, Angola, Namibia, and Kafue due to major rivers, veterinary fences, and growing human settlement/development. However, substantial highly suitable habitat occurs outside protected areas, with some WDAs playing disproportionately important roles in sustaining species’ connectivity. No single species serves as an umbrella for others when identifying critical corridors, making multi-species analyses essential for comprehensive conservation planning. Protecting corridors and core areas across KAZA depends largely on land uses outside protected areas, underscoring the need to integrate multi-species corridors into land-use planning and to promote coexistence between people and wildlife.

### **Grey Literature and Prepublication Citations**

##### **Grey Literature and Prepublication Citation 1 of 3**

Burgos-Camargo, C. G., J. D. González-Trujillo, **S. López-Casas**, **M. Rodríguez-Rocha** and **M. A. Santana-Tobar** (2026). *Macroinvertebrados Acuáticos de los Andes Tropicales: Guía Ilustrada para el Monitoreo Comunitario*. Bogota, Colombia: Wildlife Conservation Society, Colombia and Universidad Nacional de Colombia. [https://library.wcs.org/en-us/Scientific-Research/Research-Publications/Publications-Library/ctl/view/mid/40093/pubid/PUB41098.aspx](/en-us/Scientific-Research/Research-Publications/Publications-Library/ctl/view/mid/40093/pubid/PUB41098.aspx)

Abstract: Los ríos, quebradas y caños albergan una gran diversidad de formas de vida que nos dan señales sobre el estado de salud de estos ecosistemas. A través de los organismos que habitan en el agua, es posible determinar qué tan conservados se encuentran estos ambientes y detectar los efectos de actividades humanas como la deforestación, la expansión agrícola y urbana, o el vertimiento de residuos. Entre estos organismos se encuentran los macroinvertebrados acuáticos, pequeños animales visibles a simple vista que pasan al menos una etapa de su vida en el agua. Su presencia, abundancia y diversidad permiten evaluar la calidad del agua, ya que algunos grupos son sensibles a las alteraciones del ambiente, mientras que otros pueden tolerar condiciones más degradadas. En Colombia, los ríos andinos son ecosistemas fundamentales para el bienestar de numerosas comunidades, pues proveen agua, alimento y múltiples beneficios ambientales. Sin embargo, enfrentan transformaciones profundas que afectan su funcionamiento ecológico y ponen en riesgo la biodiversidad, la salud humana y las actividades productivas y recreativas que dependen de ellos. En este contexto, el monitoreo comunitario se consolida como una herramienta clave para la observación, el cuidado y la protección de los ecosistemas acuáticos. La participación activa de las comunidades fortalece el conocimiento local, permite identificar cambios tempranos en los ríos y promueve su protección. Esta guía ha sido elaborada para apoyar a las comunidades locales en el reconocimiento de la integridad de los ecosistemas a través del monitoreo participativo con macroinvertebrados acuáticos. Su contenido ofrece herramientas prácticas y accesibles para reconocer estos organismos y comprender su utilidad como indicadores de la salud de los ecosistemas andinos. Asimismo, está diseñada para apoyar su identificación a nivel de orden y familia mediante una metodología clara y fácil de aplicar. Es importante aclarar que esta cartilla incluye únicamente las familias más comúnmente encontradas en ríos y quebradas andinas, por lo que no pretende abarcar la totalidad de la diversidad presente en estos ecosistemas. En caso de surgir dudas o de registrarse hallazgos de organismos no descritos aquí, se recomienda acudir a la Red Colombiana de Limnología, donde personas expertas podrán brindar orientación técnica y apoyo especializado para determinar con mayor precisión los organismos observados.

##### **Grey Literature and Prepublication Citation 2 of 3**

**Germaná, C.**, **C. Alvarez** and **A. Cóndor** (2026). *Guía para la Identificación y Reporte de Otras Medidas Efectivas de Conservación Basadas en Áreas (OMEC) del Perú*. Lima, Peru: Wildlife Conservation Society, Peru. [https://library.wcs.org/en-us/Scientific-Research/Research-Publications/Publications-Library/ctl/view/mid/40093/pubid/PUB41097.aspx](/en-us/Scientific-Research/Research-Publications/Publications-Library/ctl/view/mid/40093/pubid/PUB41097.aspx)

Abstract: El Marco Mundial de Biodiversidad de Kunming-Montreal (MMBK-M), adoptado en la COP 15 de Biodiversidad celebrada en diciembre del 2022 en Montreal, establece objetivos y metas ambiciosas para detener y revertir la perdida de la biodiversidad a nivel global. La Meta 3 – también conocida como meta 30x30 - plantea que al menos el 30% de las zonas terrestres, de aguas continentales y de las zonas marinas y costeras sea conservado y gestionado eficazmente mediante diversos esquemas de conservación para el 2030. Entre estos esquemas se encuentran las Otras Medidas Efectivas de Conservación Basadas en Áreas (OMEC), que comprenden distintas formas de gestión del territorio que, de manera directa o indirecta, conservan biodiversidad. Para que un área puede ser reconocida y reportada como OMEC, el Convenio de Diversidad Biológica (CDB) ha establecido un conjunto de criterios adoptados en el Perú a través de la Resolución Ministerial N.º 339-2023-MINAM, que aprueba los lineamientos para el reporte de OMEC del Perú a la Base de Datos Mundial sobre OMEC En el Perú existen diversas modalidades de gestión del territorio - tanto a nivel normativo como en implementación - que pueden ser consideradas y reportadas como OMEC; por ello, en el caso Peruano, una OMEC es la oportunidad de reconocer esfuerzos de conservación existentes fuera de áreas protegidas, contribuyendo así a la meta global y a la Estrategia Nacional de Diversidad Biológica al 2050. Luego de unos años de evaluar un gran número de áreas bajo distintas modalidades existentes en la Amazonía y en los Andes, desde WCS consideramos pertinente compartir las metodologías, herramientas y procesos requeridos desarrollados entre el MINAM, SERFOR, INIA y distintos aliados de la sociedad civil, con otras instituciones o personas interesadas en aportar a la meta 30x30 desde el Perú. En ese sentido, la presente guía busca orientar a los gestores de estas áreas su proceso de evaluación y reporte como OMEC, sobre la base de los procedimientos establecidos por el Ministerio de Ambiente y las herramientas que se vienen utilizando. La guía se estructura en tres capítulos. El primero presenta el marco general en el que se desarrolla este proceso. El segundo aborda la importancia, definición y criterios que permiten identificar a las OMEC. Finalmente, el tercero describe las herramientas y procedimientos necesarios para la identificación y reporte de una OMEC en el Perú. Este contenido está complementado con tutoriales disponibles en línea para brindar mayor precisión y apoyo práctico a lo largo del proceso.

This is a Wildlife Conservation Society (WCS) Library webpage showcasing WCS-authored research publications, organized by week with the most recent publications listed first. The page highlights three weekly periods of publications from 2026.

**WCS-AUTHORED PUBLICATIONS, 10-16 August 2026** (4 peer-reviewed, 3 grey literature):
- Botero-Cañola et al. studied medium-large mammals in Colombia's Serranía de San Lucas using camera traps, finding elevation and Forest Integrity Index as key predictors of habitat use. Documented 24 species including 5 of conservation concern.
- Millicent et al. developed a GIS-based framework for landfill site selection in Nigeria, finding only 9.2% of the study area suitable.
- Rey Faura et al. quantified foraging energetics of Magellanic penguins in Argentina's Beagle Channel, estimating colony prey intake of 6-15 tons.
- Sousa et al. delineated multi-species corridors across the KAZA TFCA landscape, finding central KAZA provides the best-connected habitat.
- Grey literature includes guides on aquatic macroinvertebrates for community monitoring (Colombia), OECM identification (Peru), and a study on avian biodiversity offsets in Uganda.

**WCS-AUTHORED PUBLICATIONS, 3-9 August 2026** (10 peer-reviewed):
- Arona & Schiavini studied feral dogs in Tierra del Fuego, finding a 230% increase in dog detections over 5 years and 66% decline in chilla foxes.
- Hill et al. examined gendered perceptions of resilience in Fijian communities post-Cyclone Winston.
- King et al. piloted community-based zoonotic disease surveillance in rural Alaska (COHNA project).
- Marchenkova et al. documented Far Eastern leopard population recovery in Russia, with density increasing nearly threefold (0.89 to 2.64/100km²).
- Negret et al. evaluated area-based governance mechanisms for achieving GBF goals, finding protected areas most effective at reducing deforestation (49-53%).
- Noguera et al. developed a theory of change for wildlife health surveillance globally.
- Wallace et al. studied giant anteater activity patterns in Bolivia, finding diurnal behavior in forests (81.1%) but nocturnal in grasslands (66.5%).
- Other studies cover wild pigs in Alberta, civet interactions in Cambodia, and ringed seal haul-out behavior in the Arctic.

**WCS-AUTHORED PUBLICATIONS, 20 July-2 August 2026** (9 peer-reviewed):
- Bedriñana-Romano et al. challenged fin whale migratory assumptions off South America, documenting a "seasonally inverted migration."
- Bielmyer-Fraser et al. found anthropogenic microparticles in all 35 white shark fecal samples tested.
- Forero-Medina et al. presented CONTRAFACTUAL, a tool for counterfactual analysis of conservation areas in Colombia.
- Claire et al. studied tail-directed abnormal repetitive behaviors in zoo felids, with 6.5% overall prevalence and highest in clouded leopards (30%) and jaguars (28%).
- Hayes et al. found high temperatures alter core behaviors of mountain goats, a cold-adapted species.
- Other studies include an IUCN assessment of furrowed wood turtles, and fin whale migration research.

_Animal Conservation_ provides a forum for rapid publication of novel, peer-reviewed research into the conservation of animal species and their habitats. Subjects covered include conservation translocations, population biology, epidemiology, evolutionary ecology, population genetics, biodiversity, biogeography, palaeobiology and conservation economics. The journal is essential reading for conservation biologists, policy-makers and students.

### [Habitat Fragmentation Drives Disappearance of Specialised Forest Birds in Tropical Urban Landscapes, While Omnivores Thrive at the Forest Edge](https://zslpublications.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/acv.70097 "Habitat Fragmentation Drives Disappearance of Specialised Forest Birds in Tropical Urban Landscapes, While Omnivores Thrive at the Forest Edge")

[Sharifah Nur Atikah](https://zslpublications.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/authored-by/Atikah/Sharifah+Nur),[Muhammad Syafiq Yahya](https://zslpublications.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/authored-by/Yahya/Muhammad+Syafiq),[Kang Woei Ong](https://zslpublications.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/authored-by/Ong/Kang+Woei),[Ruzana Sanusi](https://zslpublications.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/authored-by/Sanusi/Ruzana),[Ahmad Razi Norhisham](https://zslpublications.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/authored-by/Norhisham/Ahmad+Razi),[Badrul Azhar](https://zslpublications.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/authored-by/Azhar/Badrul),

*   First Published: 11 August 2026

#### Graphical Abstract

[![Image 11: Habitat Fragmentation Drives Disappearance of Specialised Forest Birds in Tropical Urban Landscapes, While Omnivores Thrive at the Forest Edge Issue , ](https://zslpublications.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/cms/asset/2dcda28e-5c74-4da7-ac77-15e7602f6709/acv70097-toc-0001-m.jpg)](https://zslpublications.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/cms/asset/2dcda28e-5c74-4da7-ac77-15e7602f6709/acv70097-toc-0001-m.jpg "Show full-size graphical abstract")
This study assessed the impact of habitat fragmentation on avian assemblages by comparing four urban forest fragments to a contiguous tropical rainforest in Greater Kuala Lumpur, Malaysia. The results indicate that while contiguous forests are irreplaceable for supporting high species richness and forest interior specialists, fragmented patches can still maintain comparable feeding guild abundances through species turnover. Ultimately, integrating landscape-scale planning with targeted microhabitat interventions, such as preserving native fruiting trees and understory complexity, can significantly enhance the supplementary conservation value of these urban remnants.

[![Image 12: Jaguar Conservation Units as an Effective Tool in a Payment for Ecosystem Services Scheme for an Apex Predator Issue , ](https://zslpublications.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/cms/asset/d8a794f7-ba05-4ec1-b331-b3932cc81347/acv70094-toc-0001-m.jpg)](https://zslpublications.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/cms/asset/d8a794f7-ba05-4ec1-b331-b3932cc81347/acv70094-toc-0001-m.jpg "Show full-size graphical abstract")
Jaguar Conservation Units can be operationalized by linking confirmed breeding populations to rural property boundaries, creating transparent spatial units for conservation action and payments for ecosystem services. Applied to Mato Grosso do Sul, Brazil, the framework delineated three operational JCUs encompassing 14,197 rural properties and estimated annual livestock losses from jaguar predation at approximately US$13.1 million. Linking payments to legal compliance, habitat retention, conflict mitigation and jaguar monitoring offers a scalable pathway for coexistence in privately owned landscapes.

[Lauren J. Moore](https://zslpublications.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/authored-by/Moore/Lauren+J.),[Silviu O. Petrovan](https://zslpublications.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/authored-by/Petrovan/Silviu+O.),[Adam J. Bates](https://zslpublications.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/authored-by/Bates/Adam+J.),[Helen L. Hicks](https://zslpublications.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/authored-by/Hicks/Helen+L.),[Philip J. Baker](https://zslpublications.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/authored-by/Baker/Philip+J.),[Sarah E. Perkins](https://zslpublications.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/authored-by/Perkins/Sarah+E.),[David E. Wembridge](https://zslpublications.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/authored-by/Wembridge/David+E.),[Richard W. Yarnell](https://zslpublications.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/authored-by/Yarnell/Richard+W.),

*   First Published: 28 July 2026

#### Graphical Abstract

[![Image 15: Beyond the Individual: Multisite Population-Level Consequences of Road Mortality on a Declining Mammal Issue , ](https://zslpublications.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/cms/asset/4e16d581-acaf-44ca-9e4c-34c53b902c79/acv70082-toc-0001-m.jpg)](https://zslpublications.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/cms/asset/4e16d581-acaf-44ca-9e4c-34c53b902c79/acv70082-toc-0001-m.jpg "Show full-size graphical abstract")
We used a comparative study design to quantify population densities, structure, survival, cause-specific mortality and female productivity in four West-European hedgehog (Erinaceus europaeus) populations, and to forecast the impact of road mortality on population viability. Losses to road mortality were offset by juvenile recruitment and survival in relatively large (> 36 individuals) populations, but not in smaller (< 15 individuals) populations. Population viability was unaffected by current road mortality rates in the largest populations. In contrast, simulations of current road mortality in the two smallest populations halved their population sizes in five years and accelerated the time to extinction by up to 18 years compared to baseline scenarios with no road mortality. However, simulations of 40% annual proportional loss to road mortality catalysed declines in all four populations. This study demonstrates that even low road mortality rates may have detrimental effects for small populations with low per-capita growth.

[![Image 18: The Dilemma of Ground-Nesting Bird Conservation Impacted by Rewilded Megaherbivore Populations Issue , ](https://zslpublications.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/cms/asset/59057ab3-4cb7-4094-8543-e6e84ebb6d79/acv70090-toc-0001-m.jpg)](https://zslpublications.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/cms/asset/59057ab3-4cb7-4094-8543-e6e84ebb6d79/acv70090-toc-0001-m.jpg "Show full-size graphical abstract")
The “disturbance-predation trade-off” framework explaining divergent reproductive fates of ground-nesting birds under Milu rewilding disturbance. The reintroduction of the flagship species, Père David’s deer (Milu, Elaphurus davidianus), at the Jiangsu Dafeng Milu National Nature Reserve has generated an unforeseen “ecological trap” paradox for sympatric ground-nesting waterbirds. Following habitat transformation engineered by the expanding Milu population, the ground-nesting avifauna exhibited a striking divergence in nest-site selection. Species such as the Little Tern (Sternula albifrons), Common Tern (Sterna hirundo), and Kentish Plover (Anarhynchus alexandrinus) selected bare-ground nesting sites in habitats with residual deer populations. Conversely, Saunders’s Gull (Saundersilarus saundersi) nested solitarily and exclusively in dense seepweed grounds remote from deer-occupied areas. Infrared camera monitoring revealed that while deer activity presents a conspicuous physical disturbance and trampling risk, their presence establishes a “biological shield” (predator deterrent zone) that drives predator avoidance among dominant avian species like the Oriental Magpie (Pica pica) and Grey-headed Lapwing (Vanellus cinereus). By balancing this “disturbance-predation trade-off” and amplifying collective defense, the mixed-colony nesters maintained a 68.75% combined nest survival rate. In sharp contrast, the solitary-nesting strategy of Saunders’s Gulls to avoid deer exposed them to a lethal predator community (including rats, feral dogs, and snakes), while the dense vegetation inadvertently reduced their early-warning capabilities, culminating in a catastrophic 0% reproductive success. These findings underscore that single-species recovery metrics can mask significant ecological dysfunction among sympatric taxa. Consequently, conservation frameworks must transition from single-species metrics to multi-taxa management, strategically deploying a “habitat mosaic by design” with low- to moderate-deer activity buffer zones to optimize predator deterrence while minimizing trampling risks.

Headstarting, involving the collection of wild early life-stage individuals, rearing them in captivity, and releasing them into a new or existing population once independent, has recently been identified as a potential translocation technique to assist small breeding populations of waders declining due to low levels of productivity. # Elephants Live Longer in the Wild, Study Shows

![African Elephant on the river bank](/sites/default/files/2024-12/E7GW73%20%281%29.jpg)

### General Inquiries

[[email protected]](/cdn-cgi/l/email-protection#92f3f4e0fbf1f3fce5fbfef6fefbf4f7d2f3e5f4bcfde0f5)

Tel:+254 711 063 000

Ngong Road, Karen, P.O. Box 310  
 00502 Nairobi, Kenya

Elephants have a much longer lifespan in the wild than in captivity, according to a new study from Science.

The study, which compared female African elephants in [Kenya's](https://www.awf.org/where-we-work/kenya) Amboseli National Park with those in zoos, found that the wild elephants lived three times as long on average, surviving to a median age of 56 years compared with 17 years for elephants living in captivity. The findings were similar for Asian elephants kept in captivity to support the logging industry.

Common health problems for elephants in zoos include herpes, tuberculosis, arthritis, and obesity. The effect of captivity on this highly intelligent, social and wide-ranging species also likely has psychological effects, as sometimes evidenced by unusual aggressiveness or repetitive behaviors.

The findings of this study highlight the importance of implementing conservation strategies that ensure elephants and other species have the space and resources they need to thrive. Through its Africa Heartland Program, AWF works to combine parks, private lands and community areas into large conservation landscapes that give elephants and other wildlife the room they need to thrive. It is our belief that such [large-landscape conservation](https://www.awf.org/living-with-wildlife) is the soundest strategy for securing the future of Africa's magnificent wildlife across the continent.

# Wild Elephants Live Longer Than Their Zoo Counterparts

Wild elephants in protected areas of Africa and Asia live more than twice as long as those in European zoos, a new study has found.

ByMaryann Mott

Published December 11, 2008

•4 min read

Wild [elephants](http://animals.nationalgeographic.com/animals/article/elephants-index.html) in protected areas of Africa and Asia live more than twice as long as those in European zoos, a new study has found.

Animal welfare advocates have long clashed with zoo officials over concerns about the physical and mental health of elephants in captivity.

British and Canadian scientists who conducted the six-year study say their finding puts an end to that debate once and for all.

"We're worried that the whole system basically doesn't work and improving it is essential," said lead author Georgia Mason, a zoologist at the University of Guelph in Canada.

Obesity and stress are likely factors for the giant land mammals' early demise in captivity, she said.

Until these problems are resolved, the authors are calling for a halt to importing wild elephants and breeding them in facilities unless an institution can guarantee long, healthy lives for its elephants. The study will be published tomorrow in the journal *Science*.

(Related: ["Zoo Life Shortens Elephant Lives in Europe, Study Says"](http://news.nationalgeographic.com/news/2002/10/1025_021025_Elephants.html) [October 25, 2002].)

## Wild and Long-Lived

Mason and colleagues looked at data from more than 4,500 wild and captive African and Asian elephants.

The data include elephants in European zoos, which house about half of the world's captive elephants; protected populations in Amboseli National Park in [Kenya](https://www.nationalgeographic.com/travel/destination/kenya); and the Myanma Timber Enterprise in [Myanmar (Burma)](https://www.nationalgeographic.com/travel/destination/myanmar-burma), a government-run logging operation where Asian elephants are put to work.

Only the survival rates of females were analyzed because of their importance to future populations.

The findings show that captive elephants live considerably shorter lives.

For [African elephants](https://www.nationalgeographic.com/animals/mammals/facts/african-elephant), the median life span is 17 years for zoo-born females, compared to 56 years in the Amboseli National Park population.

For [Asian elephants](https://www.nationalgeographic.com/animals/mammals/facts/asian-elephant), the results are "much more worrying because they are the rarer of the two species," Mason said.

Zoo females only live 19 years—about half the life span of the Myanma timber elephants, which, on average, survive until 42.

What's more, the team discovered that Asian elephants bred and born in captivity died earlier than those imported into zoos from the wild.

"That really surprised us," Mason said.

"Something is happening very, very early in life in these zoo animals, and it's got to be happening before the age of three or four … the average age when wild-caught animals arrive in [zoos]."

Mason doesn't know why captive-bred elephants are dying sooner than their wild-caught counterparts.

But if healthy adults are not able to live long enough reproduce, then the captive populations in Europe won't be self-sustaining—a problem that American zoos already face.

## Survival Strategies

To keep zoo elephants alive longer, the authors recommend routine screening for obesity (something that's done in U.S. captive elephant populations), as well as monitoring stress via a chemical known as interleukin-6.

Checking this biological marker, which shows that the body's immune system is battling sickness, would allow zoo officials to intervene before the animal is seriously ill, Mason said.

Robert Wiese, collections director at the San Diego Zoo in California, was not part of this study. He said making a comparison between the lifespan of captive and wild elephants may seem deceptively simple.

"There are just so many confounding issues, especially in small sample sizes [of] zoo animals, that it's hard to really separate and make sure you're comparing apples to apples," he said.

## Huge Improvements

In 2004 Wiese co-authored a paper in the journal *Zoo Biology* showing the opposite of Mason's findings: that zoo elephants live as long as those in the wild.

He said that within the last decade accredited facilities have made huge improvements in the care of captive elephants by providing better nutrition to combat obesity, as well as environmental enrichment activities that reduce stress.

"Typically anti-zoo critics throw … in our face the things that the zoo community has already identified as issues that we need to work on," Wiese said.
