args.summary:
The Whale Sanctuary Project webpage compiles scientific research and publications documenting the negative welfare impacts of captivity on cetaceans (whales, dolphins, and porpoises). Key resources include:

- A major review paper in *PeerJ* (October 2025) by Lori Marino PhD and colleagues showing that despite incremental improvements, most captive cetaceans continue to suffer from major welfare problems in marine parks and zoos.
- A January 2024 white paper on orca welfare at Loro Parque Zoo, documenting early deaths, mishandled breeding, self-harming stereotypies, and hyperaggression.
- A September 2021 paper in *Reviews in the Neurosciences* on how impoverished captive environments affect cetacean and elephant brains.
- A 2020 presentation on neuroethical issues of keeping large mammals in captivity for entertainment.
- A June 2019 article in *Journal of Veterinary Behavior* on chronic stress in captive orcas, linking it to effects on the brain and immune system.
- A July 2018 article in *Nature's Newsletter* by Dr. Marino arguing that "the nature of orcas and other cetaceans is entirely incompatible with life in the tanks."
- Policy papers on dolphin-human interaction programs and a 2011 *PLoS ONE* paper proposing non-captive research methods for cetacean cognition.

The overarching message is that scientific evidence consistently demonstrates poor welfare, short lifespans, and psychological/physical ailments in captive cetaceans, supporting the need for alternatives like sea sanctuaries.

## Abstract

Orcas are large, deep-diving cetaceans who are known for their global distribution, wide-ranging behavior, intelligence, and social complexity. They possess one of the largest and most complex [brains](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/agricultural-and-biological-sciences/protocerebrum) in the mammalian kingdom. However, they are the third most common species of cetaceans kept in aquariums and marine theme parks. Most spend many years, and sometimes decades, in captivity. At the time of writing, 60 individuals are held in concrete tanks globally. The scientific data on how both wild-caught and captive-born orcas fare in captivity are increasingly robust in demonstrating that they cannot thrive under artificial circumstances in concrete tanks. In captivity, orcas exhibit a wide range of abnormal behaviors and often die at an early age from infections and other health conditions that are uncommon in a wild setting. Though numerous papers and reports describe these adverse effects, they do not offer a clear and systematic explanation for why captive orcas suffer chronic stress and how it affects their well-being. We describe likely mechanisms for the high levels of morbidity and mortality in captive orcas, including the impact of chronic stress on physiology and illness. We conclude that orcas are poor candidates for maintenance in captivity and suggest that a radical shift is required in their treatment, to meet their complex needs.

## Introduction

Orcas (_Orcinus orca_, also known as killer whales) are part of the worldwide commercial trade in cetaceans and are the third most commonly confined cetacean species after bottlenose dolphins (_Tursiops truncatus_) and beluga whales (_Delphinapterus leucas_). As of January 2019, 60 orcas were held in concrete tanks globally ([www.orcahome.de/orcastat](http://www.orcahome.de/orcastat), last accessed 11 January 2019). A slight majority (56.7%) were born in captivity, and a further 26 were captured at a very young age; 18 of these captured animals were recently taken from Russian waters. Most of these individuals have spent years, and sometimes decades, in captivity ([www.orcahome.de/orcastat](http://www.orcahome.de/orcastat)).

Despite decades of advances in veterinary care and husbandry (Gulland et al., 2018), cetaceans in captive facilities (e.g., marine theme parks, aquariums, zoos) consistently display behavioral and physiological signs of stress and frequently succumb to premature death by infection or other health conditions. The breadth of available scientific data demonstrates that, by every appropriate metric, captive orcas do not fare as well as their free-ranging counterparts (e.g., Woodley et al., 1997, Small and Demaster, 1995, Jett and Ventre, 2015, Robeck et al., 2015).

In this study, we summarize how orcas are especially vulnerable to the negative effects of the constricted artificial environments they experience in marine theme parks, aquariums, and zoos. First, we describe the complex needs of orcas based on their evolutionary history, brain anatomy, physiology, and cognitive-behavioral characteristics. Then we describe the morbidity and mortality patterns seen in captivity, as well as how these patterns are associated with a failure to meet the complex needs of this species. We conclude by describing mechanisms that could explain the relationship between conditions of captivity, stress, and the high rates of morbidity and mortality observed in captive orcas.

Generally, individuals who experience greater enclosure complexity express higher diversity of behaviours and show better physiological well-being. However, positive outcomes of providing habitat complexity should be species-specific, and not all species would benefit from it. Thus, it is important to provide and constantly evaluate the habitat complexity of zoo animals. Complexity can change temporally and spatially. We discuss in this paper how habitat complexity can positively influence animal welfare, and provide some ideas on how to add habitat complexity and functional structures for captive animals. The complexity of the habitat refers to its physical geometry, which includes abiotic and biotic elements. Habitat complexity is important because it allows more species to coexist and, consequently, more interactions to be established among them. The complexity of the habitat links the physical structure of the enclosure to the biological interactions, which occur within its limits. Enclosure complexity should vary temporally, to be able to influence the animals in different ways, depending on the period of the day and season and throughout the year. In the present paper, we discuss how habitat complexity is important, and how it can positively influence the physical and mental states of zoo animals. args.summary:
This is a review article published in the Journal of Veterinary Behavior (January–February 2020, Volume 35, Pages 69-82) titled "The harmful effects of captivity and chronic stress on the well-being of orcas (Orcinus orca)." The authors include Lori Marino, Naomi A. Rose, Ingrid N. Visser, Heather Rally, Hope Ferdowsian, and Veronica Slootsky.

The article argues that orcas are poor candidates for captivity due to their large, complex brains, wide-ranging behavior, social complexity, and deep-diving nature. As of January 2019, 60 orcas were held in concrete tanks globally, with 56.7% born in captivity and 26 captured at a very young age. Orcas are the third most commonly confined cetacean species after bottlenose dolphins and beluga whales.

Key findings include:
- Captive orcas exhibit a wide range of abnormal behaviors and often die at an early age from infections and health conditions uncommon in wild settings.
- A 1979 review showed infectious diseases were the primary cause of death in captive orcas, a pattern that remains largely unchanged.
- Between 1971 and 2017, there were 35 documented orca deaths at SeaWorld facilities alone.
- The authors describe mechanisms linking captivity conditions, chronic stress, and high rates of morbidity and mortality.
- The article concludes that orcas cannot thrive under artificial circumstances and that a radical shift in treatment is needed to meet their complex needs.

The paper has been cited by 42 sources as of the time of publication, and includes 237 references. It discusses orca evolution, phylogeny, brain anatomy, behavioral characteristics, causes of illness and death, and the association between stress, disorder, and death.

![Three dolphins performing at a theme park.](/cdn-cgi/image/width=1280,format=auto/siteassets/images/wildlife/wildlife-interactions/dolphins-performing-at-theme-park.jpeg)

# The Case Against Marine Mammals in Captivity

In *The Case Against Marine Mammals in Captivity* report, we provide scientific evidence and ethical arguments to support the case that it is unacceptable to house marine mammals in captivity for the purpose of public display and tourist entertainment.

[**Read the executive summary**](/siteassets/reports-programmatic/the_case_against_marine_mammals_in_captivity_5th_exec_summary_final_us.pdf "the_case_against_marine_mammals_in_captivity_5th_exec_summary_final_us.pdf")

[**Read the full report**](/siteassets/reports-programmatic/the-case-against-marine-mammals-in-captivity.pdf "The-Case-Against-Marine-Mammals-in-Captivity.pdf")

## Report Highlights

* Wild cetaceans (whales and dolphins) travel 40-100 miles a day, achieve speeds of 30 miles per hour, and dive hundreds of feet deep. Even in the largest facilities, they have less than 0.0001% (one millionth) of their natural habitat range.
* One 2014 study found that a captive male orca spent nearly 70% of his time virtually motionless.
* Captive marine mammals suffer from a huge range of health problems, including extreme stress, neurotic behaviors, and abnormal levels of aggression.
* Bottlenose dolphins are six times more likely to die immediately after capture from the wild and transfer between facilities.
* Annual mortality rates for captive orcas have improved over the years, but they still don’t match healthy populations in the wild.
* The number of ocean theme parks in China has jumped from 39 in 2015 to 76 in early 2019.
* Dolphin sea pen enclosures in Asia and the Caribbean are at extreme risk from hurricanes and tsunamis, and damage the environment, including coral reefs and mangroves.

### Interview with Dr Naomi Rose

Dr Rose is the report’s lead author and AWI’s marine mammal scientist.

### Captivity is cruel

Keeping marine mammals captive, whether taken from the wild or bred in captivity, causes immense physical and psychological suffering – from capture, to transport, to a lifelong existence in small barren tanks.

The inadequate space provided in captivity suppresses natural behaviors such as consistent cardiovascular exercise, foraging for prey, and social interaction with large groups of closely bonded pod mates.

![Orca in captivity.](/cdn-cgi/image/width=1280,format=auto/siteassets/images/wildlife/marine-wildlife/orcas-and-whales/orca-in-captivity.png) 

Orcas are among the most intelligent species on the planet. This orca, in a small barren holding tank, literally has nothing to do while they wait for their cue in the orca show.

> Marine mammals simply cannot thrive in captivity. Almost all marine mammal species are wide-ranging predators and the best we can provide for them are barren concrete boxes or small sea pen corrals.

### Profit over welfare

Marine mammal exhibits prioritize the needs of the visiting public and economic factors over the needs of the animals. Enclosures are designed to make the animals readily visible, not necessarily comfortable, and the efficiency of maintenance dictates slick surfaces as opposed to naturalistic textures and substrates.

Some facilities display marine mammals in sea pens rather than traditional aquariums. While sea pens simulate more natural conditions, they are subject to alternative problems such as noise pollution from boat traffic and coastal development, and physical pollution from land-based features such as runoff from roads and sewage outfall.

The habitat of marine mammals is difficult and frequently impossible to re-create.

![A young child petting dolphins.](/cdn-cgi/image/width=1280,format=auto/siteassets/images/wildlife/wildlife-interactions/young-child-petting-dolphins.png) 

Posing like this for a “photo op” with tourists is a completely unnatural behavior for dolphins. This is not education.

### Inadequate conditions lead to physical and mental suffering

* Stress-related conditions such as ulcers, stereotypical behaviors including pacing and self-mutilation, and abnormal aggression frequently develop in predators denied the opportunity to forage.
* Diseases afflict captive marine mammals more frequently or more intensely than their free-ranging counterparts; captive cetaceans have been known to suffer from infections not known to afflict wild dolphins.
* The public display industry is not transparent with veterinary records and publishes very few welfare-related studies in the scientific literature, despite having direct access to the relevant data.

Many facilities offer direct interaction with marine mammals through feeding sessions or attractions such as swimming with dolphins. These interactions endanger both the animals and the human participants by increasing the chances of disease transmission and physical injuries, as well as stress for the animals.

### The argument for education and conservation

The public display industry often justifies marine mammal exhibits by claiming that they serve a valuable educational function and that people learn important information from seeing live animals.

However, a study found that fewer than half of reviewed dolphinaria provided any information on conservation or provided educational materials for children or teachers.

It can also be argued that viewing captive animals gives the public a false picture of the animals’ natural lives. For example, many actions performed by dolphins in shows that are portrayed as “play” or “fun” are actually displays that in free-ranging animals would usually be considered aggressive or a sign of disturbance.

Similarly, it is often misleadingly claimed that marine mammal exhibits serve a valuable conservation function.

In reality, fewer than 5 to 10 percent of zoos, dolphinaria, and aquaria are involved in substantial conservation programs and the majority of marine mammals currently being bred in captivity are neither threatened nor endangered.

In fact, most captive-breeding programs simply ensure a supply of animals for display or trade, creating in many cases larger populations of animals with questionable genetic backgrounds.

It would appear that for dolphinaria and aquaria to state that they are actively involved in conservation is little more than a marketing tool or a way to justify imports of animals–particularly because the overwhelming majority of marine mammal species currently being bred in captivity is neither threatened nor endangered, including bottlenose dolphins.

> ## There is about as much educational benefit to be gained in studying dolphins in captivity as there would be studying mankind by only observing prisoners held in solitary confinement.

### Wildlife. Not Entertainers

The Case Against Marine Mammals in Captivity (CAMMIC) report is part of our global campaign to end the abuse and suffering of wild animals for tourist entertainment.

Around the world, hundreds of thousands of wild animals are trapped, confined, and forced to behave unnaturally to entertain tourists.

[**Explore Wildlife. Not Entertainers Campaign**](/take-action/wildlife-not-entertainers/)

![Mother and daughter riding a dolphin.](/cdn-cgi/image/width=1280,format=auto/siteassets/images/wildlife/wildlife-interactions/mother-and-daughter-riding-a-dolphin.png) 

Many people consider swimming with dolphins a thrill of a lifetime, but for the dolphins, it is just a job. As wild animals, they do not want to be with us as much as we want to be with them.

*Summary:*  
An adult female killer whale (*Orcinus orca*) was transported to the Port of Nagoya public aquarium in June 2010. While the animal was being maintained in the aquarium there was a gradual decrease in body weight. On October 1st, 2010 the whale exhibited signs of gastrointestinal disease and died on January 14th, 2011. At necropsy examination the gastric compartments were filled with a large number of variably-sized rocks (total weight 81.4 kg) and there was marked ulceration in the third compartment. There were multifocal tubercle-like nodules within the lungs and on sectioning there were numerous abscesses and pulmonary cavities. Microscopically, there was severe suppurative pneumonia associated with fungal hyphae that were infrequently septate and often branched. Numerous bacterial colonies were also present. The hyphae demonstrated immunohistochemical cross-reactivity with Rhizomucor spp. and Cunninghamella bertholletiae was cultured. Bacteriological culture revealed the presence of Proteus mirabilis, Pseudomonas aeruginosa and Pseudomonas oryzihabitans. This case represents the first documentation of zygomycosis associated with C. bertholletiae in a marine mammal.

*Summary:*Orca behaviors interacting with humans within apparent friendship bonds are reviewed, and some impediments to the human evaluation of delphinid intelligence are discussed. The subsequent involvement of these orcas and their offspring in aggressive incidents with humans is also documented and examined. This is particularly relevant given that the highest recorded rates of aggressive incidents have occurred among orcas who had previously established unstructured human friendship bonds prior to their inclusion within oceanaria performances. It is concluded that the confinement of orcas within aquaria, and their use in entertainment programs, is morally indefensible, given their high intelligence, complex behaviors, and the apparent adverse effects on orcas of such confinement and use.   
  
*Abstract:*   
Based on neuroanatomical indices such as brain size and encephalization quotient, orcas are among the most intelligent animals on Earth. They display a range of complex behaviors indicative of social intelligence, but these are difficult to study in the open ocean where protective laws may apply, or in captivity, where access is constrained for commercial and safety reasons. From 1979 to 1980, however, we were able to interact with juvenile orcas in an unstructured way at San Diego’s SeaWorld facility. We observed in the animals what appeared to be pranks, tests of trust, limited use of tactical deception, emotional self-control, and empathetic behaviors. Our observations were consistent with those of a former Seaworld trainer, and provide important insights into orca cognition, communication, and social intelligence. However, after being trained as performers within Seaworld’s commercial entertainment program, a number of orcas began to exhibit aggressive behaviors. The orcas who previously established apparent friendships with humans were most affected, although significant aggression also occurred in some of their descendants, and among the orcas they lived with. Such oceanaria confinement and commercial use can no longer be considered ethically defensible, given the current understanding of orcas’ advanced cognitive, social, and communicative capacities, and of their behavioral needs.

*Summary:*A bottlenose dolphin was tested on its ability to echoically discriminate horizontal angular differences between arrays of vertically oriented air-filled PVC rods. The blindfolded dolphin was required to station in a submerged hoop 2 radial m from the stimuli and indicate if an array with two rods (S+) was to the right or the left of a single rod (S-). The angular separation between the two rods (thetaw) was held constant within each experiment while the angle between the S+ and the S- stimuli (thetab) varied to produce angular differences (Deltatheta=thetab-thetaw) ranging from 0.25 to 4°. In experiment I, thetaw was maintained at 2° and in experiment II, thetaw was maintained at 4°. Resulting 75% correct thresholds (method of constant stimuli) were 1.5 and 0.7°, respectively. The two main findings of this study are: (1) decreasing the number of targets does not aid in localization, and (2) increasing the space between the rods enhances localization. Taken as a whole, the experiments suggest dolphins have a well-developed ability to resolve spatial information through sonar.

An approximately 10-yr-old male killer whale of Icelandic origin ("Keiko") developed bilateral axillary skin lesions soon after its arrival at a Mexico City oceanarium in 1985." ..."Studies are underway to characterize this presumptive viral disease and to address the potential immunological aspects of its pathogenesis. These studies include evaluation and characterization of the physiological and immunological status of the whale, isolation and characterization of the papilloma-associated virus, and subsequently the design and implementation of potential treatment regimens."   
  
*Note:*   
This report is noteworthy because it mentions the word "virus" in the title ("papillova*viral*-like") and throughout the paper, and it states that this virus is the "first case" found in a killer whale, strongly suggesting that Keiko was infected with a virus foreign to wild populations, without quite stating clearly that Keiko actually carried any virus. At the time the paper was written many spokespeople for the marine park industry were stating publicly that Keiko should never be released because he carried a contagious virus that could infect wild populations. In 1993, prior to this report, one of its authors, ([Cornell](http://www.orcanetwork.org/Main/index.php?categories_file=Captivity%20Studies#preliminary)), had written a report stating that Keiko's skin problems were the result of environmental stresses and not related to any virus. In 1998, after Bossart, *et al.*'s report was published, a group of six veterinarians and specialists appointed by the USDA examined Keiko and found him negative for 48 suspected viruses. (See [USDA](#Summary)) report, below.) Bossart, *et al.*'s frightening viral theory was apparently incorrect.

Bruck, Jason N. (2013). **Decades-long social memory in bottlenose dolphins**. Royal Society Publishing DOI: 10.1098/rspb.2013.1726 Published 7 August 2013.

ABSTRACT  
Long-term social memory is important, because it is an ecologically relevant test of cognitive capacity, it helps us understand which social relationships are remembered and it relates two seemingly disparate disciplines: cognition and sociality. For dolphins, long-term memory for conspecifics could help assess social threats as well as potential social or hunting alliances in a very fluid and complex fission–fusion social system, yet we have no idea how long dolphins can remember each other. Through a playback study conducted within a multi-institution dolphin breeding consortium (where animals are moved between different facilities), recognition of unfamiliar versus familiar signature whistles of former tank mates was assessed. This research shows that dolphins have the potential for lifelong memory for each other regardless of relatedness, sex or duration of association. This is, to my knowledge, the first study to show that social recognition can last for at least 20 years in a non-human species and the first large-scale study to address long-term memory in a cetacean. These results, paired with evidence from elephants and humans, provide suggestive evidence that sociality and cognition could be related, as a good memory is necessary in a fluid social system.

Hanna, Pepper, Beri Brown, Kelley Winship, Dianne Cameron, Heather M. Hill, and Stan Kuczaj II. (2017). **A Killer Whale’s (*Orcinus orca*) Response to Visual Media**. International Journal of Comparative Psychology, Issue 30.

ABSTRACT  
Environmental enrichment is critical for maintaining cognitive welfare for animals in human care, but is subject to individual preferences. The interest in a video-based enrichment was assessed for a single killer whale (*Orcinus orca*) in human care. The adult female was presented 20 video recordings featuring cetaceans, elephants, or humans with each video presented in two conditions: (1) with sound and (2) without sound. Four additional presentations in which the television displayed a blank screen served as controls. All sessions were videotaped and coded for time spent viewing the recordings, behavioral responses, and visual laterality. The killer whale spent significantly more time at the television when programs were on screen compared to when the television was present but blank. She was more likely to watch videos accompanied by sound than those presented without sound. Videos were more likely to be viewed monocularly rather than binocularly, with a right eye preference when viewing the videos the first time they were presented. The highest rates of behavioral responses occurred during videos of cetaceans. These results demonstrate that one killer whale responded to video recordings of different stimuli, suggesting that video recordings may be used as a form of enrichment for cetaceans and that not all video content and formats are equally interesting.

Herman, Louis M. (2005). **Intelligence and rational behavior in the Bottlenosed Dolphin**. In *Rational Animals*, Susan Hurley and Matthew Nudds, editors.

ABSTRACT  
A rational animal is defined as one that can perceive and represent how its world is structured and functions, and can make logical inferences and draw conclusions that enable it to function effectively and productively in that world. Further, a rational animal is able to incorporate new evidence into new perspectives of the world and can then modify its behaviours appropriately—in effect creating a new or revised model of the world in which it is immersed. Rational behaviour is necessarily built on the bedrock of general and specific intellectual capacity. Intelligence, a multidimensional trait, may appear to various degrees in various behavioural, cognitive, or social domains. Data and observations are presented on dolphin cognitive performance and on apparent rational responses within four intellectual domains within the context of a variety of empirical studies that we have conducted. These domains are: (a) the declarative (semantic or representational) domain (does the dolphin display knowledge or understanding about things?); (b) the procedural domain (does the dolphin exhibit competency in means, operations, or methods?); (c) the social domain (does the dolphin reveal social awareness and appropriate responsiveness in social interactions or relations?); and (d) the domain of the self (does the dolphin exhibit knowledge or awareness of itself?). In each case, the particular experimental paradigms are briefly outlined and instances of apparent inferenctial or creative acts within each paradigm are given.

Herman, L. M., Matus, D. S., Herman, E. Y. K., Ivancic, M., and Pack, A. A. (2001). **The Bottlenosed Dolphin's (*Tursiops truncatus*) Understanding of Gestures as Symbolic Representations of its Body Parts.** Animal Learning & Behavior, 29, 250-264.

ABSTRACT  
We assigned gestural symbols to nine different body parts of a bottlenosed dolphin (*Tursiops truncatus*) (rostrum, mouth, melon, pectoral fin, dorsal fin, side, belly, genitals, tail). The dolphin was first trained to touch any floating object it chose with the body part indicated by a gestural symbol. In Experiment 1, we tested the dolphin's ability to now touch specific gesturally referenced objects using specific gesturally referenced body parts. In Experiment 2, we tested its ability to either touch or toss gesturally referenced objects with gesturally referenced body parts, or to simply display those body parts, or shake them back and forth. The acts of touching, tossing, displaying, and shaking were each associated with specific gestures and appeared in random sequences within test sessions. The results demonstrated highly significant levels of performance throughout these tasks, including many successes on the first occasions of new body-part uses. These findings provided strong evidence that the gestural symbols we used for body parts were semantically processed and understood by the dolphin as representing those body parts. In addition, the dolphin's ability to use its different body parts in the same way (e.g., touching objects with each of the nine referenced body parts), and to use the same body part in different ways (e.g., displaying or shaking its dorsal fin, or touching or tossing objects with its dorsal fin), suggested a body-image representational system for conscious awareness and conscious control of body parts similar to that postulated for humans and revealed through human brain lesion studies.

Jacobs, Bob, Heather Rally, Catherine Doyle, Lester O’Brien, Mackenzie Tennison and Lori Marino. **Putative neural consequences of captivity for elephants and cetaceans.** [Reviews in the Neurosciences](https://www.degruyter.com/journal/key/revneuro/html), <https://doi.org/10.1515/revneuro-2021-0100>

ABSTRACT  
The present review assesses the potential neural impact of impoverished, captive environments on large-brained mammals, with a focus on elephants and cetaceans. These species share several characteristics, including being large, wide-ranging, long-lived, cognitively sophisticated, highly social, and large-brained mammals. Although the impact of the captive environment on physical and behavioral health has been well-documented, relatively little attention has been paid to the brain itself. Here, we explore the potential neural consequences of living in captive environments, with a focus on three levels: (1) The effects of environmental impoverishment/enrichment on the brain, emphasizing the negative neural consequences of the captive/impoverished environment; (2) the neural consequences of stress on the brain, with an emphasis on corticolimbic structures; and (3) the neural underpinnings of stereotypies, often observed in captive animals, underscoring dysregulation of the basal ganglia and associated circuitry. To this end, we provide a substantive hypothesis about the negative impact of captivity on the brains of large mammals (e.g., cetaceans and elephants) and how these neural consequences are related to documented evidence for compromised physical and psychological well-being.

John Jett, Jeffrey M. Ventre (2015). **Captive killer whale (*Orcinus orca*) survival.** Journal of Marine Mammal Science.

ABSTRACT  
Killer whales (*Orcinus orca*) were first placed into captivity in 1961 and are now found in theme parks around the world. Despite successful breeding of captive killer whales since 1985 there is growing concern for their welfare in captivity, which often includes claims of poor survival. We employed Kaplan-Meier and Cox Proportional hazards models and annual survival rate analyses on 201 captive killer whales to discern how sex, facility (U.S. vs. foreign), captive-born vs. wild-captured, pre- vs. post-1 January 1985, and animal age upon entering captivity affect survival. Overall median survival estimate was 6.1 yr, with no difference between male and female survival. Killer whales in U.S. facilities (12.0 yr) demonstrated a significantly higher median survival than those in foreign facilities (4.4 yr), as did whales entering captivity post-1 January 1985 (11.8 yr) vs. those entering prior to 1 January 1985 (3.9 yr). Median survival for captive-born (14.1 yr) was significantly higher than wild-captured killer whales (5.5 yr), though the two failed to differ among the post-1 January 1985 cohort. Facility location and pre- vs. post-1 January 1985 were predictors of the hazard rate. Survival of captive killer whale cohorts has generally improved through time, although survival to age milestones are poor when compared to wild killer whales.

John Jett, Jeffrey M. Ventre, Courtney S. Vail (2012). **Evidence of Lethal Mosquito Transmitted Viral Disease in Captive *Orcinus orca*.** Florida Marine Mammal Health Conference.

ABSTRACT  
Two recently discovered studies document the presence of viral diseases carried by a mosquito vector in captive killer whales, *Orcinus orca*. In both cases, the transmission of these diseases was implicated in the cause of death for these animals. In the first case, a 25-year-old male orca, Kanduke, died suddenly and unexpectedly in the summer of 1990 at Sea World of Florida in Orlando. The necropsy in this instance identified the St. Louis encephalitis virus as the cause of death. Buck et al (1993) subsequently wrote a peer-reviewed paper describing the presence of this avian virus in the tissue of Kanduke. In the second case , a 14-year-old male orca, Taku, also died suddenly and without notable premonitory signs of illness in 2007 at Sea World of Texas in San Antonio. The necropsy in this case confirmed the presence of West Nile Virus in brain tissue and suggested the observed pathologies were consistent with those caused by West Nile Virus in other animals.   
  
This initial evidence suggests a direct causal link between orcas maintained in public display facilities and premature death due to viruses transmitted through a mosquito vector. Further analysis is required to determine the presence of, and exposure to, these viruses in captive cetacean populations and stemming from the shallow and static environments where loafing and other surface behaviors increase susceptibility to transmission through mosquito bite. The West Nile Virus has been isolated in some populations of wild dolphins who may be similarly susceptible as a result of sustained surface behaviors in shallower coastal waters. Additionally, anecdotal eyewitness reports of mosquitoes being observed on the dorsal surfaces of killer whales in a captive environment reveals the additional risks associated with confinement and housing of this species in subtropical environments.   
  
The occurrence of avian-borne viruses in captive killer whales requires further inquiry, and suggests the possibility of such viruses in other cetaceans maintained in captivity. This information is critical to the debate about keeping cetaceans in captivity and may provide additional explanation for past or future illnesses and death in these facilities. Free-ranging, wild killer whales are not stationary and suspended with their dorsal surfaces exposed for extended periods of time, thereby providing an opportunity for transmission via mosquitoes carrying avian viruses. No data has been found that documents these diseases in their wild counterparts.

ABSTRACT  
Orcas are large, deep-diving cetaceans who are known for their global distribution, wide-ranging behavior, intelligence, and social complexity. They possess one of the largest and most complex brains in the mammalian kingdom. However, they are the third most common species of cetaceans kept in aquariums and marine theme parks. Most spend many years, and sometimes decades, in captivity. At the time of writing, 63 individuals are held in concrete tanks globally.   
  
The scientific data on how both wild-caught and captive-born orcas fare in captivity is increasingly robust in demonstrating that they cannot thrive under artificial circumstances in concrete tanks. In captivity, orcas exhibit a wide range of abnormal behaviors and often die at an early age from infections and other health conditions that are uncommon in a wild setting. Though numerous papers and reports describe these adverse effects, they do not offer a clear and systematic explanation for why captive orcas suffer chronic stress and how it affects their well-being.   
  
We describe likely mechanisms for the high levels of morbidity and mortality in captive orcas, including the impact of chronic stress on physiology and illness. We conclude that orcas are poor candidates for maintenance in captivity and suggest that a radical shift is required in their treatment, in order to meet their complex needs.

INTRODUCTION  
Millions of people visit zoos, marine parks and aquariums every year. Ostensibly, these places provide an opportunity to look at, connect with and appreciate the beauty and behavior of the animals. Indeed, everyone is drawn to the majesty and mystery of animals who look and live so differently than we do, but nonetheless seem so similar to us. But more is going on than meets the eye. Exactly what are we learning about other animals in these places? How is the zoo experience different for the animals than it is for the visitors? And what might we learn about ourselves by casting a more examining eye on the institution of zoos and aquariums?   
Most zoo visitors don’t think about what it means that the animals on display have been removed from their native habitats. When they do think about it, people often come to the conclusion that captivity is a necessary evil: Zoos and aquariums are necessary because it is important for people to be able to look at other animals and because this human experience actually helps other animals in the wild. Subsequently, the price we pay for this (or, more accurately, the price the animals pay) is justified. But this rationalization sidesteps a fundamental question: Why do zoos exist in the first place? How did they begin? To understand why zoos endure so tenaciously in Western culture, we need to look at their historical origins.

This is an Orca Network Archives webpage compiling scientific studies and reports on captive orcas (killer whales) and other cetaceans. The page presents a bibliography of over 30 papers with summaries covering multiple aspects of captivity.

Key studies include:

1. **Health and Disease**: Abdo et al. (2012) documents the first case of pulmonary zygomycosis in a captive orca that died after ingesting 81.4 kg of rocks. Bossart et al. (1996) discusses papillomaviral-like papillomatosis in Keiko, though later evaluations found him negative for 48 suspected viruses. Jett et al. (2012) presents evidence of mosquito-transmitted viral diseases (St. Louis encephalitis and West Nile Virus) causing deaths in captive orcas.

2. **Behavior and Aggression**: Anderson et al. (2016) concludes that confinement of orcas in aquaria is "morally indefensible" given their intelligence, noting that orcas who established friendship bonds with humans showed the highest rates of aggression after being trained as performers.

3. **Survival Statistics**: Jett and Ventre (2015) found overall median survival of captive orcas was 6.1 years, with U.S. facilities (12.0 yr) higher than foreign (4.4 yr), and captive-born (14.1 yr) higher than wild-captured (5.5 yr).

4. **Cognitive Research**: Multiple studies by Herman, Pack, Reiss, and Marino document dolphin intelligence, including understanding of symbolic gestures, mirror self-recognition, and decades-long social memory.

5. **Chronic Stress**: Marino et al. (2019) describes mechanisms for morbidity in captive orcas, concluding they are "poor candidates for maintenance in captivity."

6. **Keiko's Case History**: Cornell's 1993 report details Keiko's health problems due to poor water quality and heat, concluding his skin condition was likely contact dermatitis from environmental issues rather than viral. A 1998 expert panel found Keiko negative for 48 suspected viruses.

7. **Navy Programs**: Bowers and Henderson (1972) describes the US Navy's killer whale program where both whales eventually escaped or died. Brill and Friedl (1993) concluded reintroduction technology didn't exist (contradicted by existing research).

8. **Reintroduction Successes**: Claridge and Balcomb (1993) documents a dolphin inadvertently released after 17 years of captivity, positively photo-identified up to eight months later with wild dolphins.

9. **Neural Consequences**: Jacobs et al. (2021) hypothesizes about negative impacts of captivity on brains of large-brained mammals including cetaceans and elephants.

10. **Critical Evaluation of Zoos**: Marino et al. (2010) finds no compelling evidence that zoos promote attitude change or conservation education in visitors.

--- SOURCE 2: Red Wolf Recovery Program | U.S. Fish & Wildlife Service ---
URL: https://www.fws.gov/project/red-wolf-recovery-program

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service (FWS) webpage details the Red Wolf (Canis rufus) Recovery Program. The red wolf was declared extinct in the wild in 1980, but a captive breeding program (now the AZA SAFE program) saved the species. Since 1987, recovery efforts have focused on the Eastern North Carolina Red Wolf Population (ENC RWP) across five counties. The population peaked at an estimated 120 wolves in 2012 but declined dramatically due to human-caused mortality and hybridization with coyotes.

As of June 2026, the known/collared adult/subadult population is 22, with 12-16 pups. Four family groups were tracked: Milltail (6 pups born, 2 surviving), West Alligator River (7 pups born, cross-fostered with 3 SAFE pups from St. Louis Zoo, 1-5 surviving), Boundary (2 pups surviving), and Pungo (8 pups born, 7 surviving). A cross-foster with an 8-day age difference (the largest ever attempted) was successful. Three acclimation pens were active but produced no pups. Five adult/subadult mortalities occurred since December 2025 (three under investigation). The SAFE captive population has approximately 280 wolves across 52 facilities.

A revised Recovery Plan was released on September 29, 2023, with a vision for multiple viable wild populations coexisting with humans. Management includes releases from SAFE, pup fostering, adaptive management, the Prey for the Pack habitat program, and the Red Wolf Center public education facility. A hotline (1-855-4-WOLVES) is available for reports. The public is urged to maintain at least 100 yards distance from wolves.
</summary>

--- SOURCE 4: Limited contributions of released animals from zoos to North American conservation translocations ---
URL: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7380022

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This scientific article, published in *Conservation Biology* (2018), investigates the role of zoos in providing captive-bred animals for conservation translocations (reintroductions, reinforcements) in North America (Canada, US, Mexico, Caribbean, Central America). The authors analyzed the North American Conservation Translocations (NACT) database, comprising 1,863 articles published before 2014, to assess the extent of zoo involvement.

**Key Findings:**
- Of 279 animal species translocated, 162 species (58%) involved captive-bred populations.
- Captive breeding by zoos contributed to only 40 species (14% of all translocated species, 25% of those bred in captivity).
- Zoo contributions varied by taxon: highest for amphibians (42%), followed by terrestrial invertebrates (29%), mammals (19%), birds (17%), reptiles (15%), fish (2%), and marine invertebrates (0%).
- 54 zoos contributed animals; 50 were North American, 42 AZA-accredited (only 18% of AZA institutions).
- While the proportion of zoo-bred animals in translocations increased over time (1974-2014, r=0.325, p=0.0313), the overall contribution remains low.
- Zoo staff co-authorship on translocation papers increased from 0% (1974) to 42% (2013).

The authors conclude that while zoos contribute to conservation through education, funding, and expertise, their direct contribution of animals for release is limited. They recommend increased collaboration between zoos, governments, and academic institutions, and suggest zoos prioritize threatened species and expand captive breeding programs linked to foreseeable releases.
</summary>

URL: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Species_Survival_Plan

SUMMARY:
<summary>
The Species Survival Plan (SSP) is an American program developed in 1981 by the Association of Zoos and Aquariums (AZA) to help ensure the survival of selected species in zoos and aquariums, most of which are threatened or endangered in the wild. SSP programs focus on animals that are near threatened, threatened, endangered, or otherwise in danger of extinction, using captive breeding programs to aid their chances of survival. These programs help maintain healthy and genetically diverse animal populations within AZA-accredited zoos and involve cooperative population management, research, conservation genetics, public education, reintroduction, and in situ conservation projects. Species selection is guided by Taxon Advisory Groups (TAGs) who curate Regional Collection Plans. As of 2025, there are nearly 300 existing SSP programs (295 species). The SSP has been successful in ensuring viable populations exist in zoological settings even if species become functionally extinct in the wild. Successful reintroduction programs include the black-footed ferret, California condor, northern riffleshell, golden lion tamarin, Karner blue butterfly, Oregon spotted frog, palila finch, red wolf, and Wyoming toad. An SSP master plan is a document produced by the SSP coordinator that sets ex situ population goals and management recommendations to achieve maximum genetic diversity and demographic stability for a species.

SUMMARY:
<summary>
# California Condor Recovery Program (U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service)

## Overview
The California Condor Recovery Program is an international multi-entity effort led by the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service, with partners across state, federal, tribal, and non-governmental organizations. The program aims to establish robust, self-sustaining condor populations within their historical range. Key components include addressing threats in the wild, captive breeding, release and monitoring at field sites, and public education.

## Historical Context
- **1967**: California condor listed as endangered under the Endangered Species Preservation Act of 1966
- **1979**: USFWS established the California Condor Recovery Program
- **1982**: Only 22 condors survived in the wild (23 worldwide)
- **1987**: All remaining wild condors were placed into a captive breeding program
- **1992**: USFWS began reintroducing captive-bred condors to the wild
- **2004**: First successful wild-hatched chick since program began
- **2008**: Major milestone — more condors flying free in the wild than in captivity for the first time

## Current Status
- As of 2022: **561 total condors** (347 in the wild, 214 in captivity)
- As of the most recent data: **410 birds** total; **300+ wild free-flying** condors
- The 1996 Recovery Plan goals for downlisting from Endangered to Threatened: Establish two wild, geographically distinct, self-sustaining populations, each with at least 150 birds and 15 breeding pairs, plus maintain a third captive population.

## Species Description
- **Scientific name**: *Gymnogyps californianus*
- **Largest land bird in North America**: 9.5-foot wingspan, 3-3.5 feet tall, 17-25 pounds
- **Range**: Historically from California to Florida and western Canada to northern Mexico. Currently reintroduced in southern California, Big Sur (central California coast), near the Grand Canyon (Arizona), and Baja California (Mexico).
- **Habitat**: Remote country for foraging, roosting, and nesting; open grasslands and oak savanna foothills. Condors can fly 150 miles a day in search of food.
- **Breeding**: Reach sexual maturity at 5-7 years; one egg per clutch; incubation 54-58 days; chicks dependent on parents for 1-2 years.
- **Behavior**: Carrion eaters (do not kill for food); can reach speeds of 55+ mph and altitudes of 15,000 feet; highly intelligent and social birds.

## Recent Key Developments (2023)
- HPAI (Highly Pathogenic Avian Influenza) response: Incident Command Team implementing conservation strategies including vaccine trials, field monitoring, and bi-weekly updates.
- November 2023: Vaccinated California condors were released as part of ongoing HPAI protection efforts.
- September 2023: Investigation into the shooting of an endangered condor found in Hollister, California (July 2022).

## Library Resources
- 2025 California Condor Population Status Report (published Feb 2026)
- 2024 California Condor Population Status Report (published Feb 2025)
</summary>

--- SOURCE 13: Endangered Przewalski’s Horse, Equus przewalskii, Cloned from Historically Cryopreserved Cells ---
URL: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11898140

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This scientific article, published in *Animals* (Basel) on February 20, 2025, reports the successful cloning of two Przewalski's horses (*Equus przewalskii*) from historically cryopreserved cells. The clones, named Kurt (SB8268) and Ollie (SB9029), are genetic copies of Studbook Number 615 (Kuporovitch), a stallion that lived from 1975 to 1998 and was underutilized in the species' genetic management program.

**Key Background:** All ~1800-3000 living Przewalski's horses descend from just 12 wild founders captured between 1898 and 1947. The species was saved from extinction through ex situ breeding, but its complex management history—including attempts to purge domestic horse ancestry—led to significant loss of genetic diversity. SB615, who had domestic horse ancestry, was bred during only 4 out of 21 potential breeding seasons, and only 61 of 8,316 horses born (0.7%) descended from him.

**Methodology:** The clones were produced via cross-species somatic cell nuclear transfer (SCNT) using fibroblast cells cryopreserved in 1980 from the San Diego Zoo Wildlife Alliance's Frozen Zoo®. Domestic horse (*Equus caballus*) oocytes and surrogate mothers were used. Of 11 reconstructed embryos transferred to surrogate mares, 7 resulted in pregnancies and 2 resulted in live births (both healthy, requiring no interventions).

**Verification:** Identity was confirmed via microsatellite genotyping (complete match) and whole genome sequencing of one clone (Kurt), which showed 98% identical SNVs (5,347,267 of 5,454,492) compared to the donor. Mitochondrial genome analysis confirmed Kurt's maternal ancestry derives from a domestic horse, as expected from cross-species SCNT.

**Significance:** This is the fifth endangered species ever successfully cloned and the first time multiple viable clones of an endangered species survived past the neonatal period. The clones represent an opportunity to restore valuable founder genetics to the global population. They are expected to reach sexual maturity between late 2025 and 2028. The work emphasizes the value of biobanking and assisted reproductive technologies for conservation.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
The Przewalski's horse, Equus przewalskii, was saved from extinction by ex situ breeding and reintroduction into the wild., This milestone represents the fifth endangered species ever successfully cloned and one of the first true applied conservation cloning efforts., A total of 9,250,892 SNVs were called across all five individuals, of which 5,454,492 SNVs were called for Kurt and Kuporovitch collectively; of those, 5,347,267 (98%) were identical., This is the first time that multiple healthy clones surviving the perinatal period have been produced for an endangered species., The clones present an opportunity to restore valuable founder genetics to the global population.
</key_excerpts>

URL: https://www.ebsco.com/research-starters/history/captive-bred-condors-and-ferrets-are-reintroduced-wild

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This article (authored by Vernon N. Kisling Jr., published 2021) covers the successful reintroduction of captive-bred California condors and black-footed ferrets to prevent extinction, focusing on efforts from the 1980s-1990s. 

**California Condor:** By 1987, only 14 wild condors remained. A captive propagation program (U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service, 1976) combined with the California Condor Recovery Plan (1974) brought all remaining birds into captivity at San Diego and Los Angeles zoos. By 1992, the captive population had grown sufficiently to begin releases back into the wild. By 2006, the wild population had risen to about 200 individuals.

**Black-Footed Ferret:** The species declined due to prairie dog population loss (habitat loss and poisoning). After a ferret was found in Wyoming in 1981, 18 specimens were captured (1985-1987) and bred at Sybille Wildlife Research Unit. The captive population grew to 134 by 1991. Releases began in fall 1991 in southeastern Wyoming (not Meeteetse, where a canine distemper epidemic had eradicated the wild population). By 2005, the wild population had built up to about 500.

**Significance:** These programs serve as models for species recovery. Key lessons include the need for interagency cooperation, improved captive breeding programs, and early intervention before populations become too small. The article highlights the potential of biotechnology, reproductive techniques, and genetics in conservation. It emphasizes the importance of integrating human interests with habitat preservation and cooperation among governments, zoos, and private landowners.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"The reintroduction of captive-bred animals to prevent a species from becoming extinct is a technique that developed in the 1980's and 1990's from interdisciplinary studies in conservation management, small population and endangered species population biology, reproductive biology, wildlife veterinary medicine, genetics, and biotechnology.", "From fewer than a couple dozen condors, the population in the wild had risen to about 200 by 2006, as the captive-bred birds had begun to reproduce in the wild. Similarly, the black-footed ferret population in the wild had slowly built up to about 500 by 2005.", "Above all else, the evaluations highlighted how crucial it is that the probability of the extinction of a species be determined before the population becomes too small to be able to respond.", "The California condor, whose nearest relative is the Andean condor of South America, belongs to the family of New World vultures."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 15: Przewalski's Horse Project - Revive & Restore ---
URL: https://reviverestore.org/projects/przewalskis-horse

SUMMARY:
<summary>
The Przewalski's Horse Project is a conservation initiative led by Revive & Restore, in partnership with the San Diego Zoo Wildlife Alliance and ViaGen Pets and Equine, aimed at restoring genetic diversity in the critically endangered Przewalski's horse (Equus przewalskii) through strategic conservation cloning. The Przewalski's horse is the last truly wild horse species, having diverged from domestic horses over 500,000 years ago. All 2,000+ living Przewalski's horses today are descendants of just 12 individuals due to a severe historic bottleneck.

Since 2018, the project has worked to restore lost genetic variation. In 2020, the first cloned Przewalski's horse, named Kurt, was born on August 6, 2020, from a cell line cryopreserved since 1980 at the San Diego Zoo Wildlife Alliance Frozen Zoo. On February 17, 2023, a second cloned foal named Ollie (Kurt's genetic twin) was born from the same cell line, named in honor of Dr. Oliver Ryder, Director of Conservation Genetics at San Diego Zoo Wildlife Alliance. Both Kurt and Ollie may become the first cloned animals to restore lost genetic variation to their species. Reintroductions since the 1990s have established wild herds in China and Mongolia, but restoring genetic variation is essential for the species' long-term survival.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"It is an enormously hopeful, unprecedented step to have the capacity to restore genetic diversity. Kurt's birth was a major milestone for Przewalski's horse conservation. His success will serve as a model for saving endangered wildlife through the use of cloning." — Oliver Ryder, Director of Conservation Genetics, San Diego Zoo Wildlife Alliance
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 2: What Do We Know About Children’s and Adolescents’ Formal and Non-Formal Learning in the Zoo? A Systematic Literature Review ---
URL: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12729533

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This article presents a systematic literature review on children's and adolescents' formal and non-formal learning in zoos and aquariums. While six prior reviews focused on adult learning, none specifically targeted younger visitors. The author searched ERIC and Web of Science databases, yielding 858 peer-reviewed articles, of which 51 met inclusion criteria after title/abstract and full-text screening (interrater agreement: κ = 0.91 for both steps). Studies were analyzed via qualitative content analysis with two raters (one human, one AI).

Key findings:
- Studies were published between 2003-2024, with most from the US, and most participants aged ~10 years on average.
- Learning trips (56% of studies) were the predominant visit type, followed by family outings and camps.
- 25 learning arrangements were identified; the most commonly examined were keeper talks, guided tours, touch tanks, and enrichment activities.
- Knowledge was the most frequently studied dependent variable (55% of studies), followed by attitude, motivation, interest, behavior, learning behavior, and communication.
- 69% of studies investigated causal relationships; 35% used three or more measurement points; 57% lacked a control group.
- Only 21% of studies followed the recommended three-step approach (preparation, on-site learning, follow-up).
- Positive effects were found for: zoo visits/learning trips, lectures/guided tours, educational programs, enrichment construction, direct animal contact, theater plays, parent-child conversations, camps, and virtual devices.
- Children with special educational needs were not examined in any study.
- Significant differences emerged between visit types in the study of behavior (p=0.008), motivation (p=0.022), and communication (p=0.003).

The review identifies research gaps and suggests directions for future studies, including the need for more controlled designs, research on children with special needs, and broader outcome variables beyond conservation education.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
While adult learning in zoos and aquariums has been systematically reviewed, no previous literature review has focused on children's and adolescents' learning., A search in two databases identified 858 peer-reviewed articles, of which 51 met inclusion criteria and were analysed in detail., The results indicate differences in research focus in different countries and that zoos and aquariums are productive learning environments for various types of visiting., Learning methods including touch tanks, keeper talks and guided tours were found to positively influence knowledge, attitudes and behaviour., The review also highlights current research gaps and suggests directions for future studies.
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 3: Frontiers | Zoos as educational and conservation spaces: perspectives from (future) teachers ---
URL: https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/education/articles/10.3389/feduc.2025.1680014/full

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is an original research article published in Frontiers in Education (December 19, 2025) titled "Zoos as educational and conservation spaces: perspectives from (future) teachers" by Wolf, Dierkes, and Kleespies from Goethe University Frankfurt.

**Purpose:** The study investigates how teachers and trainee teachers perceive zoos as extracurricular learning places, given the critical role teachers play in deciding whether school classes visit zoos.

**Methods:** 126 teaching students and 303 teachers from the Frankfurt area (Hesse, Germany) participated in paper or online surveys. The questionnaire covered three areas: emotional attitudes toward zoos, perception of zoos' tasks (education, research, conservation), and perception of zoos as extracurricular learning places. Participants also reported prior zoo experiences. Data were analyzed using PCA, Kruskal-Wallis, Mann-Whitney U, and Spearman correlation tests.

**Key Results:**
- Overall neutral to slightly positive attitudes toward zoos across all areas (emotional mean=2.71, tasks mean=3.45, extracurricular learning mean=3.52 on a 5-point Likert scale).
- **No gender differences** found.
- **Significant age differences**: Younger generations (18-24) had more negative perceptions than older groups (55+), particularly regarding zoo tasks and educational value.
- **Teaching profession differences**: Primary school teachers viewed zoos more positively as extracurricular learning places compared to high school and middle school teachers, though significance weakened after adjustment.
- Strong correlations found between all three domains (emotional attitudes, task perception, and learning place perception).

**Conclusions:** The study recommends that zoos develop more educational programs targeting secondary schools and provide clearer information about their conservation and educational functions to address more skeptical views among younger teachers. The findings highlight the need for zoos to increase communication with educators about their multifaceted work.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
The results reveal no difference between the genders, but significant differences between age groups, with younger generations having more negative perceptions than older ones., teachers from primary schools have a more positive view of the zoo as an extracurricular place of learning compared to those from high schools., It is therefore important to educate future teachers about the opportunities of zoos and the various ways in which they can be integrated into the classroom., The study demonstrated that the perception of the zoo's tasks exerts a more significant influence on the perception of the zoo as an extracurricular place of learning than do emotional attitudes.
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 4: "Do Zoos and Aquariums Promote Attitude Change in Visitors? A Critical " by Lori Marino, Scott O. Lilienfeld et al. ---
URL: https://www.wellbeingintlstudiesrepository.org/acwp_zoae/8

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage presents a 2010 critical research article by Marino, Lilienfeld, Malamud, Nobis, and Broglio published in Society & Animals, hosted on the WBI Studies Repository (WellBeing International). The article evaluates the methodological soundness of a 2007 study by Falk et al., conducted by the American Zoo and Aquarium Association (AZA), which claimed to be the first direct evidence that zoo and aquarium visits produce long-term positive effects on visitors' attitudes toward animals. The authors conclude that the Falk et al. study contains at least six major threats to methodological validity that undermine its conclusions. They find no compelling evidence that zoos and aquariums promote attitude change, education, or conservation interest in visitors, though they call for further investigation using methodologically sophisticated designs.
</summary>

URL: https://www.thezooscientist.com/conservation-research

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage, titled "The Zoo Scientist," is a curated collection of scientific papers and research summaries related to zoo and aquarium science, conservation, animal welfare, and related fields. It covers a wide range of studies published between 2020 and 2026, organized chronologically.

**Key Research Areas and Findings:**

- **Conservation Breeding & Reintroduction:** The "Saving Wildcats" project in Scotland (Barclay et al., 2026) produced 56 kittens (2022-2025), with 28 released (89% 6-month survival) and 24 kittens born in the wild. A program for the New England cottontail (Brown & Puccia, 2022) bred over 600 kits from 139 founders, releasing over 250. A long-term program for the Chiricahua leopard frog (Harris et al., 2022) increased occupied sites from 37 to 155 over 25+ years.

- **Animal Welfare & Behavior:** Studies examined behavioral responses to solar eclipses, visitor pressure, and observer presence. A systematic review (Kelly et al., 2025) found abnormal behavior consistently higher in zoos with lower foraging and reproductive behaviors. Research on captive big cats (Øgelund Nielsen et al., 2026) showed individuals born in the most recent decade lived almost 5 years longer on average than those born in the early 20th century.

- **Ex Situ Management & Husbandry:** A systematic evidence map (Martin et al., 2025) extracted 1,070 articles covering 424 husbandry interventions across 637 species. Studies covered paternal care in orangutans, moulting patterns in puffins, cooperative behavior in porcupines, and nursing behaviors in black rhinos.

- **Zoo Research Collaboration & Methodology:** The "ManyZoos" consortium (Barrett et al., 2025) aims to foster multi-institutional research collaborations. A guide for successful zoo-university collaborations (Schulz et al., 2022) surveyed 117 staff from 59 US zoos. Biologgers, environmental DNA, acoustic research, and thermal imagery were explored as research tools.

- **Conservation Science & Extinction Prevention:** A study in Science (Smith et al., 2023) reviewed 95 species that went extinct in the wild since 1950, noting 12 recovered wild status and 11 lost while in human care. SUMMARY:
<summary>
This study investigated zoo education communication strategies and their effectiveness globally, using a two-phased, mixed-methods approach. Phase 1 consisted of an online survey with 176 zoos across 50 countries (categorized into three regions: Asia-Pacific n=24; Europe, Middle East, and Africa n=107; North and South America n=45). Key findings showed that 97% of zoos use signs at animal enclosures, 72% use pamphlets, and 69% use worksheets. For educational activities, 95% of zoos reported using at least one person-to-person education strategy, with animal feedings (83%), animal contact areas (78%), zookeeper talks (74%), and docents (74%) being most common. Animal shows were offered by 54% of zoos (75% in the Americas).

Phase 2 involved in-depth case studies at nine zoos (with annual visitation of 500,000+), including interviews with 28 staff members and 540 visitor interviews. The case studies revealed high consistency between survey responses and direct observations, though some discrepancies existed where zoos omitted strategies they actually employed. However, the authors noted significant variation in the quality of person-to-person education. For example, some animal shows contained limited educational content and appeared mainly for entertainment. Only one zoo provided extensive docent training; at others, docents "lacked even basic knowledge about the animals or facilities within the zoo" and sometimes acted more as crowd control.

Visitor interviews showed that 95% read at least some exhibit signs: 5% read all, 33% read most, 20% read half, 37% read some, and 5% read none. The most common reason for not reading all signs was watching animals (33%). Other reasons included insufficient time (14%), already being familiar with information (13%), difficulty reading/accessing signs (10%), attending to children (7%), and not finding the animal interesting (6%). The researchers noted wide variation in signage quality regarding educational content, readability, design, condition, and placement, with placement significantly affecting visitor engagement.
</summary>

--- SOURCE 8: Engaging internal and external audiences to develop and promote zoo-based conservation efforts ---
URL: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11023405

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This PLOS ONE article (2024 Apr 17) describes a multi-phase, evidence-based process used by Denver Zoo to develop a conservation action campaign (CAC) aimed at driving behavior change among zoo visitors. The study used the Transtheoretical Model of Behavior Change (TTM) as a framework.

**Phase 1:** Internal zoo staff and volunteers (n=111 from all divisions) participated in workshops using a modified nominal group technique. They brainstormed 605 conservation actions, which were consolidated into 164 unique actions and coded into 5 themes (Support conservation organizations, Internal outcomes, Help protect wildlife and habitats, Help protect the environment, Organizational actions). Top-scoring actions included resource sustainability, habitat conservation, and reducing carbon footprint.

**Phase 2:** The top 45 actions were narrowed to 20 by leadership, and a survey was sent to 3,192 zoo visitors (401 completed responses, 12.6% response rate). The survey used TTM stages to assess readiness for each action. Key findings: Members were more likely to donate and purchase sustainable seafood; older adults were more likely to have installed low-flush toilets; people without children were more likely to donate, volunteer, and learn about wildlife protection. MaxDiff scaling showed actions perceived as having the greatest positive impact were "Dispose of waste properly when recreating outdoors" (0.41) and "Participate in nature restoration/clean-ups" (0.35). The actions perceived as having the least impact were "Spend time in nature" and "Purchase shade-grown coffee" (both -0.45).

**Phase 3:** A second survey using visitor intercepts on zoo grounds (collected Nov 2022) asked participants which of 10 actions they were most interested in, along with perceived barriers and benefits. This phase was ongoing at the time of publication.

The research concluded that the campaign should focus on habitat restoration/remediation and purchasing wildlife-friendly coffee and other products. Visitors' responses tended to align with self-transcendent values. The study demonstrates how zoos can use evidence-based decision-making to select conservation actions that resonate with their communities.
</summary>

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This academic article, published in *Evaluation and Program Planning* (Volume 88, October 2021), investigates the challenges and successes of implementing a zoo conservation-education program called "When Balloons Fly" (WBF) at Zoos Victoria in Melbourne, Australia. The program aims to raise awareness about marine debris and encourage the use of bubbles instead of balloons outdoors.

The study used a process evaluation approach, surveying 24 Zoos Victoria professionals (April-May 2018) and conducting follow-up interviews with 4 participants. The research applied a re-contextualized version of Greenhalgh et al.'s (2004) model of diffusion in service organisations to identify barriers and enablers to implementation.

- Key challenges: staffing availability, role continuity, and resource constraints.
- Recommendations focus on streamlining delivery, improving project management, and prioritizing staff/resource availability alongside effective communication.

**Background context:** The study notes that evaluation of zoo conservation-education programs has yielded mixed results. The authors argue that understanding implementation processes (not just outcomes) is critical for program effectiveness. The paper highlights that while zoos have enormous potential to promote sustainability (with hundreds of millions of annual visitors worldwide), evidence of their effectiveness in encouraging social change is still developing.

**Conclusion:** Attention to the organisational context is critical for promoting and evaluating the success of conservation-education programs, and must be given significant attention alongside program characteristics and staff capability.

The AZA has provided a path to reaccreditation requiring investments in technology (broadband), capital upgrades (veterinary center), infrastructure (modern exhibits), and operations (competitive salaries).

The Zoo's current operating/capital budget (~$5 million) lags significantly behind peers. For comparison, the Akron Zoo—which received public funding support—grew from 100,000 to 400,000 annual visitors and now generates $56.2 million in economic impact. Erie Zoo receives only 4% of its revenue from government support, compared to 57% for Akron, 25% for Pittsburgh Zoo, and 20% for Buffalo Zoo.

A modernization effort (the Wild Open Spaces campaign raised $8 million privately) could transform the Zoo from a local attraction to a regional destination. Doubling the budget to be competitive could conservatively double its economic impact to $46.1 million annually. The report concludes that the Erie Zoo is a worthy investment—a self-sustaining community asset that needs public funding support to reach its full potential as an economic engine for Northwest Pennsylvania.

URL: https://www.facetsjournal.com/doi/10.1139/facets-2017-0083

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This study, published in FACETS in March 2018, is the first to quantify the research productivity of zoos and aquariums by analyzing peer-reviewed publications from Association of Zoos and Aquariums (AZA) members between 1993 and 2013. The authors found that 228 AZA-accredited institutions published 5,175 peer-reviewed manuscripts over the 21-year period, with publication output increasing over time (from 114 in 1993 to 437 in 2013). Most publications were in zoology (31.9%) and veterinary science (31.6%) subject areas, with articles classified as "biodiversity conservation" averaging only 7% of total publications annually. The top five journals were the Journal of Zoo and Wildlife Medicine, Zoo Biology, American Journal of Primatology, Marine Mammal Science, and Biology of Reproduction. Regression analyses showed that AZA organizations with larger financial assets generally published more, and organizations with research-affiliated mission statements had significantly higher publication output. The top publishing institutions were the Smithsonian National Zoological Park, Mote Marine Laboratory and Aquarium, and Chicago Zoological Society. The study recommends that institutions aspiring for higher research productivity need a dedicated research focus and adequate institutional support through research funding and staffing. The authors also suggest that zoos and aquariums could increase their visibility by publishing more in biodiversity conservation journals rather than only specialist zoo and veterinary journals.

<summary>
This webpage from Defenders of Wildlife provides comprehensive information about the endangered black-footed ferret, North America's only native ferret species. The black-footed ferret population is fragile at only about 400 animals total, with less than 300 left in the wild. They are nearly entirely dependent on prairie dogs, which make up more than 90% of their diet, and they live in prairie dog burrows, spending about 90% of their time underground.

**Reasons for endangerment:** Black-footed ferrets historically inhabited large areas of prairie dog colonies across the Great Plains. Their numbers declined rapidly when prairie dog towns were plowed or poisoned for farming and ranching, and most devastatingly due to sylvatic plague (an exotic bacteria-borne virus from Asia). In the 1980s, the last known wild ferrets were found on a ranch in Meeteetse, Wyoming, and brought into captivity by the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service, which began a successful breeding and reintroduction program that continues today.

**Recovery efforts:** Recovery involves off-site controlled breeding centers, head-starting in healthy prairie dog towns, and finding new large landscapes where conflicts with agriculture can be minimized. Vaccinations and pesticide applications for flea control help sustain populations. Defenders of Wildlife works as an official member of the FWS Black-footed Ferret Recovery Implementation Team, helping reintroduce ferrets to Fort Belknap Reservation in Montana, and assisting ranchers in Kansas fight a century-old state law requiring the death of all prairie dogs.

**Biology:** Mating season is March to April; gestation is 41 to 43 days; kits are born in May and June; average litter size is 3-4 kits. Kits are born blind and helpless, staying below ground until about two months old. As of 2018, ferrets have been reintroduced in multiple locations within their former range in the Great Plains across several U.S. states, Canada, and Mexico.

The Arabian oryx was declared extinct in the wild by 1972 due to centuries of poaching for meat, horns, and hides, worsened by motorized hunting methods in the 1940s-1950s. 

Conservation efforts began with "Operation Oryx," led by the Phoenix Zoo and the Fauna and Flora Preservation Society with funding from the World Wide Fund for Nature. Wildlife biologists captured the remaining wild oryx (two males, one female) and obtained additional captive individuals from the London Zoo, the king of Saudi Arabia, and the sheikh of Kuwait. Between 1962 and 1964, nine oryx were collected at the Phoenix Zoo (chosen for its Sonoran Desert climate) to start the "World Herd." The breeding program was highly successful: by 2002, 225 oryx births had been facilitated at the Phoenix Zoo, and individuals were transferred to other zoos and international breeding programs.

The first reintroduction occurred in 1982 in Oman, followed by releases in Saudi Arabia (1986), the United Arab Emirates, and Jordan. In 1986, the IUCN changed the Arabian oryx's status from extinct to endangered. Ongoing challenges include continued poaching (Oman's population dropped from 400 to 100 between 1996-1999), livestock overgrazing, and prolonged drought (560 oryx died from drought between 1999-2008). As of 2011, the Arabian oryx became the first species to be downgraded from "extinct in the wild" to "vulnerable" on the IUCN Red List. Current estimates indicate roughly 1,220 wild individuals (mostly in protected areas) and about 6,000 captive individuals worldwide.
</summary>

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This article presents a systematic literature review on children's and adolescents' formal and non-formal learning in zoos and aquariums. While six prior reviews focused on adult learning, none specifically targeted younger visitors. The author searched ERIC and Web of Science databases, yielding 858 peer-reviewed articles, of which 51 met inclusion criteria after title/abstract and full-text screening (interrater agreement: κ = 0.91 for both steps). Studies were analyzed via qualitative content analysis with two raters (one human, one AI).

Key findings:
- Studies were published between 2003-2024, with most from the US, and most participants aged ~10 years on average.
- Learning trips (56% of studies) were the predominant visit type, followed by family outings and camps.
- 25 learning arrangements were identified; the most commonly examined were keeper talks, guided tours, touch tanks, and enrichment activities.
- Knowledge was the most frequently studied dependent variable (55% of studies), followed by attitude, motivation, interest, behavior, learning behavior, and communication.
- 69% of studies investigated causal relationships; 35% used three or more measurement points; 57% lacked a control group.
- Only 21% of studies followed the recommended three-step approach (preparation, on-site learning, follow-up).
- Positive effects were found for: zoo visits/learning trips, lectures/guided tours, educational programs, enrichment construction, direct animal contact, theater plays, parent-child conversations, camps, and virtual devices.
- Children with special educational needs were not examined in any study.
- Significant differences emerged between visit types in the study of behavior (p=0.008), motivation (p=0.022), and communication (p=0.003).
