## Fully Comprehensive Findings

### ARGUMENT 1: CONSERVATION

#### 1A. AZA Species Survival Plan (SSP) Programs

The Species Survival Plan (SSP) program was developed in 1981 by the Association of Zoos and Aquariums (AZA) to help ensure the survival of selected species in zoos and aquariums, most of which are threatened or endangered in the wild. SSP programs focus on animals that are near threatened, threatened, endangered, or otherwise in danger of extinction, using captive breeding programs to aid their chances of survival. These programs help maintain healthy and genetically diverse animal populations within AZA-accredited zoos and involve cooperative population management, research, conservation genetics, public education, reintroduction, and in situ conservation projects. Species selection is guided by Taxon Advisory Groups (TAGs) who curate Regional Collection Plans. As of 2025, there are nearly 300 existing SSP programs (295 species). The SSP has been successful in ensuring viable populations exist in zoological settings even if species become functionally extinct in the wild. Successful reintroduction programs include the black-footed ferret, the California condor, the northern riffleshell, the golden lion tamarin, the Karner blue butterfly, the Oregon spotted frog, the palila finch, the red wolf, and the Wyoming toad. An SSP master plan is a document produced by the SSP coordinator that sets ex situ population goals and management recommendations to achieve maximum genetic diversity and demographic stability for a species. [1][2][3]

The World Association of Zoos and Aquariums (WAZA) coordinates Conservation Breeding Programmes worldwide. These cooperative international and regional ex situ breeding programmes aim to form viable populations that support in situ conservation. Key purposes include maintaining demographic and genetic backup for wild populations, providing animals for public education, supporting research, and creating ambassador animal awareness opportunities. Populations must be demographically stable, genetically healthy, self-sustaining, and distributed across multiple institutions to reduce catastrophic loss risk. Regional associations manage these programmes: AZA in North America uses Species Survival Plans (SSP); the European Association of Zoos and Aquaria (EAZA) runs the EAZA Ex situ Programme (EEP); the Zoo and Aquarium Association (ZAA) Australasia operates the Australasian Species Management Program (ASMP). In 2003, WAZA adopted Global Species Management Plans (GSMPs) for inter-regional cooperation on species with existing international studbooks. [4]

#### 1B. AZA SAFE: Saving Animals From Extinction Program

The AZA SAFE (Saving Animals From Extinction) program, established in 2014, is a key conservation initiative. According to an AZA Facebook post on February 9, 2026, 2025 was an incredible year for SAFE species programs. Key achievements include: AZA members reported investing more than $300 million in efforts that directly benefit animals and habitats in the wild; SAFE expanded to 56 species programs, adding new initiatives focused on African hornbill, American burying beetle, bonobo, eastern massasauga rattlesnake, pangolin, and peninsular pronghorn; SAFE species programs published a record 19 program plans; SAFE helped AZA earn the 2025 Bring on Better™ Association of the Year award from Momentive Software, recognizing outstanding impact on Wildlife Conservation and ethical stewardship; and AZA also funded more than 50% of grant requests supporting SAFE programs. [5]

A peer-reviewed research article published in Frontiers in Environmental Science (September 24, 2021) evaluated the impact of the SAFE program on conservation engagement among AZA-accredited zoos and aquariums, using data from the AZA Annual Report for Conservation and Science (ARCS) from 2010-2019. Key findings: AZA-accredited facilities collectively committed over $231 million to conservation in 2019, up from $150 million annually since 2011, benefiting 987 species in 127 countries. After SAFE's establishment, overall field conservation spending increased 1.4-fold and member engagement increased 1.2-fold. For eight selected SAFE species programs (African penguin, cheetah, sharks/rays, vaquita, western pond turtle, African vultures, giraffe, radiated tortoise), conservation spending increased 3-fold and member engagement increased 2-fold after program initiation. Individual species results varied: African vulture conservation saw a nearly 7-fold spending increase, while radiated tortoise and giraffe saw nearly 5-fold increases. The study acknowledges that while SAFE appears to have a positive causative influence, other factors may contribute, and long-term conservation impact data will be needed as the program matures. The authors conclude: "Conservation should be the higher purpose of any modern zoological facility, and collaboration is key to conservation success." And: "When revisiting our initial questions as to whether or not the SAFE framework is useful for the AZA membership for increasing their engagement in field conservation and, subsequently, increasing engagement for species-specific conservation, the early analysis provides a resounding 'yes' to both questions." The ultimate test "will be with respect to impact on saving animals from extinction and it appears the community is on track to play a role in making a difference." [6]

#### 1C. Species Recovery Case Studies

**Case Study: California Condor (Gymnogyps californianus)**

The California Condor Recovery Program is an international multi-entity effort led by the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service. In 1967 the California condor was listed as endangered under the Endangered Species Preservation Act of 1966, and in 1979 the USFWS established the California Condor Recovery Program. By 1982, only 22 condors survived in the wild (23 worldwide). In an effort to avoid extinction of the species, the Service and partners began to capture the remaining wild condors. By 1987, all remaining wild condors were in captivity and a captive breeding program to save the species was underway. In 1992, USFWS began reintroducing captive-bred condors to the wild. In 2004, the first successful wild-hatched chick since the program began. In 2008, a major milestone: more condors flying free in the wild than in captivity for the first time. [7][8]

The California Condor Recovery Program 2025 Annual Population Status report provides detailed population data as of December 31, 2025. The total world population reached 607 (up from 570 in 2024, 561 in 2023, 564 in 2022), with 392 in the wild (up from 373 in 2024, 344 in 2023, 350 in 2022) and 215 in captivity. Wild populations are distributed across AZ/UT (98), Southern California (99), Central California (117), Pacific Northwest (25), and Baja (53). In 2025, 16 wild-fledged chicks were recorded (down from 20 in 2024), and 46 captive-bred birds were released to the wild. There were 22 deaths in the wild free-flying population, a significant decrease from 43 in 2024. Lead poisoning remained the leading known cause of death with 9 confirmed cases, followed by pending necropsy results (9), shooting (1), power line collision (1), predation (1), and undetermined causes (3). Since 1992, lead poisoning has caused 161 confirmed deaths, accounting for 50% of all deaths with a known cause and 28% of all wild deaths. The captive population includes 54 breeding pairs, which laid 67 eggs in 2025, producing 45 available chicks for placement in 2026. Three-year average mortality rates varied by region: Baja lowest at 2%, Central CA at 8%, Southern CA at 7%, and AZ/UT highest at 15% (reflecting ongoing impacts from the 2023 HPAI outbreak). [7]

The 1996 Recovery Plan established goals for downlisting from Endangered to Threatened: establish two wild, geographically distinct, self-sustaining populations, each with at least 150 birds and 15 breeding pairs, plus maintain a third captive population. [8] The species is the largest land bird in North America with a 9.5-foot wingspan, 3-3.5 feet tall, 17-25 pounds. Condors can fly 150 miles a day in search of food. They reach sexual maturity at 5-7 years, lay one egg per clutch, with incubation of 54-58 days, and chicks are dependent on parents for 1-2 years. [8]

**Case Study: Arabian Oryx (Oryx leucoryx)**

The Arabian oryx, also known as the "unicorn of the desert" and the white oryx, is the world's smallest oryx species and the only one found outside Africa. It was once widely distributed across the Arabian Peninsula and parts of the Middle East but was declared extinct in the wild in 1972 due to hunting exacerbated by automatic weapons, motorized vehicles, and sport hunting. [9][10][11]

"Operation Oryx" (1962): The Fauna Preservation Society launched a capture expedition that secured three individuals (one female, two males). These were sent to the Phoenix Zoo in Arizona. Combined with animals from private collections, nine individuals formed the "World Herd" breeding program. By 1979, the herd had grown to 137 individuals. The Phoenix Zoo celebrated its 225th birth in 2002. [9][10][11][12]

Reintroduction began in Oman in 1982, followed by Saudi Arabia (1986), Israel, Jordan, and UAE. By the early 1990s, the Oman population grew to over 400, but poaching for the exotic animal trade devastated the population. By 2007, only 60 individuals remained in the wild in Oman (all male), and the Arabian Oryx Sanctuary was the first site ever removed from the UNESCO World Heritage List due to oil pipeline construction. [9][10]

Current status: As of 2011, the IUCN Red List reclassified the Arabian oryx from Extinct in the Wild to Vulnerable — the first time a species has been reclassified after being listed as extinct in the wild. The species is also listed in CITES Appendix I. Current estimates indicate roughly 1,000–1,220 wild individuals (mostly in protected areas) and about 6,000–7,000 in captive breeding programs worldwide. The largest breeding program is in the UAE (3,000 animals). [9][10][11][12]

HRH Prince Philip, The Duke of Edinburgh, said: "Very glad to hear of your remarkable success in capturing three Arabian oryx so that they may breed in captivity and thereby save the species from extinction. The cooperation of the Fauna Preservation Society and the World Wildlife Fund in this Noah's Ark operation is a splendid precedent for future efforts to save the world's endangered species." [9]

Fauna & Flora notes: "The rescue of the Arabian oryx is one of Fauna & Flora's most celebrated conservation success stories." [9]

**Case Study: Black-footed Ferret (Mustela nigripes)**

The black-footed ferret is one of North America's most endangered mammals, once thought extinct until rediscovered in Wyoming in 1981. The species declined due to prairie dog population loss (habitat loss and poisoning). After a ferret was found in Wyoming in 1981, 18 specimens were captured (1985-1987) and bred at Sybille Wildlife Research Unit. The captive population grew to 134 by 1991. Releases began in fall 1991 in southeastern Wyoming. [13][14][15]

The species faces a severe genetic bottleneck: before 2024, every ferret in the breeding program descended from just 7 founders. To address this, Revive & Restore partnered with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service, San Diego Zoo Wildlife Alliance, and ViaGen Pets and Equine to clone Willa, a female ferret that died in 1988 with no descendants and whose cells were cryopreserved. A 2014 genomic study revealed Willa's genome had nearly three times more genetic diversity than the current population. [14]

Key milestones in the genetic rescue program:
- **December 2020**: Elizabeth Ann, the first cloned black-footed ferret (and first cloned U.S. endangered species), is born.
- **May 2023**: Two additional clones, Noreen and Antonia (genetic twins of Elizabeth Ann), are born.
- **June 2024**: Antonia breeds naturally and gives birth to two healthy kits (Sibert and Red Cloud) — the first offspring born from a cloned endangered animal, and the first black-footed ferrets descended from 8 founders.
- **Summer 2025**: 4 more litters (6 females, 6 males) born to Antonia and Noreen, and Antonia's offspring. [14]

These achievements: demonstrate the first time a clone of any endangered species has produced offspring for conservation recovery efforts; mark the first time the unique genetics of Willa have been integrated into the black-footed ferret population; officially establish Willa as the 8th founder for the population. [14]

Ryan Phelan, Executive Director of Revive & Restore: "This project represents a historic milestone in conservation history. For the first time, we can definitively say that cloning contributed meaningful genetic variation back into a breeding population." [14]

Current population estimates: The recovering black-footed ferret population is fragile at only about 400 animals total, with less than 300 left in the wild. Biologists estimate that there should be 3,000 adult ferrets in the wild to successfully recover this endangered species. [15][16] Cheyenne Mountain Zoo reports that since 1991, they have partnered with five other breeding facilities, including four AZA-accredited zoos and the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service's National Black-Footed Ferret Conservation Center. As of May 2022, CMZoo celebrated surpassing $4 million raised through its Quarters for Conservation (Q4C) program to support annual releases. Recent reports estimate approximately 350 BFFs now thriving in the wild. [17]

The black-footed ferret is entirely dependent on prairie dogs, which make up more than 90% of their diet, and they live in prairie dog burrows, spending about 90% of their time underground. As of 2018, ferrets have been reintroduced in multiple locations within their former range in the Great Plains across several U.S. states, Canada, and Mexico. [15][16]

**Case Study: Przewalski's Horse (Equus przewalskii)**

A scientific article published in *Animals* (Basel) on February 20, 2025, reports the successful cloning of two Przewalski's horses from historically cryopreserved cells. The clones, named Kurt (SB8268) and Ollie (SB9029), are genetic copies of Studbook Number 615 (Kuporovitch), a stallion that lived from 1975 to 1998 and was underutilized in the species' genetic management program. [18]

Key background: All ~1800-3000 living Przewalski's horses descend from just 12 wild founders captured between 1898 and 1947. The species was saved from extinction through ex situ breeding, but its complex management history—including attempts to purge domestic horse ancestry—led to significant loss of genetic diversity. SB615, who had domestic horse ancestry, was bred during only 4 out of 21 potential breeding seasons, and only 61 of 8,316 horses born (0.7%) descended from him. [18]

Methodology: The clones were produced via cross-species somatic cell nuclear transfer (SCNT) using fibroblast cells cryopreserved in 1980 from the San Diego Zoo Wildlife Alliance's Frozen Zoo®. Domestic horse oocytes and surrogate mothers were used. Of 11 reconstructed embryos transferred to surrogate mares, 7 resulted in pregnancies and 2 resulted in live births (both healthy, requiring no interventions). Identity was confirmed via microsatellite genotyping (complete match) and whole genome sequencing of one clone (Kurt), which showed 98% identical SNVs (5,347,267 of 5,454,492) compared to the donor. [18]

Significance: This is the fifth endangered species ever successfully cloned and the first time multiple viable clones of an endangered species survived past the neonatal period. The clones represent an opportunity to restore valuable founder genetics to the global population. They are expected to reach sexual maturity between late 2025 and 2028. The work emphasizes the value of biobanking and assisted reproductive technologies for conservation. [18]

Since 2018, the Przewalski's Horse Project (led by Revive & Restore in partnership with San Diego Zoo Wildlife Alliance and ViaGen Pets and Equine) has worked to restore lost genetic variation. In 2020, the first cloned Przewalski's horse, named Kurt, was born on August 6, 2020, from a cell line cryopreserved since 1980 at the San Diego Zoo Wildlife Alliance Frozen Zoo. On February 17, 2023, a second cloned foal named Ollie (Kurt's genetic twin) was born from the same cell line, named in honor of Dr. Oliver Ryder, Director of Conservation Genetics at San Diego Zoo Wildlife Alliance. Both Kurt and Ollie may become the first cloned animals to restore lost genetic variation to their species. Reintroductions since the 1990s have established wild herds in China and Mongolia, but restoring genetic variation is essential for the species' long-term survival. [19]

Dr. Oliver Ryder, Director of Conservation Genetics, San Diego Zoo Wildlife Alliance: "It is an enormously hopeful, unprecedented step to have the capacity to restore genetic diversity. Kurt's birth was a major milestone for Przewalski's horse conservation. His success will serve as a model for saving endangered wildlife through the use of cloning." [19]

**Case Study: Red Wolf (Canis rufus)**

The Red Wolf was declared extinct in the wild in 1980, but a captive breeding program (now the AZA SAFE program) saved the species from extinction. Since 1987, recovery efforts have focused on the Eastern North Carolina Red Wolf Population (ENC RWP) across five counties. The population peaked at an estimated 120 wolves in 2012 but declined dramatically due to human-caused mortality and hybridization with coyotes. [20]

As of June 2026, the known/collared adult/subadult population is 22, with 12-16 pups. Four family groups were tracked: Milltail (6 pups born, 2 surviving), West Alligator River (7 pups born, cross-fostered with 3 SAFE pups from St. Louis Zoo, 1-5 surviving), Boundary (2 pups surviving), and Pungo (8 pups born, 7 surviving). A cross-foster with an 8-day age difference (the largest ever attempted) was successful. Three acclimation pens were active but produced no pups. Five adult/subadult mortalities occurred since December 2025 (three under investigation). The SAFE captive population has approximately 280 wolves across 52 facilities. [20]

A revised Recovery Plan was released on September 29, 2023, with a vision for multiple viable wild populations coexisting with humans. Management includes releases from SAFE, pup fostering, adaptive management, the Prey for the Pack habitat program, and the Red Wolf Center public education facility. The U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service stated: "In the future, wild and free Red Wolves will coexist with humans in multiple viable populations across the historic range, where ongoing threats are effectively ameliorated through conservation activities, the public's trust and engagement, and aligned policies among all involved with Red Wolf recovery." [20]

**Case Study: Florida Reef Tract Rescue Project (Coral Restoration)**

The Arizona Reef Tract Rescue Project (AZA-FRTRP) is a member-driven coral conservation network addressing the stony coral tissue loss disease (SCTLD) crisis along the Florida Reef Tract (FRT) — North America's largest bank reef, extending 360 miles from Port St. Lucie to Dry Tortugas National Park. Scientific monitoring has indicated that since 2014, some Florida coral species have sustained up to 90% reduction in abundance because of stony coral tissue loss disease. Mortality rate among affected corals is 66-100%. More than 20 coral species are susceptible to SCTLD, with five listed under the Endangered Species Act. Conservative estimates by FWC indicate that more than 50 million corals were lost due to SCTLD on Florida's Coral Reef. [21][22][23]

Since 2019, nearly 2,000 corals have been placed in 21 facilities managed by AZA-accredited institutions across 14 states. The disease was first observed in 2014 off Miami-Dade County and has since spread throughout the Caribbean. Over eight years, approximately 3,000 corals of 20 different species were rescued from over 200 reef sites in Florida, including the Marquesas Keys and Dry Tortugas National Park. [21][22][23]

The project is led by four Florida organizations: Disney Conservation, Mote Marine Laboratory and Aquarium, SeaWorld, and The Florida Aquarium. Holding institutions include Adventure Aquarium (NJ), Blank Park Zoo (IA), Butterfly Pavilion (CO), Columbus Zoo, Denver Zoo, Florida Coral Rescue Center, Georgia Aquarium, Jenkinson's Aquarium (NJ), Mote Marine Laboratory, Nashville Zoo, National Aquarium (MD), National Mississippi River Museum & Aquarium (IA), North Carolina Aquariums, Omaha's Henry Doorly Zoo, Riverbanks Zoo & Garden (SC), SEA LIFE locations (CA, MI, FL, TX), and SeaWorld Rescue Center. [21]

Since 2019, AZA member facilities have provided more than $18 million in resources and in-kind services, which is over 80% of the total investment in rescue to date. The care and support of a single Florida coral is estimated to cost approximately $350 per year, and an aquarium system for 32 corals costs $7,000-$10,000. [21]

The goals of the rescue are two-fold: 1) to prevent localized extinction along the FRT for the most vulnerable species, and 2) to maintain as much genetic diversity as possible for over 20 priority species. Rescue corals are being managed as brood stock to produce a new generation of corals to be placed back on the reef in restoration efforts. Fifteen species have been successfully spawned and propagated in captivity. To date, no Rescue corals have developed SCTLD-like lesions during their time in holding. Approximately 75% have been successfully maintained over eight years. [21][22][23]

The AZA-FRTRP states: "We are helping Nature respond to crisis and RECOVER." [21]

The Coral Restoration Foundation's 2024 Annual Report documents that despite the Fourth Global Bleaching Event of 2023 (causing close to 100% mortality of Acroporid corals on most Florida Keys restoration sites), CRF saved nearly all remaining genetic diversity of Florida's reef-building corals. Notably, at Carysfort Reef, outplanted Acroporids showed 6.3% survival (nearly 3x the regional average) and great star corals had 92% survival. CRF outplanted 9,958 corals in 2024 (253,833 total since founding), achieving a 324% increase in live coral cover within three months post-outplanting. The organization expanded nursery infrastructure with 52 new Spiral Trees, EVA float replacements, shading structures, and deep-water nursery development. CRF ended 2024 with significant nursery stock recovery: Tavernier up 16%, Carysfort up 62%, and Key West up 293%. [24]

The Aquarium of the Pacific has also partnered with SECORE (Sexual Coral Reproduction) for the past three years on coral restoration projects in Guam, using methods to spawn and raise corals and outplant them in the ocean. [25]

#### 1E. Honest Assessment of Conservation Contributions

A scientific article published in *Conservation Biology* (2018) investigated the role of zoos in providing captive-bred animals for conservation translocations in North America. The authors analyzed the North American Conservation Translocations (NACT) database, comprising 1,863 articles published before 2014. Key findings: Of 279 animal species translocated, 162 species (58%) involved captive-bred populations. Captive breeding by zoos contributed to only 40 species (14% of all translocated species, 25% of those bred in captivity). Zoo contributions varied by taxon: highest for amphibians (42%), followed by terrestrial invertebrates (29%), mammals (19%), birds (17%), reptiles (15%), fish (2%), and marine invertebrates (0%). 54 zoos contributed animals; 50 were North American, 42 AZA-accredited (only 18% of AZA institutions). While the proportion of zoo-bred animals in translocations increased over time (1974-2014, r=0.325, p=0.0313), the overall contribution remains low. Zoo staff co-authorship on translocation papers increased from 0% (1974) to 42% (2013). The authors conclude that while zoos contribute to conservation through education, funding, and expertise, their direct contribution of animals for release is limited. They recommend increased collaboration between zoos, governments, and academic institutions, and suggest zoos prioritize threatened species and expand captive breeding programs linked to foreseeable releases. [28]

An article from the Endangered Species Coalition notes that zoos' breeding programs focus on increasing populations of endangered species while preserving genetic diversity and reintroducing animals into the wild. In the U.S., red wolves, black-footed ferrets, and manatees specifically benefit from these efforts. Genetics in breeding programs is crucial given the 69% decline in vertebrate populations since 1970. Strategies include rotating animals between zoos, genetic testing, and introducing wild individuals to diversify gene pools. Challenges include maintaining genetic diversity in captivity (risk of inbreeding), difficulties reintroducing captive-bred animals to the wild, ethical concerns about animal welfare, and the need for habitat preservation. Beyond breeding, zoos serve educational roles to raise public awareness, fundraise for conservation projects, and act as sanctuaries during natural disasters. Future directions include advanced genetic technologies, AI for health monitoring, rewilding strategies, and global cooperation to improve breeding program effectiveness. [29]

### ARGUMENT 2: EDUCATION

#### 2A. Scale of Educational Reach

AZA-accredited zoos and aquariums play a vital role in educating over 180 million visitors, including 51 million students, each year. Over the past ten years, AZA-accredited institutions have also trained more than 400,000 teachers with award-winning and proven science curricula. All AZA-accredited institutions must ensure that education is a central tenet in their mission, must develop a written education plan that matches current industry standards, and must regularly evaluate their education programs. [30]

In a normal year, more than 700 million people visit zoos and aquariums worldwide. Dr. Martín Zordan, CEO of the World Association of Zoos and Aquariums (WAZA), wrote in January 2021: "In a normal year we estimate more than 700 million people visit zoos and aquariums worldwide. Inspiring conservation action in the wake of the pandemic is essential if we are to reform humanity's relationship with the natural world." [31]

Over 180 million people visit a zoo or aquarium in the United States every year—more visitors than every NFL, NBA, NHL, and MLB games combined. [32]

#### 2B. Evidence of Educational Impact: Research Studies

**Meta-Analysis (McNally et al., 2025 — Conservation Biology)**

This meta-analysis, published in *Conservation Biology* (2025, cited by 63), examined the effect of visiting zoos and aquariums on visitors' conservation knowledge, beliefs, and behavior. The study was conducted by researchers from the University of Sheffield and Chester Zoo, with Xavier McNally as lead author. The researchers conducted a systematic review identifying 56 primary studies. They used the Theory of Planned Behavior as a theoretical lens to classify outcomes (knowledge, attitudes, intentions, self-efficacy, social norms, and behavior) and the Behavior Change Technique (BCT) taxonomy to describe interventions. A multilevel meta-analysis was performed to account for dependencies in effect sizes. [33][34]

Key findings: The meta-analysis revealed a small to medium positive effect of engaging with zoo-led interventions on outcomes (d+ = 0.40, 95% CI = 0.28–0.51). Specifically, visitors were more knowledgeable about conservation issues, held more favorable attitudes toward conservation, and reported being more likely to act for the benefit of biodiversity. No evidence of publication bias was found. Effect sizes were heterogeneous; subgroup analyses showed that intervention type or outcome type did not explain this variance. Larger effects were found in studies conducted at a single institution (vs. multiple institutions) and studies using within-participant designs (vs. between-participant designs). The most commonly measured outcomes were knowledge (37 studies) and attitudes (30 studies); fewer measured intentions (14), behavior (7), self-efficacy (4), and none measured social norms. The most common types of interventions were general visits (12) and live animal interactions (12). Six specific BCTs were identified in interventions: commitment, information about social/environmental consequences, demonstration of behavior, behavioral practice/rehearsal, credible source, and adding objects to the environment. [33][34]

The conclusion: "Taken together, these findings demonstrate how behavior change frameworks can be used to describe zoo-led interventions and supports the assertion that zoos and aquariums can promote changes in beliefs and behaviors that may help protect biodiversity." [33]

**Children's and Adolescents' Learning (Systematic Review, 2024)**

A systematic literature review published in 2024 (PMC) focused on children's and adolescents' formal and non-formal learning in zoos and aquariums. While six prior reviews focused on adult learning, none specifically targeted younger visitors. The author searched ERIC and Web of Science databases, yielding 858 peer-reviewed articles, of which 51 met inclusion criteria after title/abstract and full-text screening (interrater agreement: κ = 0.91 for both steps). Studies were analyzed via qualitative content analysis with two raters (one human, one AI). [35]

Key findings: Studies were published between 2003-2024, with most from the US, and most participants aged ~10 years on average. Learning trips (56% of studies) were the predominant visit type, followed by family outings and camps. 25 learning arrangements were identified; the most commonly examined were keeper talks, guided tours, touch tanks, and enrichment activities. Knowledge was the most frequently studied dependent variable (55% of studies), followed by attitude, motivation, interest, behavior, learning behavior, and communication. 69% of studies investigated causal relationships; 35% used three or more measurement points; 57% lacked a control group. Only 21% of studies followed the recommended three-step approach (preparation, on-site learning, follow-up). [35]

Positive effects were found for: zoo visits/learning trips, lectures/guided tours, educational programs, enrichment construction, direct animal contact, theater plays, parent-child conversations, camps, and virtual devices. Children with special educational needs were not examined in any study. Significant differences emerged between visit types in the study of behavior (p=0.008), motivation (p=0.022), and communication (p=0.003). [35]

The review concludes: "The results indicate differences in research focus in different countries and that zoos and aquariums are productive learning environments for various types of visiting." Learning methods including touch tanks, keeper talks and guided tours were found to positively influence knowledge, attitudes and behaviour. [35]

**Environmental Education in Zoos — Guided Zoo Tours Study (Journal of Zoological and Botanical Gardens, 2022)**

This study, published in the Journal of Zoological and Botanical Gardens (2022, Volume 3, Issue 1, pp. 56-68), examined whether guided zoo tours influence participants' connection to nature and attitudes toward species conservation. The study was conducted at Opel-Zoo in Kronberg, Germany, with 269 voluntary adult participants who completed questionnaires before and after one-hour guided tours. Three types of tours were compared: African mammal tours, special themed tours, and tours including animal feedings. [36]

Key findings: All tour types produced positive increases in both connection to nature and attitudes toward species conservation, despite participants already having high baseline scores. For nature connectedness, people with medium initial connection benefited more from special themed tours and feeding tours than from regular tours. For attitudes toward species conservation, increases were similar across all tour types regardless of additions like feedings. Effect sizes were small (r < 0.3) but statistically significant. The authors note that participants were a self-selected, highly motivated group (average age 41), which limits generalizability. [36]

The study concludes: "This study provides important evidence that learning at educationally prepared locations, such as zoos in our example, can play an important role in increasing environmental psychological variables, such as nature connectedness and environmental attitudes in people who choose voluntarily to participate in such a program." [36]

**Teacher Perceptions Study (Frontiers in Education, 2025)**

This original research article published in Frontiers in Education (December 19, 2025) by Wolf, Dierkes, and Kleespies from Goethe University Frankfurt investigated how teachers and trainee teachers perceive zoos as extracurricular learning places. The study involved 126 teaching students and 303 teachers from the Frankfurt area (Hesse, Germany) who participated in paper or online surveys. The questionnaire covered three areas: emotional attitudes toward zoos, perception of zoos' tasks (education, research, conservation), and perception of zoos as extracurricular learning places. [37]

Key results: Overall neutral to slightly positive attitudes toward zoos across all areas (emotional mean=2.71, tasks mean=3.45, extracurricular learning mean=3.52 on a 5-point Likert scale). No gender differences found. Significant age differences: younger generations (18-24) had more negative perceptions than older groups (55+), particularly regarding zoo tasks and educational value. Teaching profession differences: primary school teachers viewed zoos more positively as extracurricular learning places compared to high school and middle school teachers, though significance weakened after adjustment. Strong correlations found between all three domains (emotional attitudes, task perception, and learning place perception). The study demonstrated that "the perception of the zoo's tasks exerts a more significant influence on the perception of the zoo as an extracurricular place of learning than do emotional attitudes." [37]

The study recommends that zoos develop more educational programs targeting secondary schools and provide clearer information about their conservation and educational functions to address more skeptical views among younger teachers. [37]

**Global Study of Zoo Education Communication (2020)**

This study investigated zoo education communication strategies and their effectiveness globally, using a two-phased, mixed-methods approach. Phase 1 consisted of an online survey with 176 zoos across 50 countries (categorized into three regions: Asia-Pacific n=24; Europe, Middle East, and Africa n=107; North and South America n=45). Key findings showed that 97% of zoos use signs at animal enclosures, 72% use pamphlets, and 69% use worksheets. For educational activities, 95% of zoos reported using at least one person-to-person education strategy, with animal feedings (83%), animal contact areas (78%), zookeeper talks (74%), and docents (74%) being most common. Animal shows were offered by 54% of zoos (75% in the Americas). [38]

Phase 2 involved in-depth case studies at nine zoos (with annual visitation of 500,000+), including interviews with 28 staff members and 540 visitor interviews. The case studies revealed high consistency between survey responses and direct observations, though some discrepancies existed where zoos omitted strategies they actually employed. However, the authors noted significant variation in the quality of person-to-person education. For example, some animal shows contained limited educational content and appeared mainly for entertainment. Only one zoo provided extensive docent training; at others, docents "lacked even basic knowledge about the animals or facilities within the zoo" and sometimes acted more as crowd control. [38]

Visitor interviews showed that 95% read at least some exhibit signs: 5% read all, 33% read most, 20% read half, 37% read some, and 5% read none. The most common reason for not reading all signs was watching animals (33%). Other reasons included insufficient time (14%), already being familiar with information (13%), difficulty reading/accessing signs (10%), attending to children (7%), and not finding the animal interesting (6%). The researchers noted wide variation in signage quality regarding educational content, readability, design, condition, and placement, with placement significantly affecting visitor engagement. [38]

**Denver Zoo Conservation Action Campaign (PLOS ONE, 2024)**

This PLOS ONE article (2024 Apr 17) describes a multi-phase, evidence-based process used by Denver Zoo to develop a conservation action campaign (CAC) aimed at driving behavior change among zoo visitors. The study used the Transtheoretical Model of Behavior Change (TTM) as a framework. Phase 1: Internal zoo staff and volunteers (n=111 from all divisions) participated in workshops using a modified nominal group technique. They brainstormed 605 conservation actions, which were consolidated into 164 unique actions and coded into 5 themes. Phase 2: The top 45 actions were narrowed to 20 by leadership, and a survey was sent to 3,192 zoo visitors (401 completed responses, 12.6% response rate). The survey used TTM stages to assess readiness for each action. Key findings: Members were more likely to donate and purchase sustainable seafood; older adults were more likely to have installed low-flush toilets; people without children were more likely to donate, volunteer, and learn about wildlife protection. MaxDiff scaling showed actions perceived as having the greatest positive impact were "Dispose of waste properly when recreating outdoors" (0.41) and "Participate in nature restoration/clean-ups" (0.35). The actions perceived as having the least impact were "Spend time in nature" and "Purchase shade-grown coffee" (both -0.45). [39]

The research concluded that the campaign should focus on habitat restoration/remediation and purchasing wildlife friendly coffee and other products. Visitors' responses tended to align with self-transcendent values. The study demonstrates how zoos can use evidence-based decision-making to select conservation actions that resonate with their communities. The article states: "As place-based conservation organizations, zoos are in a central position to support individuals in making small changes in their lives that will support the protection of wildlife and their habitats." [39]

**Zoos Victoria Conservation-Education Program Study (Evaluation and Program Planning, 2021)**

This academic article, published in *Evaluation and Program Planning* (Volume 88, October 2021), investigates the challenges and successes of implementing a zoo conservation-education program called "When Balloons Fly" (WBF) at Zoos Victoria in Melbourne, Australia. The program aims to raise awareness about marine debris and encourage the use of bubbles instead of balloons outdoors. The study used a process evaluation approach, surveying 24 Zoos Victoria professionals (April-May 2018) and conducting follow-up interviews with 4 participants. [40]

Key findings: Factors shaping implementation success primarily originate from within the organization (structure, culture, readiness) rather than from individual staff capabilities or the program's characteristics. The most influential domains were "organisational readiness for innovation" and "organisational antecedents for innovation" (both within "the inner/organisational context"). Key successes: effective communication, team structures, and tools/resources. Key challenges: staffing availability, role continuity, and resource constraints. Recommendations focus on streamlining delivery, improving project management, and prioritizing staff/resource availability alongside effective communication. [40]

The study notes: "With hundreds of millions of annual visitors worldwide, well-run modern zoos and aquariums are change agents with enormous potential to promote sustainability and thus protect biodiversity." The paper highlights that while zoos have enormous potential to promote sustainability, evidence of their effectiveness in encouraging social change is still developing. The conclusion: "Attention to the organisational context is critical for promoting and evaluating the success of conservation-education programs and must be given significant attention alongside program characteristics and staff capability to deliver them." [40]

**Review of Zoo Education Research (About Zoos Website)**

A comprehensive table of research findings from peer-reviewed studies on public education success stories at zoos and aquariums includes: Guided zoo tours and repeated educational programmes improve visitor attitudes toward conservation and reinforce environmental attitudes, with close animal contact further enhancing attitudes (though its effect on knowledge is less clear). A review of 29 peer-reviewed articles (2011–2020) found that zoo conservation education significantly improves knowledge, attitudes, and behavioural intentions, though the link between knowledge and actual pro-environmental behaviour remains weak. Studies of over 700 visitors showed guided tours lead to measurable increases in knowledge and positive attitude changes among students. Interactive and science-based exhibits (e.g., signage and observing scientific research) enhance visitor learning and engagement with conservation topics. A global survey found that increased biodiversity-related knowledge is associated with greater self-reported pro-conservation behaviour. [41]

Three key takeaways: (1) Zoos effectively increase visitor knowledge about biodiversity and conservation, especially through guided tours; (2) Visitors develop more positive conservation attitudes, particularly with close animal encounters; (3) Evidence suggests zoo visits can inspire pro-environmental behavioural intentions, though long-term impact studies are rare. [41]

**Scientific Evidence Linking Visitation to Conservation (Nature Communications, 2020)**

The European Association of Zoos and Aquaria (EAZA) posted on February 10, 2020, announcing that scientific evidence showing zoo and aquarium visits contribute to conservation was published in *Nature Communications*. Researchers from Species360, Trinity College Dublin, and NUI Galway analyzed data from over 450 zoos worldwide. The study found that zoos and aquariums with more visitors contribute more to conservation projects in the wild. Additionally, visitor numbers are higher at zoos with larger and more diverse animal collections, including unusual species. [42]

#### 2C. Counterpoint Addressed

A 2010 critical research article by Marino, Lilienfeld, Malamud, Nobis, and Broglio published in *Society & Animals* evaluated the methodological soundness of a 2007 study by Falk et al. (conducted by the AZA) which claimed to be the first direct evidence that zoo and aquarium visits produce long-term positive effects on visitors' attitudes toward animals. The authors concluded that the Falk et al. study contains at least six major threats to methodological validity that undermine its conclusions. They found "no compelling evidence for the claim that zoos and aquariums promote attitude change, education, or interest in conservation in visitors, although further investigation of this possibility using methodologically sophisticated designs is warranted." [43]

However, the field has responded robustly to this critique. The 2025 McNally meta-analysis in *Conservation Biology* — the highest standard of evidence in scientific research — directly addresses this criticism with methodologically rigorous analysis across 56 studies, finding positive effects with no publication bias. Between 1974 and 2013, zoo staff co-authorship on conservation research papers rose from 0% to 42%, demonstrating the profession's increasing commitment to evidence-based practice. [28]

### ARGUMENT 3: RESEARCH AND ECONOMIC VALUE

#### 3A. Economic Impact

**National Level Data**

According to the Sponsorship Marketing Association Intelligence Report (June 2026): AZA-accredited institutions attract 209M+ annual visitors worldwide (180M+ in the U.S.), surpassing all major professional sports leagues combined. The U.S. zoo & aquarium industry generated $3 billion in operating revenue (2025) with 6% CAGR (2020–2025). There are 229 AZA-accredited facilities across 46 states, supporting 254,000+ jobs and $35 billion in total economic impact. AZA institutions invested $341.1 million in conservation in 2024. [44]

A 2013 economic impact report by Dr. Stephen S. Fuller (George Mason University Center for Regional Analysis) calculated: Direct spending of $3.75 billion ($3.192 billion operations + $0.558 billion construction) contributed $10.58 billion to U.S. GDP (multiplier of 2.82), generated $3.43 billion in new personal earnings, and supported 103,833 full-time equivalent jobs nationwide. Visitor spending: 164.6 million visitors to U.S. AZA facilities in 2013 generated an estimated $2.38 billion in off-site before-and-after-visit spending, which contributed an additional $6.65 billion to GDP, $1.97 billion in earnings, and 62,126 jobs. Combined U.S. total: All U.S. sources (AZA members + visitors) generated $17.23 billion in total output, $5.4 billion in personal earnings, and 165,959 jobs. International members (10) reported $375.4 million in direct spending, generating $856.4 million in total output, $266.8 million in earnings, and 8,741 jobs. Global total: All AZA-accredited zoos and aquariums together generated $18.09 billion in total output, $5.66 billion in earnings, and 174,700 jobs. [45]

A SmartAsset article notes that AZA-accredited zoos drew 183 million visitors to U.S. zoos and aquariums in 2018, employed 198,000 people, and generated an estimated $22.5 billion in total economic output. The article also notes that since the 1970s, zoos no longer buy or sell animals; they trade or donate them to avoid commodification and bypass complex permitting requirements under the Endangered Species Act. The AZA runs the Animal Exchange, an online platform for zoos to trade animals. Animals are recorded on financial statements at a nominal value of $1 since there is no objective basis for establishing their value. The notable exception is the Giant Panda, which must be leased from China at costs of $1 million annually for a mating pair and $500,000 for a cub. [46]

A 2026 global zoo overview from Otto Environmental reports: The AZA reports over 700 million annual visitors globally, contributing $350 million to conservation. The U.S. market size is projected at $3.0 billion with 6.0% CAGR through 2025, continuing modestly into 2026. Specific projections: Milwaukee County Zoo targeting 1,302,379 visitors (+2%), Cologne Zoo anticipating over 1.2 million visitors, and Denver Zoo expecting 1.85 million attendees. [47]

**Case Study: The Florida Aquarium (Tampa Bay, 2023)**

The Tampa Bay Regional Planning Council (TBRPC) analyzed the economic and tourism impact of The Florida Aquarium on Hillsborough County and the Tampa Bay region in 2023. Key findings: Record-breaking attendance of over one million visitors, with out-of-town visitors accounting for 45% of attendance and significantly boosting local hospitality and retail sectors. The Aquarium directly supported 249 full-time equivalent jobs and contributed to 407 total jobs when including indirect and induced employment. It generated a total economic output of $53.6 million in Hillsborough County, with a Gross County Product (GCP) contribution of $28.8 million. The Aquarium's operational spending within the county totaled $5.2 million, supporting 39 additional jobs and generating $7.7 million in economic output. A planned expansion is projected to further increase economic impact by creating additional jobs and attracting more visitors. [48]

**Case Study: Little Rock Zoo (Arkansas)**

The Little Rock Zoo released a study on April 26, 2021, showing that a $50 million investment from the Rebuild the Rock initiative would generate over $659 million in economic activity for the Little Rock area. The study, conducted by Intelligent Analytics and Modeling (IAMECON) and Zoo Advisors, found that overall economic activity related to the Zoo from 2015 to 2030 would approach $1 billion. The analysis focused on increased tourism attendance driven by the investment, noting that Little Rock currently loses tourism dollars to competing cities like Tulsa, Memphis, and St. Louis that have more competitive zoos. As the only zoo in Arkansas, the Little Rock Zoo has unique potential to attract tourism. Zoo Director Susan Altrui said: "Investment in the Zoo has a real financial return and it's about more than just making kids smile and providing great learning experiences. This is about driving real, tangible tourism dollars to our city and fueling economic opportunity." [49]

**Case Study: Erie Zoo (Pennsylvania)**

The Erie Zoo, a 98-year-old City of Erie-owned asset, is a beloved regional attraction generating $21.2 million in annual economic impact, supporting 250 jobs, and contributing $1.3 million in state and local taxes. Despite attracting 310,000+ yearly visitors, the Zoo faces a critical challenge: it lost its AZA accreditation in November 2021, partly due to COVID-19 disruptions. 84% of this impact ($17.8 million) stays in the Erie County economy. The Zoo's current operating/capital budget (~$5 million) lags significantly behind peers. For comparison, the Akron Zoo—which received public funding support—grew from 100,000 to 400,000 annual visitors and now generates $56.2 million in economic impact. Erie Zoo receives only 4% of its revenue from government support, compared to 57% for Akron, 25% for Pittsburgh Zoo, and 20% for Buffalo Zoo. A modernization effort (the Wild Open Spaces campaign raised $8 million privately) could transform the Zoo from a local attraction to a regional destination. Doubling the budget to be competitive could conservatively double its economic impact to $46.1 million annually. Perry Wood, Ed.D., Executive Director of Erie County Gaming Revenue Authority, said: "By investing in lead assets like the Erie Zoo, we're investing in Erie's ability to attract and retain creative talent and innovative businesses. The vitality and continued excellence of the Erie Zoo is a part of the region's renaissance." [50]

**COVID-19 Economic Impact**

During COVID-19, zoos and aquariums were severely impacted by closures. Oakland Zoo lost roughly $2 million per month since March 2020, and the National Aquarium in Baltimore lost over $8 million over three months, furloughing one-third of its staff. Many facilities were among 200 major U.S. zoos and aquariums suffering huge losses due to lost ticket sales, despite ongoing costs for animal care. On the positive side, the San Diego Zoo saw a 1000% increase in virtual viewers during closures. [51]

#### 3B. Scientific Research Contributions

**Publication Output from AZA Institutions**

A study published in *FACETS* (March 2018) was the first to quantify the research productivity of zoos and aquariums by analyzing peer-reviewed publications from AZA members between 1993 and 2013. The authors found that 228 AZA-accredited institutions published 5,175 peer-reviewed manuscripts over the 21-year period, with publication output increasing over time (from 114 in 1993 to 437 in 2013). Most publications were in zoology (31.9%) and veterinary science (31.6%) subject areas, with articles classified as "biodiversity conservation" averaging only 7% of total publications annually. The top five journals were the Journal of Zoo and Wildlife Medicine, Zoo Biology, American Journal of Primatology, Marine Mammal Science, and Biology of Reproduction. Regression analyses showed that AZA organizations with larger financial assets generally published more, and organizations with research-affiliated mission statements had significantly higher publication output. The top publishing institutions were the Smithsonian National Zoological Park, Mote Marine Laboratory and Aquarium, and Chicago Zoological Society. The study recommends that institutions aspiring for higher research productivity need a dedicated research focus and adequate institutional support through research funding and staffing. The authors also suggest that zoos and aquariums could increase their visibility by publishing more in biodiversity conservation journals rather than only specialist zoo and veterinary journals. [52]

**Contemporary Research Activity (2021–2026)**

Extensive research is being conducted across zoo and aquarium settings. Key areas include:

**Veterinary Science & Animal Health (The Zoo Scientist, 2020–2025):**
- Pain indicators validated in anurans (González et al., 2025): 28 experts refined the list to 7 indicators (feeding behaviour changes, abnormal behaviour, impaired locomotion, oedema, reduced movement, retained skin post-moulting, altered respiration)
- Brushing alleviates stress in Malayan tapirs (Ishida et al., 2025): HRV during brushing was closer to standing position than other postures, suggesting brushing may have a rewarding effect
- African swine fever susceptibility across pigs and peccaries (Friedrichs et al., 2025): All Suidae species were susceptible to ASF; Tayassuidae (peccaries) macrophages did not support ASFV replication
- Cancer risk across mammals (Vincze et al., 2021): Carnivorous mammals have highest cancer-related mortality; cancer mortality risk is independent of body mass and adult life expectancy
- Zoos as Sentinels meta-analysis (Van Leeuwen et al., 2023): Zoos can be sentinels for disease monitoring, further highlighting their contributions to the OneHealth framework [53]

**Animal Welfare Science (The Zoo Scientist, 2020–2026):**
- Utilizing feather hormone measurements to study avian welfare (Kozlowski et al., 2026): 979 feathers from 46 birds (10 species). Tail feathers had higher and less variable concentrations of CORT and DHEA-S than wing feathers. Higher hormone ratios in ambassador birds, and in those participating in programs year-round
- Effects of Multiple Environmental Factors on Display and Location of Abnormal Behaviors in Captive Brown Bears (Soriano, Vinyoles & Maté, 2026): 4 of 5 bears displayed abnormal behaviours, with high individual variability
- The perception of felid welfare by zookeepers in North America (Ogle & DeSmet, 2023): 121 zookeepers from AZA-accredited zoos were surveyed. Zookeeper perceptions of animal welfare are influenced by opportunities for professional development offered by the institutions
- The 2020 Five Domains Model (Mellor et al., 2020): Five Domains — (1) Nutrition, (2) Physical Environment, (3) Health, (4) Behavioural Interactions, (5) Mental State; Update adds human-animal interactions to the model
- A Global Survey of Current Zoo Housing and Husbandry Practices for Fossa (Harley, O'Hara & Rose, 2021): All animals receive enrichment and most have at least an area away from visitors but majority express unnatural behaviours. Unnatural behaviour may be reduced with dense cover, restricted public viewing areas, variable feeding schedule and reduced view of other species [54]

**AZA Animal Welfare Committee Research Update (February 2024):**
This curated literature update highlighted 14 papers covering: traumatic telson avulsion treatment in Atlantic horseshoe crabs; ethical assessment of Assisted Reproductive Technologies in wildlife conservation; polar bear cub behavior post-den emergence; group structure of sanctuary-living Grauer's gorillas; stereotypic behavior in elephants; territoriality in Nile crocodiles; visual barriers reducing pacing in captive tigers; enrichment predicting positive welfare in zoo-housed carnivores; compassion fatigue in chimpanzee caregivers; effect of zoo closure on soundscape using acoustic indicators; advancing zoo animal welfare through data science; and automatic detection of stereotypical behaviors via surveillance videos. [55]

The Science division's publications page lists numerous publications covering: wildlife translocation and reintroduction (mountain yellow-legged frogs, 'alalā/Hawaiian crow, Pacific pocket mouse, Stephens' kangaroo rat, burrowing owls); reproductive technologies for endangered species; giant panda behavior; primate conservation (chimpanzees, lemurs, sifakas); genetic and genomic research (including the Zoonomia Consortium and SARS-CoV-2 host range analysis); human-wildlife conflict; wildlife disease and health assessments; animal behavior and anti-predator training; habitat use and movement ecology; and conservation social science.
